(p. 191)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Kahf

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book and has not placed in it any crookedness. [He made it] upright, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, ﴾ ﴿wherein they will remain forever,﴾ ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak only a lie.﴾

In the opening of this noble surah, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, taught His servants to praise Him for the greatest blessing He bestowed upon them, which is His sending down to our Prophet ﷺ this Mighty Qur'an, which has no crookedness in it but is in perfect uprightness. Through it He brought them out of darkness into light. He made clear to them in it the beliefs, the lawful and the unlawful, and the causes of entering Paradise and Hellfire. He warned them in it against everything that harms them and urged them in it toward everything that benefits them. Thus it is the greatest blessing upon creation. For this reason their Lord taught them how to praise Him for this great blessing, by His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book﴾ — the verse [Al-Kahf: 1].

What He indicated here of the great favour and bounty upon His creation by sending down this Mighty Qur'an, which warns those who do not act upon it and gives good tidings to those who do, He mentioned in many places. Such as His saying:

﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a conclusive proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light. As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾ [An-Nisa': 174];

and His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and reminder for a people who believe﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 51];

and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ. And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [An-Naml: 76–77];

and His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and mercy for the believers﴾ [Al-Isra': 82];

and His saying: ﴿Say, "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing"﴾ — the verse [Fussilat: 44];

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 106–107];

and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, but it was out of mercy from your Lord﴾ — the verse [Al-Qasas: 86];

and His saying: ﴿Then We bequeathed the Book to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds by permission of Allah. That is the great bounty﴾ [Fatir: 32].

This is an explicit statement from Him, Majestic and Exalted, that the bestowal of this Book is a great bounty. Verses of this kind are very numerous.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ [Al-Kahf: 1], meaning He did not place in the Qur'an any crookedness; that is, there is absolutely no deviation in it, neither in its wording nor in its meanings. Its reports are all truthful, its rulings are just, and it is free of all defects in its wording and meanings, its reports and its rulings. This is because His saying "'iwajan" (crookedness) is an indefinite noun (nakira) in a context of negation (siyaq al-nafy), so it generalizes the negation of all kinds of crookedness.

What He, Majestic and Exalted, mentioned here, that there is no crookedness in it, He also made clear in many other places, such as His saying: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example that perhaps they may remember﴾ ﴿an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they may fear Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 27–28]; and His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [Al-An'am: 115]. So His saying "sidqan" (in truth) means in its reports, and His saying "'adlan" (in justice) means in its rulings. And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa': 82]. Verses of this kind are very numerous.

As for His saying in this noble verse: "qayyiman" (upright), meaning straight, with no inclination in it and no deviation. What He mentioned here, that it is upright with no inclination or deviation, He also made clear in other places, such as:

His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to be separated until there came to them clear evidence, a messenger from Allah, reciting purified scriptures, within which are upright writings﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1];

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ — the verse [Al-Isra': 9];

and His saying: ﴿And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be invented other than by Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yunus: 37];

and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the righteous﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 1–2];

and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then elaborated from one who is Wise and Acquainted﴾ [Hud: 1];

and His saying: ﴿But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [Ash-Shura: 52];

and other verses besides these.

This which we have explained of His saying "qayyiman" is the statement of the majority (al-jumhur) and it is the apparent meaning. Based on this, it is an emphasis in meaning of His saying: ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ [Al-Kahf: 1], because a thing may be straight in appearance while in reality it is not free of some crookedness. For this reason He, exalted is He, combined the negation of crookedness with the affirmation of uprightness. In His saying "qayyiman" there are two other interpretations:

The first: that the meaning of its being "qayyiman" is that it is a guardian (qayyim) over what came before it of the heavenly Books, that is, it is dominant (muhaymin) over them. According to this interpretation, the verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian (muhaymin) over it﴾ — the verse [Al-Ma'idah: 48].

And because of its dominance over the Books before it, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ﴾ — the verse [An-Naml: 76]; and He said: ﴿Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93]; and He said: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾ — the verse [Al-Ma'idah: 15].

The second: that the meaning of its being "qayyiman" is that it is a guardian (qayyim) over the religious and worldly interests of creation. This interpretation in reality entails the first.

Know that the scholars of Arabic grammar (al-'arabiyyah) differed over the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying "qayyiman." A group held that it is a hal (circumstantial accusative, qualifying a state of the noun) from "al-Kitab" (the Book), and that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse. Its explanation according to this view: He sent down to His servant the Book in a state of being upright and not placing in it any crookedness. Al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf prevented this grammatical analysis, saying: indeed His saying: ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ [Al-Kahf: 1] is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the silah (relative clause) of the relative pronoun, which is the clause ﴿sent down to His servant the Book﴾, and what is coordinated with the silah is included within the scope of the silah. So making "qayyiman" a hal from "al-Kitab" leads to separating the hal from its companion (sahib al-hal) by part of the silah, and that is not permissible.

Another group held that "qayyiman" is a hal from "al-Kitab," and that the problem Zamakhshari mentioned does not arise. They said: indeed the clause ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ is not coordinated with the silah; rather, it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). And His saying "qayyiman" is a hal after a hal. Its explanation: the meaning is: He sent down to His servant the Book in a state of not placing in it any crookedness, and in a state of being upright. Multiplicity of hal presents no difficulty. The majority hold that it is permissible for the hal to be multiple while the governing verb (amil) and the companion of the hal are one, as he indicated in the Khulasah (Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik) with his saying:

"The hal may come multiple, for a singular, know this, and for other than singular."

Whether that is with coordination or without coordination, its example with coordination is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39]; and its example without coordination is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ — the verse [Al-A'raf: 150]. And the words of the poet:

"Upon me, if you come to Layla secretly, is a visit to the House of Allah, walking barefoot on two feet."

It is related from Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur that he prevented the multiplicity of hal unless the governing element in it was the comparative form (sighat al-tafdil), as in the saying: "This is more delicious than that in unripe dates and in ripe dates (hadha busran atyabu minhu ruṭaban)." It is also related that this was prevented by al-Farisi and a group. Those who prevent multiplicity of hal say: the second hal is only a hal from the implicit pronoun in the first hal, and the first is in their view the governing element for the second, so they are overlapping states (ahwal mutadakhilah); or they make the second an adjective (na't) of the first. Among those who chose that the clause "wa lam yaj'al" is a hal, and that "qayyiman" is a hal after a hal, is al-Asfahani.

Some scholars held that His saying "qayyiman" is a badal (substitute or apposition) for His saying: ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ [Al-Kahf: 1], because the absence of crookedness from it is the meaning of its being upright. This view is attributed by al-Razi and Abu Hayyan to the author of Hall al-'Uqad (The Untying of Knots), and according to it, it is a single-word substitute (badal mufrad) from a clause.

Just as they said regarding "'arafta Zaydan abu man" (I knew Zayd, the father of whom?), that it is a substitute of a clause from a single word; and on the permissibility of that there is a difference among the scholars of Arabic.

A group claimed that "qayyiman" is a hal from the pronoun in the genitive position in His saying: ﴿and has not placed in it any crookedness﴾ [Al-Kahf: 1]. Al-Zamakhshari and others chose that "qayyiman" is an accusative governed by an omitted verb, and its estimate is: "and has not placed in it any crookedness and made it upright." Omitting the governing verb of a non-essential element (fadlah) when the context indicates it is permissible, as he said in the Khulasah:

"The governing verb of it may be omitted if it is known, and its omission may sometimes be obligatory."

And the closest of the grammatical analyses of His saying "qayyiman" is that it is an accusative governed by an omitted element, or a second hal from "al-Kitab." And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿to warn of severe punishment﴾ [Al-Kahf: 2], the lam (in "li-yundhira") is connected (muta'alliqah) with "anzala" (He sent down). Al-Hawfi said it is connected with His saying "qayyiman," but the first is the apparent one.

"Al-indhar" (warning) is informing accompanied by intimidation and threat. So every warning is an informing, but not every informing is a warning. The verb "anzara" (to warn) takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [Al-Layl: 14], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ — the verse [Sad: 40].

At the beginning of this noble surah He repeated the warning. In the first occurrence He omitted the first object of the warning, and in the second He omitted the second object, so what is mentioned becomes an indication of what is omitted in both places. The estimate of the omitted first object in the first place is: ﴿to warn those who disbelieved of severe punishment from Him﴾; and the estimate of the omitted second object in the second place is: ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son," of severe punishment from Him.﴾

In this noble verse, He, exalted is He, has indicated that this mighty Qur'an is a frightening and threatening [message] for the disbelievers, and good tidings for the believing righteous. For He said regarding its intimidation of the disbelievers: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾ [Al-Kahf: 2], and He said: ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ — the verse [Al-Kahf: 4]; and He said regarding its good tidings for the believers: ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾ — the verse [Al-Kahf: 2].

What He mentioned here, that it is a warning to these and good tidings to those, He made clear in other places, such as His saying: ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people contentious﴾ [Maryam: 97]; and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book revealed to you, so let there be no discomfort in your breast about it, that you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 1–2].

We have explained this topic at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf, and there we explained the meanings in which the warning occurs in the Qur'an. The severe punishment (ba'sun shadid) with which He warned them is the painful torment in this world and the Hereafter. And "al-bishara" (good tidings) is good news of what gladdens.

The Arabs may also use "al-bishara" for informing of what is distressing, and from it is His saying: ﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 8], and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You gave me tidings, O Sa'd, that my beloveds have shunned me, and they said: the appointment of love is the Gathering (al-hashr)."

And the saying of another:

The Shinqiti Commentary (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

؎ "The crow brings me news of my family's separation, / so I said to it: May you be bereaved; what a messenger of news you are!"

The verified position is that applying the term "good news" (bishara) to the report of what is distressing is a style (uslub) of the Arabic language. It is well known that the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) treat such usage as a metaphor (majaz), and call it a "contrarian metaphor" (isti'ara 'inadiyya), which they divide into the "sarcastic" (tahakkumiyya) and the "allusive" (talmihiyya), as is known in its proper place.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿those who do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], other verses have clarified its intended meaning, showing that a deed is not righteous except by three matters:

First: that it conforms to what the Prophet ﷺ brought. Every deed that opposes what he, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, brought is not righteous, but is void. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and He said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 80], and He said: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], and He said: ﴿Or do they have partners who have instituted for them of the religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura: 21], along with other verses.

Second: that the doer be sincere in his deed for Allah, in what is between him and Allah. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyina: 5], and He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion. And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims. Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day. Say: Allah I worship, being sincere to Him in my religion. So worship what you will besides Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 11–15], along with other verses.

Third: that the deed be founded upon the basis of faith and sound belief, because deeds are like the roof and belief is like the foundation. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], so He made faith a condition (qayd) in that.

He explained the meaning of this condition in many verses, such as:
• His saying concerning the deeds of non-believers: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23],
• and His saying: ﴿Their deeds are like a mirage﴾ [al-Nur: 39],
• and His saying: ﴿Their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows hard upon﴾ [Ibrahim: 18],
along with other verses, as has already been made clear.

The verified position is that the singular of "the righteous [deeds]" (al-salihat) in His saying ﴿do righteous deeds﴾, and in His saying (p-197) ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], and what is similar to that, is: ṣāliḥa (feminine singular). The Arabs apply the word ṣāliḥa to a good act, just as the generic noun (ism al-jins) is applied while disregarding the descriptive sense (li-tanasi al-wasfiyya), as this application has become common for ḥasana (good deed) meaning a good act.

From the Arabs' application of the word ṣāliḥa to this meaning is the saying of Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' concerning his wife Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

؎ "Daughter of the trustworthy one, may Allah reward you with righteousness, / and every husband will praise what he knows of you."

And the saying of al-Hutay'a:

؎ "How can I satirize when a righteous woman of the family of Lam / keeps coming to me in my absence?"

And a Bedouin was asked about love, and he said:

؎ "Love is a preoccupation away from every righteous woman, / and the intoxication of love banishes the intoxication of drowsiness."

As for His saying in this noble verse ﴿that they will have a good reward﴾, meaning: and that He may give them good news that they will have a good reward. The reward (ajr) is the recompense for a deed, and the recompense of their deed, expressed here as "reward," is Paradise. Therefore He said ﴿remaining therein﴾ [al-Kahf: 3], and He made the pronoun in His saying "therein" (fihi) masculine, because it refers to "reward" (ajr), which is masculine, even though what is meant by the reward is Paradise. He described their reward here as "good," and He explained the aspects of its goodness in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿A company of the first and a few of the last, on thrones woven with gold, reclining upon them facing one another﴾, up to His saying ﴿a company of the first and a company of the last﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 13–16], and His saying: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17; cf. al-Waqi'a: 39–40 as cited], along with what is similar to these, which are very many and well known.

As for His saying in this noble verse ﴿remaining therein forever﴾, meaning: abiding therein without cessation.

This meaning has been explained in many other places, such as:
• His saying: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills, a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud: 108], meaning: not cut off,
• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no cessation﴾ [Sad: 54], meaning: it has no cutting off or ending,
• and His saying: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah remains﴾ [al-Nahl: 96],
• and His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la: 17],
along with other verses.

As for His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And He may warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4], (p-198) meaning: He may warn them of severe punishment, "from Him," meaning from His presence, as has already been explained. This is the "specific following the general" ('atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), because His saying ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾ includes those who say "Allah has taken a son" and other disbelievers in general.

It has been established in the science of rhetoric (fann al-ma'ani) that the coordination of the specific over the general, when the specific is distinguished from the rest of the general's members by good or bad attributes, is a permissible elaboration (itnab maqbul), treating the difference in attributes as if it were a difference in essences.

An example of the one distinguished by good attributes is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿His angels, His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98], and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7].

An example of the one distinguished by bad attributes is the verse we are dealing with, for ﴿those who said, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ are distinguished from others by a monstrous slander, and therefore it was permissible to coordinate them over the term that includes them and others.

The verses indicating the great enormity of their slander are very numerous, such as His saying here: ﴿Immense is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Certainly you have produced a terrible thing. The heavens are about to burst from it, the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin, that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son. And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 88–92], and His saying: ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons and taken for Himself females from the angels? Indeed, you say a terrible statement﴾ [al-Isra': 40], and verses like these are many and well known.

We have already noted that the Qur'an explained that those who attributed a son to Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He above that by a great exaltation, are three categories of people: the Jews and the Christians, as He said: ﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths﴾ [al-Tawba: 30], and the third category is the polytheists of the Arabs, as He, the Exalted, said about them: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters, glory be to Him, while for themselves is what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57], and verses similar to these are many and well known.

As for His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers﴾ [al-Kahf: 5], He means that what they attributed to Him, may He be exalted, of taking a son, they have no knowledge of, because it is impossible.

The verse clearly indicates that negating an act does not indicate its possibility. Among the verses that indicate this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 57], because their wronging (p-199) of our Lord, and their having knowledge of taking a son for Him, are all rationally impossible.

So negating it does not indicate its possibility. Of this kind is the saying of the logicians: "The negative proposition does not imply the existence of the subject," as we have explained in another place.

As for what He negated from them and from their fathers, of knowledge of taking a son for Him, Glorified and Exalted is He above that by a great exaltation, He has explained it in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him and exalted above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100], and His saying concerning their fathers: ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 104], along with other verses.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Immense is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5], He means that what they said with their mouths, that Allah has taken a son, is a great and tremendous matter, as we have already shown in the verses indicating its enormity, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, you say a terrible statement﴾ [al-Isra': 40], and His saying: ﴿The heavens are about to burst from it, the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90], and that suffices as an indication of its magnitude and gravity.

Some scholars of Arabic said: His saying ﴿Immense is [the word]﴾ (kabura kalima) means exclamation of wonder (ta'ajjub), so it is equivalent to "how great is it as a word!" or "make it great as a word!"

What is established in the science of grammar is that the form fa'ula, with a damma on the 'ayn, is used to express blame and praise, so it falls under the category of ni'ma and bi'sa (the verbs of praise and blame). From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Immense is the word﴾, and so on. The poet alluded to this in al-Khulasa (Ibn Malik's Alfiyya) with his saying:

؎ "Make like bi'sa (ill-indeed) sa'a (was evil), and make fa'ula from the triliteral / like ni'ma (excellent-indeed), sealed."

His saying "like ni'ma" means: make it of the category of ni'ma, so that it includes bi'sa. When this is established, the subject (fa'il) of kabura is an omitted pronoun, and kalima is an indefinite noun serving as a specifier (tamyiz) for the omitted pronoun, according to the principle in al-Khulasa: "They raise a hidden pronoun that the specifier explains, like ni'ma qawman ma'shuruh (a people whose company is excellent)."

The object of praise or blame is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "It has become great, that word, coming out of their mouths, that saying which they uttered, namely their statement: Allah has taken a son." Some grammarians parsed kalima as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: their slander has become great while being a word coming out of their mouths. But this is nothing (laysa bi-shay').

(p-200) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "Coming out of their mouths" means that it has no basis other than their saying, and they have no proof for it except their lying and fabrication. Therefore He said: ﴿They say only a lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 5].

This meaning that Ibn Kathir mentioned has witnesses in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167], and similar verses.

Lying (kadhib) is the contradiction of a report to reality, according to the most correct opinions.

When the word kabura is used with a meaning other than advanced age, it is pronounced with a damma on the ba' in the past and present tenses, as in:
• His saying here: ﴿Immense is the word﴾, and so on,
• His saying: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3],
• His saying: ﴿Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾ [al-Isra': 51],
and similar.

If it is meant as advanced age, then in the past tense the ba' is kasra, and in the present tense it is fatha according to the regular pattern. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not consume their wealth extravagantly and hastily, lest they grow up﴾ [al-Nisa': 6].

And the saying of the madman (Majnun Layla):

؎ "I became enamored of Layla, while she had long braids, / and there had not appeared to the eyes of her breast any swelling / Two small ones grazing the goats; O would that we / had not grown up until today, nor had the goats grown up."

His saying in this verse, "two small ones" (saghiran), is a witness among the grammarians for the circumstantial clause (hal) coming from both the subject and the object together.

And His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse, ﴿Immense is the word﴾, by "the word" He means the speech which is their saying: ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾ [al-Kahf: 4].

What this noble verse indicates, that Allah calls speech by the name "word" (kalima), has been clarified by other verses, such as His saying: ﴿No! It is only a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], whose meaning is His saying: ﴿"My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99–100], and His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [Hud: 119]. The word kalima in the Qur'an comes only meaning a meaningful speech.

As for His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse: "'iwaja" is with a kasra on the 'ayn in meanings, as in this noble verse, and with a fatha when it refers to something standing upright, like a wall.

(p-201) Al-Jawhari said in his Sihah: Ibn al-Sikkit said: Everything that stands upright, like a wall or a stick, is called "'awaj" with a fatha. And "'iwaj" with a kasra is what is in land, religion, or livelihood; one says: "In his religion there is 'iwaj." End.

Hafs, from ʿĀṣim, read this word ʿiwajan (عِوَجًا) in continuous recitation (waṣl) with a pause (sakta) on the alif that replaces the tanwin, a brief pause without taking breath. This signals that qayyiman is not connected to ʿiwajan in meaning; rather, it indicates that qayyiman is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: He made it upright (qayyiman), as we mentioned earlier.

Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read min ladunhu (مِن لَدُنْهُ) with the dal sukun (بِإسْكانِ الدّالِ) along with the ishmam of a ḍamma (إشْمامِها الضَّمَّ), with kasra on the nun and the ha', and joining it with a yā' in pronunciation. As for His saying ﴿wa-yubashshira al-mu'minina alladhina﴾ (Al-Kahf: 2), the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the bā' (the single-dotted bā'), and a kasra on the shīn, shaddated. Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read yabshura with a fatḥa on the yā', a sukun on the bā', and a ḍamma on the shīn.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 18, verse 6:

Allah's statement: ﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse.﴾

Know first that the word "la'alla" (perhaps) is used to express hope regarding something loved, and apprehension regarding something feared. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr al-Muhit (The Surging Sea), inclined to the view that "la'alla" in His statement here, ﴿then perhaps you would kill yourself﴾, expresses concern on his part (ﷺ) that he might destroy himself because they do not believe in him.

Some scholars said that "la'alla" in the verse carries the sense of a prohibition. Among those who held this view is al-'Askari, and this is the meaning of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words as quoted from both of them by the author of al-Bahr al-Muhit.

According to this view, the meaning is: Do not kill yourself because they do not believe. It was also said that it is here an interrogative carrying the sense of denial. Using "la'alla" in an interrogative sense is a well-known position of the Kufan (grammarians of Kufa) school.

The most apparent of these opinions to me regarding the meaning of "la'alla" is that what is intended by it in the verse is a prohibition against grieving over them.

Using "la'alla" to imply the sense of prohibition in such a verse is an Arabic stylistic usage, indicated by the context of the speech.

Among the evidences that what is meant by it is a prohibition against this is the frequent occurrence of an explicit prohibition against it, such as:

• His statement: ﴿So let not your soul go out in pursuit of them through regrets﴾ [Fatir: 8],

• His statement: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ (p-202) [an-Nahl: 127],

• His statement: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68],

and other verses besides these. The best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

"Al-bakhi'" (the one who destroys) means the one who ruins; that is, you are destroying yourself out of intense grief over their not believing. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Ah, you who destroy yourself with grief,
for a thing the decrees have snatched from his hands!

as has already been mentioned.

As for His statement: ﴿over their traces﴾, al-Qurtubi said: "Athar-hum" is the plural of "athar," and it is also said "ithr." The meaning is: following their turning away and their aversion from you.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: The meaning of "over their traces" is: after them, that is, after your despair of their belief, or after their death in disbelief. It is said: "So-and-so died over the trace of so-and-so," meaning after him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He compared himself and them, at the time they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and what entered him of grief and sorrow over their turning away, to a man whose beloved ones and dear ones have left him; he keeps falling down in regrets over their traces, and destroys himself with passion for them and longing over their separation. "Al-asaf" here means intense sorrow. The word "asaf" is sometimes used to mean anger, as in His statement: ﴿Then when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55].

When you have verified the meaning of this noble verse, know that what Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in it of the intensity of His Prophet's (ﷺ) grief over them, and of His prohibition to him against that, is explained in many other verses, such as His statement: ﴿So let not your soul go out in pursuit of them through regrets﴾ [Fatir: 8], and His statement: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself that they will not be believers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 3], and His statement: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88], and His statement: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68], and His statement: ﴿We certainly know that what they say saddens you﴾ [al-An'am: 33], and His statement: ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ [al-Hijr: 97], as we have already set forth clearly.

His statement in this noble verse: "asafan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, the accusative of cause), meaning: destroying yourself because of grief. It is permissible to parse it as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: while you are grieving over them. Upon the principle stated in the Khulasah:

And a verbal noun in indefinite form comes as a circumstantial often, like "baghtatan Zayd ta'la" (Zayd came out suddenly).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed. And indeed, We will make what is upon it into barren, dry ground.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said concerning the meaning of this noble verse: "'Whatever is upon it' means whatever is upon the earth that may serve as an adornment for it and for its people, from the ornaments of this world and what is considered beautiful in it."

Some scholars said: "Everything upon the earth is an adornment for it without restriction." According to this view, the snakes and other harmful creatures are also an adornment for the earth, because they point to the existence of their Creator and to His attributes of perfection and majesty, and the existence of that which produces this knowledge is an adornment for the thing in which it exists.

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification (bayan) mentioned in it is that a general term is stated and then, in some places, the inclusion of some individual members of that general term is explicitly stated. An example is His saying: ﴿That, and whoever honours the rites of Allah...﴾ [al-Hajj: 32], the verse, together with His explicit statement that the camels are included in this generality, in His saying: ﴿And the camels We have made for you as among the rites of Allah...﴾ [al-Hajj: 36], the verse.

Knowing this, be aware that His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Indeed, We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7] has been explicitly followed, in other places, by mention of some of the individual members included in it. Examples are His saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], the verse, and His saying: ﴿And horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as an adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8], the verse, along with other verses.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿barren, dry ground﴾ [al-Kahf: 8] means white land with no vegetation in it. We have already mentioned the meaning of "al-sa'id" (the surface of the earth) with its Arabic evidences in the surah of al-Ma'idah.

Al-Juruz (the barren land) is land with no vegetation in it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which eat their livestock and themselves? Then will they not see?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 27]. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"The sand-dunes and the barren wastes have consumed what was in its ribs, and nothing remains but its ribs, sharp and protruding."

This is because what he meant by "al-ajraz" (barren wastes) is the desert plains in which there is no vegetation. "Al-ajraz" is the plural of "juraza," and "juraza" is the plural of "juruz," so it is a plural of a plural of "juruz," as al-Jawhari said in his Sihah.

Al-Zamakhshari said in explaining this noble verse: ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it﴾ [al-Kahf: 8], meaning of this adornment, "barren, dry ground": like white land with no vegetation in it, after it had been green and luxuriant, in the removal of its freshness and the effacing of its beauty, and the nullification of what had made it an adornment, by causing the animals to die and the plants and trees to dry up. End of quotation.

This meaning indicated here has been clarified in other places, such as His saying: ﴿The example of the worldly life is only like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, from which people and livestock eat, until when the earth takes on its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it into stubble as though it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the verses for a people who give thought﴾ [Yunus: 24]. And like His saying: ﴿And present to them the example of the worldly life: like water which We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it and then became dry stalks, scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever Capable of all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 45], along with other verses.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7] means: that We may examine them through the tongues of Our messengers.

This wisdom which He mentioned here for making what is on the earth an adornment for it (namely, the trial as to good deeds) has been shown in other places to be the wisdom behind the creation of death and life, and of the heavens and the earth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, and He is over all things competent. He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving﴾ [al-Mulk: 1-2]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7].

The Prophet (ﷺ) explained excellence (ihsan) with his saying: "It is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you," as has passed.

What we have explained, that He, Majestic and Exalted, made what is upon the earth an adornment for it in order to test His creation, and then destroys what is upon it and makes it barren, dry ground, contains the greatest admonition for people and the most powerful deterrent from following desire and preferring the transient over the everlasting. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the world is sweet and green, and indeed Allah will make you successors in it, and He will see how you act. So beware of the world, and beware of women, for the first trial of the Children of Israel was with women."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾

Am [al-Kahf: 9], in this noble verse, is the disjunctive (munqati'a) "am", which is not used for asking for clarification. Its meaning according to the majority of scholars is "bal" (rather) together with the hamza (of interrogation), and according to some scholars it means "bal" alone. So according to the first opinion the meaning is: rather, did you think (ahasibta)? And according to the second, the meaning is: rather, you thought (hasibta). Thus, according to the first opinion it combines the sense of turning away (idrab) and denial (inkar), and according to the second it is only for the transitional idrab (al-idrab al-intiqali).

The most apparent of the opinions on the meaning of this noble verse is that Allah says to His Prophet ﷺ: the story of the companions of the cave, although people consider it great and marvel at it, is not a marvelous thing in comparison to Our power and the magnificence of Our creation. For Our creating the heavens and the earth, and Our making what is on the earth an adornment for it, and then Our making it after that a barren dry ground (sa'idan juruzan), is greater and more marvelous than what We did with the companions of the cave, and than Our causing them to sleep this long time, then raising them up. Many verses indicate what we have mentioned:

Among them is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ up to His saying ﴿a barren dry ground﴾ [al-Kahf: 7-8], then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave...﴾ the verse [al-Kahf: 9]. This indicates that what is meant is that their story is not marvelous in comparison to what We created, which is greater than it.

Among them is that the Great Qur'an frequently alerts people that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, and whoever created the greater is undoubtedly capable of the lesser, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ the verse [Ghafir: 57], and like His saying: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it...﴾ up to His saying ﴿as a provision for you and for your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27-33], as we have previously discussed fully in the surahs al-Baqarah and al-Nahl.

And whoever created these great creations: such as the heaven and the earth and what is in them, there is no wonder in his keeping the people of the cave this long period, then raising them up, as is clear.

Al-kahf: the wide opening in a mountain; if it is not wide, it is a ghar (cave). It was said: every cave in a mountain is a kahf. What is narrated from Anas, that the kahf is the mountain itself, is strange and not known in the language.

The scholars differed about the meaning of al-Raqim in this verse, with many opinions. It was said: al-Raqim is the name of their dog, and this is the view of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt when he says:

"And there is none in it but al-Raqim, a neighbour, and their hunting-dog, and the people in the cave are sleeping."

It is narrated from al-Dahhak that al-Raqim is a town in Rome. It was said: it is the name of the mountain in which the cave is, and it was said: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is, and the opinions on it are many. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: I do not know what al-Raqim is, is it a book or a building?

The most apparent of the opinions to me, according to the Arabic language and some verses of the Qur'an, is that al-Raqim means al-marqum (the inscribed), so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, from raqamtu al-kitab: when I wrote the book. And from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A written book﴾ the verse [al-Mutaffifin: 9, and 83/20]. Whether we say that al-Raqim is a book which they had, in which was their law to which they adhered, or a tablet of gold in which were written their names, lineages, story, and the cause of their departure, or a rock upon which their names were engraved, Allah knows best.

The apparent view is that the companions of the cave and the inscription are one group, referred to by two things one of which is conjoined to the other, contrary to those who said: the companions of the cave are one group and the companions of the inscription are another group, and that Allah related to His Prophet in this noble surah the story of the companions of the cave and did not mention to him anything about the companions of the inscription; and contrary to those who claimed that the companions of the cave are the three who were struck by a rock that blocked the door of the cave in which they were, so they called upon Allah by their good deeds: the dutiful son to his parents, the chaste man, and the one who hired workers. Their story is famous and established in the Sahih, but interpreting the verse as referring to them is far-fetched, as you see.

Know that the story of the companions of the cave and their names, and in what place on earth they were, nothing additional from the Prophet ﷺ has been established regarding all that beyond what is in the Qur'an. The commentators have many Israelite reports on this, which we have set aside for lack of reliability in them.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: "ajaban" is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: a thing that is marvelous, or: a sign that is marvelous.

His saying: "min ayatina" is in the position of a circumstantial (hal). It has been established in the science of grammar that when the qualifier of an indefinite noun is placed before it, it becomes a hal. The original meaning is: they were a marvel existing from Our signs, so when the qualifier was placed first, it became a hal.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave, and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us our affair in the right direction."﴾

In this noble verse, He (exalted and majestic is He) mentions among the attributes of the People of the Cave that they were youths, that they took refuge in the cave, and that they called upon their Lord with this great supplication, comprehensive of every good, which is His saying about them: ﴿Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us our affair in the right direction﴾ [al-Kahf: 10].

He explained elsewhere other of their attributes and sayings, such as His saying: (p-207) ﴿Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance﴾ — up to His saying — ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will facilitate for you your affair with ease﴾ [al-Kahf: 13-16]. The word "idh" (when) in His saying here, ﴿When the youths took refuge﴾ [al-Kahf: 10], is in the accusative governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), and it was said that it is governed by His saying "ajaban" (a wonder). The meaning of His saying ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 10] is that they made the cave a shelter for themselves and a place of protection.

The meaning of His saying ﴿grant us mercy from Yourself﴾ is: give us mercy from Your presence. Here mercy includes provision, guidance, protection from what they fled from fearing the harm of their people, and forgiveness.

"Al-fityah" (the youths) is the broken plural of "fata" (youth), and it is one of the plurals of paucity (jumu' al-qillah), and the word "al-fityah" indicates their small number and that they were young men, not elderly. This is contrary to what Ibn al-Sarraj claimed, that "al-fityah" is a collective noun (ism jam') and not a broken plural. Ibn Malik, in al-Khulasah, pointed to the fact that a form like "al-fityah" is a broken plural of paucity, with his saying:

"Af'ilah, af'ul, then fi'lah, likewise af'al: these are the plurals of paucity."

"Al-tahyi'ah" means bringing near and making easy; that is, make our affair easy for us and bring it near to us in the right direction. "Rashad" means being guided and remaining steadfast upon it. As for "min" in His saying "min amrina" (from our affair), there are two possibilities. The first is that it is here for explication (al-tajrid), and in that case the meaning is: make our affair entirely right, as you say: "I met from Zayd a lion, and from Amr a sea."

The second is that it is for partition (al-tab'id), and in that case the meaning is: and make for us some of our affair, that is, the part we are in of separation from the disbelievers, right, so that through it we become rightly guided and rightly directed.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾.

In this noble verse, He, mighty and exalted, mentions that He struck upon the ears of the People of the Cave for a number of years, and He did not specify the quantity of this number here. However, He specified it in another place, which is His saying: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾ [al-Kahf: 25].

His striking upon their ears in this verse is a metaphor (kinayah) for His putting them to sleep. The object of "ḍaraba" (struck) is omitted, meaning: We struck upon their ears a barrier preventing hearing, so they heard nothing that would wake them. The meaning is: We put them to a heavy sleep in which sounds did not rouse them.

His saying, ﴿years, counted﴾, is by omission of a modifier; that is, years possessing a number (dhāt ʿadad), or it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, that is, years that are counted (ma'dūdah). We have already mentioned the verse that specifies the quantity of their number by the lunar and the solar year (p-208), as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they added nine﴾ [al-Kahf: 25] indicates.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr, regarding His saying ﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ [al-Kahf: 11]: He expressed it with "striking" to indicate strength of direct contact, adherence and necessity. From this is: ﴿and humiliation was struck upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]; and one says "ḍaraba al-jizyah" (imposed the poll-tax) and "ḍaraba al-baʿth" (imposed the sending forth). Al-Farazdaq said:

The spider has spun its web over you, and the revealed Book has decreed against you by it.

And al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur said:

"And of calamities, may you have no father, that the earth has been struck upon me with barriers."

And another said:

"Indeed, manliness, generosity and liberality are in a dome struck over the son of al-Hashraj."

He mentioned the organ which is the ears (since hearing comes from them), because sleep is not fully firm except with hearing being disabled. In the hadith: "That is a man whom Satan urinated in his ear"; that is, his sleep became extremely heavy so that he would not rise at night for prayer. End of Abu Hayyan's words.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We roused them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the span of their stay.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, majestic and exalted, mentions that among the wisdoms of raising the People of the Cave after this long sleep is that He would show people which of the two disputing parties concerning the length of their stay was more precise and more exact in reckoning it. He does not specify here anything about the two parties mentioned.

Most exegetes (tafsir, the science of Qur'anic exegesis) hold that one of the two parties was the People of the Cave, and the second party was the people of the city in whose era the youths were raised, at the time when the record of the youths' affair was among them. It has also been said that the two parties were two groups from the people of that city, among whom there were believers and disbelievers. And it has been said that the two parties were two groups of believers in the time of the People of the Cave. They differed regarding the length of their stay; this was said by al-Farra'. And from Ibn 'Abbas: the kings who succeeded one another in ruling the city are one party, and the People of the Cave are a party, along with other sayings.

What the Qur'an indicates is that both parties are from the People of the Cave, and the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We roused them that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. It seems that those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾ (p-209) were those who knew that their stay had become long. And one may say: His saying about them, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾, indicates that they did not count the span of their stay precisely. And Allah knows best.

It may be answered that ascribing knowledge to Allah does not negate knowledge (for others), as evidenced by the fact that Allah informed His Prophet of the length of their stay in His saying: ﴿And they remained in their cave...﴾ [al-Kahf: 25, the verse], then commanded him to refer knowledge to Him in His saying: ﴿Say: "Allah knows best how long they remained."﴾ [al-Kahf: 26, the verse].

His saying, ﴿We roused them﴾, means: from their long sleep. And al-Ba'th (raising, rousing) is causing movement out of stillness, so it includes the raising of the sleeper and of the dead, and other things.

We have already explained in the introduction to this blessed book that among the types of clarification (al-bayan) it contains is that Allah, majestic and exalted, mentions a wisdom for a thing in one place, while that thing has other wisdoms mentioned in other places. We clarify these, and we have given examples of this and mentioned many such things in this blessed book.

Knowing this, be aware that here, in this noble verse, He has clarified that among the wisdoms of their being raised is to make manifest to people which of the two parties was more precise regarding the span of their stay. He has clarified other wisdoms for this in other places.

Among them: that they may question one another about the length of their stay, as in His saying: ﴿And thus We roused them that they might question one another﴾, the verse [al-Kahf: 19].

And among them: informing people that resurrection is true and that the Hour is true, since the story of the People of the Cave is evidence of that. This is in His saying: ﴿And thus We made them known to the people, that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾, the verse [al-Kahf: 21].

Know that His saying, majestic and exalted, in this noble verse, ﴿Then We roused them that We might know﴾, the verse, does not indicate that He was not knowing of this before raising them, as some of the disbelieving heretics claimed. Rather, He, majestic and exalted, knows everything that will be before it comes to be; nothing of that is hidden from Him, and the verses indicating this are countless.

We have already mentioned that among the clearest proofs that He, majestic and exalted, does not gain new knowledge through testing and trial, exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation, is His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts, and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. So His saying: (p-210) ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ after His saying ﴿and that He might test﴾ is clear evidence of this.

And when you have verified this, the meaning of ﴿that We might know which of the two parties﴾ is: that We might know that knowledge which makes the reality manifest to people. This does not negate that He was knowing of it before that, without its being made known to His creation.

The scholars differed regarding His saying: ﴿aḥṣā﴾ (more precise). Some of them held that it is a past-tense verb and ''amadan'' (a span) is its object, and the ''mā'' in His saying ''li-mā labithū'' (for the span they remained) is a verbal-masdar particle (mā maṣdariyya). The sense of the statement on this view is: that We might know which of the two parties computed a span of their stay in the cave.

Among those who chose that aḥṣā is a past-tense verb were al-Fārisī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn 'Aṭiyya, and others.

Others held that aḥṣā is an elative form (ṣīghat tafḍīl, comparative/superlative form), and ''amadan'' is a specification (tamyīz, an accusative of specification). Among those who chose this was al-Zajjāj and al-Tibrīzī, and others. Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqā' permitted both views.

Those who said that aḥṣā is a past-tense verb said: it cannot be an elative form, because neither the elative form nor the form of exclamation (fi'l al-ta'ajjub) can be regularly derived from anything other than a triliteral root, and aḥṣā is quadriliteral, so neither the elative nor the exclamatory form is regularly derived from it. They said: what is said, "mā a'ṭāhu" and "mā awlāhu" (how generous he is, how beneficent he is) for the known, and "a'dā min al-jarab" (more hostile than mange) and "afläs min Ibn al-Mudhalliq" (more bankrupt than Ibn al-Mudhalliq), is anomalous (shādh) and cannot be used as a basis for analogy, so it is not permissible to read the Qur'an according to it.

Al-Zamakhsharī also argued in al-Kashshāf, that aḥṣā is not an elative form, because ''amadan'' must either be governed by ''af'al'' (the elative), but ''af'al'' does not govern; or it is governed by ''labithū'', but then the meaning is not sound on that view. He said: If you claim that it is governed by a verb implied by aḥṣā, as is implied in the line:

"And more striking to us with swords are the helmets"

i.e., we strike the helmets, then you have strayed far from the obvious, since you refused that aḥṣā be a verb and then returned, compelled, to positing and implying one. End of al-Zamakhsharī's words.

It is answered on behalf of the dissenters regarding all of this: they said, we do not concede that the elative form cannot be derived from other than the triliteral, nor do we concede that it does not govern.

The summary of the discussion on this is that there are three schools of the grammarians regarding whether the elative form is derived from ''af'ala'' as here, or is not derived from it:

The first: it is permissible to form it from ''af'ala'' without restriction. This is the apparent view of Sībawayh, and it is the school of Abū Isḥāq as Abū Ḥayyān related it from him in al-Baḥr.

The second: it is not formed from it at all, and whatever is heard from it is anomalous, to be memorized and not used as a basis for analogy. This is the view Ibn Mālik followed in al-Khulāṣa, in his words:

"Judge by rarity what is other than what has been mentioned, and do not analogize from what has been transmitted."

As we mentioned earlier in the surah of Banī Isrā'īl, in discussing His saying: ﴿But whoever is blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way﴾ [al-Isrā': 72].

The third: it is formed from ''af'ala'' only when its hamza is not for transitivity (naql) specifically, such as ''aẓlama al-layl'' (the night grew dark) and ''ashkala al-amr'' (the matter became obscure). But if the hamza is for transitivity, it is not formed from it. This is the choice of Abū al-Ḥasan Ibn 'Uṣfūr. These schools are mentioned with their proofs in the books of grammar.

As for al-Zamakhsharī's statement, "af'al does not govern," it is not correct, because the elative form does govern a specification (tamyīz) without disagreement, and on this Ibn Mālik followed in al-Khulāṣa, in his words:

"And govern the agent-meaning by the elative, as a comparative: 'you are higher in rank.'"

And ''amadan'' is a specification as already stated, so its accusative construction after the elative form presents no difficulty.

Al-Ṭabarī held that ''amadan'' is governed by ''labithū'', and Ibn 'Aṭiyya said that this is not a sound direction. Abū Ḥayyān said: it may well be sound, because the amad is the limit (ghāya), and it is an expression for the duration from the viewpoint that duration is a limit. And ''mā'' has the meaning of ''alladhī'' (that which), and ''amadan'' is in the accusative by dropping the preposition; i.e., "for what they remained of a span," i.e., a duration, and "from a span" becomes an explanation of what is ambiguous in the phrase ''mā labithū'', as in His saying: ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106], ﴿whatever mercy Allah grants to people﴾ [Fāṭir: 2]. And when the preposition was dropped, the verb reached it.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: the use of amad for limit is well known in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:

"Except for one like you, or one whom you outrun, as a steed outruns when it has gained the lead at the limit."

And we have already mentioned in the surah of al-Nisā' that 'Alī ibn Sulaymān al-Akhfash al-Ṣaghīr permitted the accusative by removing the preposition, when there is no ambiguity, in every case. But the accusative of ''amadan'' by ''labithū'' is not sound, as al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn 'Aṭiyya mentioned, and as is not hidden. End of quotation.

The Kufans permitted the accusative of the object by the elative form, and they parsed the statement of al-'Abbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī:

"I have not seen a tribe like the living tribe that greets the morning, nor like us the day we met as horsemen,
More forceful and more protective of the truth than they, and more striking to us with swords are the helmets."

They held that ''al-qawānis'' (the helmets) is a direct object of the elative form ''aḍrab'' (more striking). They said: there is no need to posit an implied verb. From here some grammarians said that ''man'' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾ [al-An'ām: 117] is in the accusative by the elative form before it, as a direct object.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: the Kufans' view, in my opinion, accords better with the sound meaning, because the elative form contains within it the meaning of the masdar (verbal noun) latent in it, so there is no barrier to its governing as the masdar governs. Do you not see that His saying, "more striking to us with swords are the helmets," means: our striking with swords of helmets exceeds the striking of others, as is clear. On the basis of what we have established, there is no barrier to ''amadan'' being in the accusative by ''aḥṣā'' as a direct object, on the grounds that it is an elative form, even though those who held that aḥṣā is an elative form parsed ''amadan'' as a specification.

**Note**

If it is asked: what is the reason for the nominative case of ''ayyu'' in His saying, ﴿that We might know which of the two parties was more precise﴾, the verse, even though it is in the accusative position as a direct object? The answer: the scholars have several answers to this. Among them: ''ayyu'' here carries the meaning of interrogation, and interrogation suspends the verb from its two objects, as Ibn Mālik said in al-Khulāṣa, joining it to what suspends the mental verb from its two objects:

"And if 'inna' or the initial lām or an oath, likewise interrogation, is the one that is necessarily so."

Among them is what al-Fakhr al-Rāzī and others mentioned: that the whole sentence is the object of knowledge, and for this reason the governance of ''li-na'lama'' did not appear on the word ''ayyu'', but it remained in its nominative state. The unsoundness of this view is not hidden, as you see.

(p-213) The author of these notes, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: the most apparent of the parsings in the verse to me is that the word ''ayyu'' is a relative-interrogative (mawṣūla istifhāmiyya). ''Ayyu'' is indeclinable because it is in construct (muḍāfa), and the head of its relative clause is omitted, according to his words in al-Khulāṣa:

"Ayyu is declined when it is not in construct, and the head of its relative clause is an omitted pronoun."

Because it is indeclinable, its accusative is not manifest. The meaning on this reading is: that We might know the party which is more precise regarding the span of their stay and distinguish it from others. And ''aḥṣā'' is an elative form as we have already explained its direction. Yes, the dissenter may say: the elative form, by the evidence of its agreement, requires that the one preferred and the one it is preferred over share in the basic act, and one of the two parties did not share with the other in the basic act of reckoning, because of its ignorance of the span from its origin. This strengthens the view of those who said that ''aḥṣā'' is a verb. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

If it is asked: what important benefit is there in people's knowing which party reckoned the span of the stay more precisely than the other, such that it would be a final cause for His saying, ﴿Then We roused them that We might know﴾, the verse? And what important benefit is there in some of them questioning others, such that it would be a final cause for His saying: ﴿And thus We roused them that they might question one another﴾?

The answer is that we have not seen anyone address this, and what appears to us, and God the Exalted knows best, is that what was mentioned of informing the people about the party that is most accurate in reckoning how long they stayed, and of their asking one another about that, necessarily entails that the reality of these youths' affair becomes manifest to the people, and that God struck upon their ears in the cave for three hundred years and they added nine, then He raised them alive with their bodies fresh, no state of theirs having changed. This is among the wondrous works of His, glorified and exalted is He, which indicate the perfection of His power and the resurrection after death. And for the sake of considering this necessary consequence, He made what we have mentioned a final cause (ʿillah ghaʾiyyah, a purposive cause), and God the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 13:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance﴾ [al-Kahf: 13].

In this noble verse, the Exalted and Majestic One tells His Prophet ﷺ that He relates to him the story of the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) in truth. Then He informed him, emphasizing it for him, that they were youths who believed in their Lord, and that Allah, exalted and majestic, increased them in guidance.

From this noble verse it is understood that whoever believes in his Lord and obeys Him, his Lord increases him in guidance, because obedience is a cause of more guidance and faith.

This meaning from this noble verse is clarified in other places, such as:

• His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accept guidance, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17],

• and His statement: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-'Ankabut: 69],

• and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Anfal: 29],

• and His statement: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124],

• and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Fath: 4],

• and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy and make for you a light by which you will walk﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Hadid: 28],

along with other verses.

These mentioned verses are explicit texts that faith increases, and it is understood from them that it also decreases, as al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, used them as evidence for that. They indicate it with a clear indication about which there is no doubt. So there is no basis, in light of them, for disagreement about the increase and decrease of faith, as you see. And Allah knows best.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And We fortified their hearts when they stood up﴾.

That is, We made their hearts firm and strengthened them to endure patiently, so that they would not panic or fear to proclaim the truth, and would bear patiently the separation from family and comfort, and fleeing with their religion into a cave in a mountain with no companion, no water and no food.

From this noble verse it is understood that whoever is in obedience to his Lord, may He be glorified and exalted, Allah, the Exalted, strengthens his heart and makes it firm to bear hardships and to exercise beautiful patience.

The Exalted has also alluded to incidents of this meaning in other places, such as His saying about the people of Badr, addressing His Prophet ﷺ and his Companions: ﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it, and to remove from you the defilement of Satan, and to strengthen your hearts and plant firmly your feet﴾ and ﴿When your Lord inspired to the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [al-Anfal: 11–12] and the verse; and His saying about the mother of Moses: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void; she was about to disclose him had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers﴾ [al-Qasas: 10].

Most of the exegetes hold that His saying "when they stood up" means before the king of their land, who was a tyrannical king calling to the worship of idols; they claim his name was Diqyanus.

Their story is mentioned in all the books of tafsir (exegesis), but we have set it aside because it is from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives traced to Jewish and Christian sources). Regarding their standing mentioned here there are many other sayings, and the governing element of His saying "إذْ" (idh, "when") is "رَبَطْنا" ("We fortified"), upon their standing up.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So they said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke besides Him any deity. We would have certainly spoken, then, an excessive transgression"﴾

[p-215] In this noble verse the Exalted mentions that these youths who believed in their Lord, and whom their Lord increased in guidance, said: indeed their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, that they would never invoke besides Him any deity, and that if they did that they would have uttered شَطَطًا (shatatan), that is, a saying of excess. Or it is a case of the noun of the verb used as an adjective (naʻt bi'l-masdar) for emphasis, as if their saying were itself excess. Al-shatat is distance from truth and rightness, and the sayings of the exegetes return to it, such as the saying of some of them that "شَطَطًا" means injustice, transgression, falsehood, error, and other sayings.

The root of the word shatat is exceeding the limit; from it comes "ashatta fi al-sawm" (he exceeded the limit in the price) when he goes beyond the bound. From it is His saying: ﴿and do not deviate﴾ [Sad: 22] and the verse, or it means distance. From it is the saying of ʻUmar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

*It will move away tomorrow, the dwelling of our neighbours, and the dwelling after tomorrow is further away.*

The use of shatat is frequent for injustice and transgression, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Will you desist, though the excessive ones are not forbidden, like a spear-thrust in which the oil and the wick go?*

This noble verse clearly indicates that whoever associates with the Creator of the heavens and the earth another deity has come with a thing of excess, far from truth and rightness, in the utmost injustice and transgression. This is because the one who deserves worship is the One who brings creation from non-existence into existence; whoever cannot create others is a creature who needs a creator to create him, provide for him and manage his affairs.

This meaning indicated by this noble verse is explained in many other verses,

• such as His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you that you may become righteous. He who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy and sent down from the sky, water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not attribute to Allah equals while you know﴾ [al-Baqara: 21–22];

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Then will you not remember?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17];

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or have they made for Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them? Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], meaning: the One, the Subduer, who is the Creator of all things, is the one deserving worship alone, may He be glorified and exalted;

• and His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿Do they associate those who create nothing and are themselves created?﴾ [al-A'raf: 191];

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they have taken besides Him deities who create nothing, while they are created﴾ [al-Furqan: 3] and the verse;

and other verses.

As for His saying, may He be glorified and exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿We would have certainly spoken, then, an excessive transgression﴾, that is: if we invoked besides Him a deity, then we would have uttered a transgression. [p-216]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair something easy.﴾

The "idh" (when) in His saying ﴿And when you withdraw from them﴾ is for causation (ta'lil), according to verification, as Ibn Hisham said. On this basis, the meaning is: because of your withdrawal from your people, the disbelievers, and from what they worship besides Allah, take the cave as a shelter and a place of refuge; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair something easy. This indicates that the believer's withdrawal from his disbelieving people and their objects of worship is among the means by which Allah shows him kindness and mercy.

This meaning is also indicated by His saying, may He be exalted, concerning His Prophet Ibrahim, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon other than Allah, and I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate.﴾ ﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped other than Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We made each a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy and granted them a true and high report.﴾ [Maryam: 48–50]. His withdrawal from them is his keeping away from them and his fleeing from them with his religion.

His saying ﴿and what they worship except Allah﴾: "ma" is a relative pronoun in the accusative position, conjoined to the object pronoun in His saying "i'tazaltumuhum" (you withdrew from them), meaning: and you withdrew from their objects of worship other than Allah. It has also been said that "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah), meaning: you withdrew from them and you withdrew from their worship of other than Allah, may He be exalted. The first is more evident.

His saying "illa Allah" (except Allah): it has been said that it is an exceptive (istithna') of the connected type (muttasil), based on the view that they used to worship Allah and the idols. It has also been said that it is a disconnected exception (munqati'), based on the view that they worshipped only the idols and did not know Allah or worship Him.

His saying "mirfaqan": that is, that by which you gain benefit (irtifaq), that is, by which you are benefited. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa', with the ra' emphasized (tafkhim). The rest of the seven read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa', with the ra' light (tarqiq). These are two readings and two dialects concerning that by which one is benefited, and concerning the human joint known as the elbow (mirfaq). Al-Kisa'i rejected the fatha of the mim and kasra of the fa' in the sense of the human joint, and said: it is with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa', and nothing other than that is permitted.

Ibn al-Anbari claimed that "min" in His saying ﴿and will prepare for you of your affair﴾ carries the sense of substitution (badaliyyah), meaning: He will prepare for you, in place of your difficult affair, a means of ease. In accordance with what he claimed, it is an ending point (ghayah), like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], meaning: in place of it and in exchange for it. From this meaning is the poet's saying:

"Would that we had for ourselves a sip of Zamzam's water, cooled, having spent the night in the Tahayan..."

meaning: in place of the water of Zamzam. And Allah knows best.

The meaning of ﴿will spread out for you﴾ is: will extend for you, as in His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura: 28].

His saying "wa-yuhayyi'" means: will make easy, bring near, and facilitate.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left, while they were in a spacious area of it. That is from the signs of Allah.﴾

Know first that we mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the types of clarification (bayan) it contains is that some scholars state an opinion regarding a verse while there is, within the verse itself, an indicator (qarinah) that points to the contrary of that opinion. We mentioned several examples of this.
