Having known this, know that the scholars differed regarding this verse into two views, and within the verse itself there is an indicator that points to the soundness of one of them and the unsoundness of the other.

As for the view which the indicator in the verse points against, it is that the People of the Cave were in a corner of the cave, and between them and the sun were natural barriers from the cave itself, which protected them from the heat of the sun at its rising and its setting, as we will mention in detail, if Allah the Exalted wills.

As for the view which the indicator in this verse points to its soundness, it is that the People of the Cave were in a spacious area of the cave, on a course that the sun reaches and faces, except that Allah prevented the light of the sun from falling upon them in a manner that breaks custom, as an honour to these righteous people who fled with their religion in obedience to their Lord, majestic and exalted.

The indicator showing this is His saying: ﴿That is from the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 17], for if the matter were as those of the first view stated, that would be a common, familiar matter with nothing strange in it, so that it could be said of it: ﴿That is from the signs of Allah.﴾ On this view which we have mentioned, to which the aforementioned indicator testifies, the meaning of the sun's inclining away from their cave to the right at its rising, and its passing them on the left at its setting, is that Allah reduces its light away from them, and pushes it to the direction of the right at rising, and to the direction of the left at setting. Allah the Exalted is capable of all things, doing what He wills. Having known this, know that the proponents of the first view differed regarding the manner of the cave's orientation. Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir, affirmed (p-219) that the verse indicates that the door of the cave was on the north side. He said: "Because He, the Exalted, informed that the sun, when it enters it at its rising, inclines away from it to the right, i.e., the shade shrinks toward the right side, as Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: 'tazawaru' means 'tamil' (inclines). That is because whenever it rises in the horizon, its ray shrinks as it rises, until nothing of it remains in that place at midday. For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when it sets, it passes them on the left﴾ [al-Kahf: 17], i.e., it enters their cave from the north side of its door, and that is from the direction of the east. This indicates the soundness of what we have said. This is clear to whoever reflects upon it and has knowledge of the science of astronomy (al-hay'ah) and the courses of the sun, moon and stars."

Its explanation: if the door of the cave were on the east side, nothing would enter it from there at setting; if it were on the qiblah side, nothing would enter it from there at rising or at setting, and the shade would not incline to the right or left; and if it were on the west side, the sun would not enter it at the time of rising, but only after midday, and it would remain in it until setting. Thus what we have mentioned is determined, and to Allah be praise. End of Ibn Kathir's words.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: The proponents of this view said that the door of the cave was open on the north side, so when the sun rose it was on the right of the cave, and when it set it was on its left. So the sun's light did not reach the interior of the cave, while good air and a suitable breeze reached it. End of al-Razi's words. Abu Hayyan said in his tafsir of this verse: This attribute with the sun requires that they had a screen from the south side and a screen from the west (dabur) side, while they were in a corner. 'Abdullah ibn Muslim said: The door of the cave faced the Bananat Na'sh (the Great Bear stars), and on this view the top of the cave was covered from rain.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Their cave faced Banat Na'sh; the sun did not enter it at rising or at setting. Allah chose for them a spacious resting place in a maqna'ah (a place not reached by the sun) where the sun does not enter upon them to harm them. End of the purpose of Abu Hayyan's words. The maqna'ah is the place which the sun does not rise upon, along with other views of the scholars.

The first view is more fitting to the Qur'anic indicator we mentioned.

Among those who relied on the first view because of the aforementioned indicator is al-Zajjaj, and al-Razi and al-Shawkani in their tafsirs inclined to it somewhat, justifying al-Zajjaj's aforementioned view by the indicator of the verse.

(p-220) Al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir: What supports the first view is His saying: ﴿That is from the signs of Allah﴾, for the turning of the sun away from them while the spacious area is directed toward a place which the sun ordinarily reaches is more fitting to the meaning of its being a sign. It is also supported by the unrestricted use of "fajwah" without limiting it to being in a particular direction. Among what indicates that fajwah means a wide place is the poet's saying:

"You clothed your people in disgrace and shame, until they were made lawful and the courtyard of the house became their open space."

End of al-Shawkani's words.

It is known that fajwah means the spacious area. It is well-known in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the aforementioned verse, and another's saying:

"We filled every valley and fajwah with men and horses, not deviating nor withdrawing."

From it is also the hadith: "When he found a fajwah, he made it..." (nass).

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose﴾, i.e., you, the addressee, would see the sun at its rising inclining over their cave; the meaning is that if you had seen them, you would have seen them thus, not that the addressee actually saw them, as His saying supports this meaning: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight﴾ [al-Kahf: 18], and address in this manner is well known in the language of the Arabs in which this great Qur'an was revealed. The root of the word tazawur is inclination (al-mayl), so the meaning of "tazawaru" is "tamilu" (inclines). Al-zawr is inclination, and from it is shahadat al-zur (false testimony), because it is an inclination away from the truth. From it is also ziyarah (visiting), because the visitor inclines toward the one visited. From this meaning is the saying of Antarah in his mu'allaqah:

"He leaned (fazarra) from the impact of the spears against his side, and complained to me with a tear and a neigh."

And the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

"My voice was lowered, I came with the gait of a bold man, and my figure was inclined (azwaru) for fear of the tribe."

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿to the right﴾ means the direction of the right, and its reality is the direction called the right. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "Dhat al-yamin" is the direction of the right of the cave, and its reality is the direction called the right, meaning the right of one entering the cave, or the right of the youths. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and when it sets, it passes them﴾, from qard in the sense of severing and cutting off, i.e., it cuts them off, keeps away from them and does not approach them. This meaning is known from the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Ghaylan Dhu al-Rummah:

"I looked at Ja'ba al-Sabiyyah a look at forenoon, while the black of the eye in the water was sunlit."

"To caravans that cut through the sand-dunes of Mushrif to the left, while on their right are the horsemen."

So his saying "yaqridna aqwaza mushrif" means they cut them and keep them away toward the left. "Aqwaz" is the plural of qawz (with fatha), which is the high part of the sand, as if it were a mountain. It is also narrated as "ajwaza mushrif," plural of jawz, from majaz, meaning the road. This which we have mentioned is the correct meaning of His saying "taqriduhum," contrary to one who claimed that "taqriduhum" means it cuts off some of its light from them and then quickly disappears like a loan that is repaid. The intent of the speaker of this view is that the sun turns away from them in the morning and touches them in the evening with a light touch, just enough that the air of the place is pleasant for them and does not rot.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: If it were from qard in the sense of lending which is then taken back, the verb would be quadriliteral, and the ta' in "taqridhum" would be damma-vocalized; but the fatha of the ta' in "taqridhum" shows that it is from qard in the sense of cutting, i.e., it cuts off some of its light for them. You have known that the correct view is the first, and we have already mentioned that fajwah means the spacious area.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿tazawaru 'an kahfihim﴾ has three seven canonical readings:

Ibn 'Amir al-Shami read "tazwarr" with sukun on the zay, dropping the alif and doubling the ra', on the pattern of tahmarr; in this reading it is from al-izwirar in the sense of inclination, like the saying of Antarah mentioned above: "fazarra min waq'i al-qana..." (the verse).

'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, the Kufans, read it with a light zay followed by an alif. In this reading its original form is "tatazawaru," from which one of the two ta's is dropped, according to the rule in the Khulasah:

"And what begins with two ta's may be shortened to one, as in tabayyana al-'ibar (the 'tabayyana' example)."

Nafi' al-Madani, Ibn Kathir al-Makki and Abu 'Amr al-Basri read "tazzawaru" with a doubled zay followed by an alif; its original form is "tatazawaru," in which the ta' was assimilated into the zay. On these two readings (I mean the reading with one ta' dropped and the reading with assimilation into the zay), it is from tazawur in the sense of inclination too, and tafa'ul may come in the sense of the bare verb itself, as here, and as in the expressions "safara," "'aqaba" and "'afa."

On the view of the one who said that in the cave there are natural barriers that prevent the sun from entering according to the arrangement of the cave, the reference in His saying: ﴿That is from the signs of Allah﴾ goes back to what was mentioned of their story, i.e., that aforementioned matter of their guidance to monotheism, their removal from among the idol-worshippers, their taking refuge in that cave, and their protection from their enemy, up to the end of their story, is from the signs of Allah.

The original form of the word "ayah" according to the verifiers is "ayayah" with three fathas; the first yaa' was changed to an alif. In such cases, when two causes of weakening (i'lal) come together, the weakening usually falls on the last, because change is usually greater at the ends, as in tawa and nawa and the like. Here the first was weakened against the usual pattern, as indicated in the Khulasah by his saying:

"If two letters both merit weakening, the first is kept sound, and the reverse may occur."

The word "ayah" is used in the Arabic language in two senses, and used in the Great Qur'an in two senses as well. As for its usage in the language, the first is that it is used to mean a sign ( 'alamah), which is the well-known usage, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the sign of His kingdom is that there will come to you the chest (tabut)...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248], and Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah's saying:

"By the sign of what she said on the morning I met her, at the place of Midfa' Aknan: 'Is this the one who is famous?'"

He means that her saying that was the sign between her and his messenger to her, mentioned in his earlier line:

"Convey to her my greetings, for indeed my visiting her is made known and denied."

In the poetry of Nabighah Dhubyani, who was pre-Islamic, the verse is interpreted as sign in his saying:

"I took for signs (ayat) remnants of her, and I recognized them after six years, and this is the seventh year."

Then he clarified that by the ayat he meant the markers of the abode, in his following saying:

"Ashes like kohl of the eye, after a long time I explain it, and a ring of stones like the stump of a pool, broken and humbled."

The second of its two senses is the use of ayah to mean a group (jama'ah). They say: "The people came with their ayah," i.e., with their group. From it is the saying of Burj ibn Musahhir or another:

"We went out from the two passes, there is no tribe like us, with our ayat we drive the milch camels, the young ones."

So his saying "bi-ayatina" means "with our group."

The meaning of "ayah" in the Qur'an has two uses. The first is its application to the cosmic, predestined sign (al-ayah al-kawniyyah al-qadariyyah), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190]. That is, they are cosmic, predestined signs by which people of sound intellect recognise that their Creator is the Lord who alone is worthy of worship, exalted is He. The cosmic, predestined ayah in the Qur'an is taken in the linguistic sense of "sign."

The second use of "ayah" in the Qur'an is its application to the legislated, religious ayah (al-ayah al-shar'iyyah al-diniyyah), as in His saying: ﴿a Messenger reciting to you the signs of Allah﴾ [At-Talaq: 11], and similar verses.

Regarding the legislated, religious ayah, it has been said that it derives from "ayah" in the linguistic sense of "sign," because it is a sign of the truthfulness of the one who brought it, or because it contains signs of its beginning and its end.

It has also been said that it derives from "ayah" in the sense of "group," because the legislated, religious ayah comprises a group and body of the words of the Qur'an.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided, and whomever He leaves astray - for them you will find no protecting friend to guide them﴾.

Exalted is He, in this noble verse, has made clear that guidance and misguidance are in His hand alone, exalted is He. Whomever He guides, there is no misguider for him, and whomever He misguides, there is no guide for him.

This meaning has been clarified in very many verses:

• such as His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided, and whomever He leaves astray - for them you will find no allies other than Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute and deaf﴾ [Al-Isra': 97];

• and His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided, and whomever He leaves astray - it is those who are the losers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 178];

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you, [O Muhammad], do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Qasas: 56];

• and His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah intends for trial - you cannot avail him anything against Allah﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 41];

• and His saying: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed, Allah does not guide those He leaves astray, and they will have no helpers﴾ [An-Nahl: 37];

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wants to guide - He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wants to leave astray - He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [Al-An'am: 125].

Verses like these are very numerous.

From these verses and their like in the Qur'an, what is derived is the invalidity of the doctrine of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree), who hold that the servant is independent in his deeds, whether good or evil, and that this is not by the will of Allah but by the will of the servant. Glorified is He, exalted is He, far above that anything should occur in His dominion without His will! And exalted is He far above that, a great exaltation! The detailed discussion of this topic will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

[p. 224] We have also clarified in our book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab, "Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book"), in the surah "al-Shams," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And inspired it [with] its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ [Ash-Shams: 8], and His saying: ﴿Then you will not find for him a protecting friend to guide him﴾ [Al-Kahf: 17], meaning: there will be no cause between him and any friend who would guide him to what is right and to guidance. That is, that will not happen, because whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him.

As for His saying "فَهو المُهْتَدِ" (fa-huwa al-muhtad, "so he is the one rightly guided"), Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited it with the yā' ("ي") pronounced in continuous recitation (wasl) but not in pause (waqf), while the rest of the Seven Readers recited it with the yā' omitted in both states.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they are asleep.﴾

Al-Husban (reckoning) means al-zann (supposing, thinking). Al-Ayqaz is the plural of yaqiz (awake), with the qaf either vowelled with a kasra or a damma. From it is the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

"When she saw that some of them had awakened, and their wakeful ones, she said: 'Advise, how do you command?'"

Al-Ruqud is the plural of raqid, which means the sleeper. That is, you, the addressee, would think them awake if you saw them, while in fact they are asleep. What supports this meaning is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, in its counterpart: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight﴾ [al-Kahf: 18] and so on. Some scholars said: the reason the observer thinks they are awake is that they are asleep with their eyes open. It was also said: it is because of how much they turn over. This view is indicated by the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, after it: ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾ [al-Kahf: 18]. The commentators' discussion here about the number of their turnings, whether many or few, has no evidence for it, and therefore we have turned away from mentioning the sayings on it.

As for His saying in this verse, "and you would think them", it was read with a fatha on the sin by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza, in accordance with analogy (qiyas). It was read with a kasra on the sin by Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i. Both are canonical readings (qira'atan sab'iyyatan), and two well-known dialects. The fatha is more analogical, and the kasra is more eloquent.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold﴾

The commentators differed in their expressions about the meaning of "al-Wasid". It was said: it is the courtyard of the house, and this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was said: al-Wasid is the door, and this is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: al-Wasid is the threshold, and it was said: the dust (al-sa'id). What the Qur'an testifies to is that al-Wasid is the door, and it is also called "asid", because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾ [al-Humazah: 8], meaning sealed shut, and this is by closing every wasid or asid, which is one of its doors. A verse from Arabic speech parallel to the verse is the saying of the poet:

"My she-camel longs for the mountains of Makkah, and between her and them are the doors of San'a, closed."

(p-225) And the saying of Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"Indeed, in the palace, if we entered, a gazelle, clapped at and closed, with a curtain over it."

So the meaning of closing (al-i'sad) in all of that is sealing and locking, because the custom in it is that it is at the wasid, which is the door, and it is said asid. On both dialects are the two readings in His saying "mu'sadah", hamzated from asid, and unhamzated from wasid.

Among the Arabs' usage of wasid for the door is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn Wahb al-'Absi, and it was said Zuhayr:

"In a wide land whose wasid is not blocked against me, and my being known there is not unfamiliar."

That is, its door is not blocked against me, meaning there are no doors in it that could be blocked against me; like the saying of another:

"And you do not see the lizard hiding in it."

If it is said: how can al-Wasid be the door in the verse, when the cave is a cavern in a mountain with no door?

The answer: the door is applied to the entrance through which one enters the thing; so there is no objection to calling the entrance to the cave a door. And whoever said al-Wasid is the courtyard does not contradict what we have mentioned, because the courtyard of the cave is its door. We have previously mentioned many times that among the kinds of clarification (bayan) which this blessed Book contains: that some scholars say a saying concerning a verse, while there is in the verse an indication that contradicts it.

Some people of knowledge said regarding this noble verse that the intended "dog" in this verse is a man among them, not a real dog, and they cited for that some anomalous readings, such as the reading "wa-kalibuhum basitun dhira'ayhi bil-wasid" and the reading "wa-kali'uhum basitun dhira'ayhi".

His saying, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿stretching out its forelegs﴾ is an indication of the falsity of that view, because stretching out the forelegs is well known as one of the characteristics of the real dog. From this is the hadith of Anas, agreed upon, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Keep straight in prostration, and let none of you stretch out his forelegs like the stretching of a dog." This meaning is well known in the speech of the Arabs, so it is an indication that it is a real dog. The reading "wa-kali'uhum" with a hamza does not negate its being a dog, because the dog protects its people and guards them, and al-kala'a means protection.

If it is said: what is the basis for the active participle "basit", which is the subject of its object "dhira'ayhi", given that it is established in grammar that the active participle, when it is not the complement of "al", does not govern except when it refers to the present or future?

The answer: the verse here is a narration of a past state, and a parallel to that in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making in the earth a successor﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and His saying: ﴿And Allah will bring out what you were concealing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72].

Know that His mention, majestic and exalted is He, in His Book of this dog, and that it was stretching out its forelegs at the threshold of their cave, in the context of honouring them, indicates that the company of the righteous is of great benefit. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in interpreting this noble verse: "Their blessing encompassed their dog, so what befell them of sleep in that state befell it too, and this is the benefit of the company of the righteous, for this dog came to have mention, report, and standing." End quote.

This meaning is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to one who said: "I love Allah and His Messenger": "You are with whom you love," agreed upon, from the hadith of Anas.

It follows from this that the company of the wicked has great harm in it, as Allah has made clear in Surah al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿A speaker among them says: Indeed, I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51], up to His saying: ﴿He said: By Allah, you had nearly ruined me, and if not for the favour of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 56-57], and so on.

As for what the commentators mention of the sayings concerning the name of their dog, some saying its name is Qitmir, and some saying its name is Humran, and other than that, we have not extended discussion on it, for lack of benefit in it.

In the great Qur'an there are many matters which Allah has not made clear to us, nor His Messenger, and nothing has been established in their clarification, and searching for them has no value and no benefit in it.

Many of the commentators go at length in mentioning the sayings about them without knowledge or benefit, and we always turn away from the like of that, such as the colour of the dog of the companions of the cave and its name, and what the slain man was struck with from the cow of the Children of Israel, and the name of the boy whom al-Khidr killed, and at which Musa objected to his killing, and the wood of Noah's ship, of what tree it was, and how long and how wide the ship was, and how many decks it had, and other matters of which there is no benefit in searching, and no evidence for verifying them.

We have previously mentioned, in Surah al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145], the ruling on eating the flesh of the dog and selling it, and taking its price if it is killed, and what of it is permissible to keep and what is not, and we explained the evidences in that and the sayings of the scholars concerning it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 19 (part 1 of 6):

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And thus We roused them, that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾

In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted mentions that He roused the People of the Cave from their long sleep so that they might question one another, meaning that some of them would ask others about the length of their stay in the cave during that sleep. Some of them said that they had remained a day or part of a day, and some of them referred the knowledge of that to Allah the Exalted.

Here He does not specify the actual length of the period about which they questioned one another. However, He specified it in another place: it was three hundred years by the solar reckoning, and three hundred and nine years by the lunar reckoning. This is in His saying: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine [more]﴾ [al-Kahf: 25], as has already been mentioned.

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city, and let him see which of its food is purest, and bring you provision from it.﴾

Concerning His saying in this verse "purest" (azka), there are two opinions among the scholars.

The first is that what is meant by "purest" (azka) is "best" (atyab), because it is lawful, not containing anything prohibited or doubtful.

The second is that what is meant by "purest" (azka) is that it is "more abundant," as in the saying of the Arabs: "zaka al-zar'u" (the crop grew), when it increased, and as in the words of the poet:

"Our tribes are seven, and you are three; and the seven are purer (azka) than three and better (atyab)."

That is, more numerous than three.

The first opinion is the one supported by the Qur'an, because Allah commanded the believers to eat what is lawful and to do righteous deeds, just as He commanded the messengers. He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Mu'minun: 51], and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things that We have provided you and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. The root z-k-w is frequently used in the Qur'an to mean purity:

• As in His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Isra': 14],
• And His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Shams: 9],
• And His saying: ﴿And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, none of you would ever have been pure﴾ [al-Nur: 21],
• And His saying: ﴿So We desired that their Lord would exchange for them one better than him in purity and nearer in mercy﴾ [al-Kahf: 81],
• And His saying: ﴿Have you killed a innocent soul without [its having killed] another?﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Kahf: 74],

along with other verses.

So "zakah" in these verses and similar ones means purity from the filth of sins and disobedience. What befits the state of these righteous, God-fearing youths is that their concern regarding their food be purity and lawfulness (al-halbah), not abundance. Some scholars have said: their acquaintance with the city was that in it there were believers who concealed their faith and disbelievers, and that they wished to buy food from the believers rather than the disbelievers, and that this is what they meant by "purity" in His saying: ﴿purest food﴾. It has also been said that there were People of the Book and Magians in it, and Allah knows best.

The word "al-warq" in His statement: ﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours﴾ [al-Kahf: 19] means silver. The scholars of the Maliki school and others derived from this noble verse several issues of jurisprudence:

The first issue: the permissibility and validity of agency (wakalah). This is because their statement: ﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours﴾, up to the end of the verse, indicates that they appointed this one who was sent as their agent to buy food. Some scholars said: the verse does not indicate the permissibility of agency absolutely, but only in cases of dissimulation (taqiyyah) and fear, because if they had all gone out to buy their needs, their enemies would have known about them, in their assumption, and so they were excused. Thus the verse indicates the appointment of an excused person and not others. To this view Abu Hanifah went, and it is also the opinion of Sahnun from the companions of Malik regarding agency for litigation.

Ibn al-Arabi said: It seems that Sahnun took it from Asad ibn al-Furat and ruled by it during his judgeship, and perhaps he did so for people of injustice and tyranny, to deal justly with them and to humiliate them, and this is the truth, for agency is a form of assistance, and it is not for the people of falsehood. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: The words of Ibn al-Arabi are good. As for people of religion and virtue, they may appoint agents even if they are present and healthy. The evidence for the validity of agency for a healthy present person is what the two Sahihs and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "A man had a claim against the Prophet ﷺ for a young camel, so he came demanding it. He said: 'Give him [one].' They sought its equal but found only one above it in age. He said: 'Give him [that].' The man said: 'You have fulfilled [the debt] for me; may Allah fulfill [His favor] for you.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The best of you are those who are best in repaying.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari.

This hadith, along with its authenticity, indicates the permissibility of appointing an agent who is present and physically healthy, for the Prophet ﷺ ordered his companions to give on his behalf the young camel that was owed, and that is an appointment by him of them for that. The Prophet ﷺ was neither sick nor traveling. This refutes the view of Abu Hanifah and Sahnun in their saying that it is not permissible to appoint a present, healthy person except with the consent of his opponent. This hadith contradicts their view. End of al-Qurtubi's words.

And what is in it is not hidden; for Abu Hanifah and Sahnun only differed concerning agency for litigation without the permission of the opponent, and they did not differ concerning agency in the handing over of a right.

On this occasion, we will mention, if Allah wills, the evidences from the Book and the Sunnah for the validity and permissibility of agency, and some of the issues in need of it, as a reminder of other matters.

Know first that the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus all indicate the permissibility and validity of agency in general. From the verses that indicate this is His statement here: ﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours﴾, and His statement: ﴿and those who work on it [zakah]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60], for their working on it is an appointment of them to collect it.

Some scholars also took as evidence His saying: ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face﴾ [Yusuf: 93], for it is an appointment by Yusuf of them to cast his shirt over his father's face so that he would regain his sight.

Some also took as evidence His saying concerning Yusuf: ﴿Make me in charge of the storehouses of the land﴾ [Yusuf: 55], for it is an appointment over what is in the storehouses of the land.

As for the Sunnah, many hadiths indicate the permissibility and validity of agency. Among them is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier in al-Qurtubi's words, which indicates appointing an agent for repaying a debt, and it is a hadith agreed upon. The group (of compilers) except al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Rafi' from the Prophet ﷺ something similar.

Among them is the hadith of "Urwah ibn Abi al-Ja'd al-Bariqi: that the Prophet ﷺ gave him a dinar to buy a sheep for him. He bought two sheep with it, then sold one for a dinar and brought him a dinar and a sheep, and he prayed for him for blessing in his trade." It was such that had he bought dust, he would have profited from it. Narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni. In it is the appointment of an agent for buying.

Among them is the hadith of "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I wished to go out to Khaybar, so I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'I wish to go out to Khaybar.' He said: 'When you come to my agent, take from him fifteen wasqs; if he asks you for a sign, place your hand on his collarbone.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni. In it is the explicit statement from him ﷺ that he had an agent.

Among them is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the authentic hadith: "And go out in the morning, O Unays, to this woman's [husband]; if she confesses, stone her." This is explicit in the appointment of an agent for carrying out the prescribed punishments.

Among them is the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded me to look after his camels, to give away their meat, skins and saddlecloths in charity, and not to give the butcher anything from them, and he said: 'We will give him from our own.'" Agreed upon. In it is the appointment of an agent for supervising the camels, giving away their meat, skins and saddlecloths in charity, and not giving the butcher anything from them.

Among them is the hadith of "Uqbah ibn 'Amir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ gave him sheep to distribute among his companions, and one young goat remained, so he mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: 'Sacrifice it yourself.'" Also agreed upon. In it is agency in distributing sacrificial animals. Hadiths of this kind are numerous, and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated in their Sahihs a sufficient portion of them, and we have mentioned some of them here.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in the Book of Agency, the following text: The Book of Agency (meaning in Sahih al-Bukhari) contains twenty-six hadiths; of them six are mu'allaq (suspended), and the rest are mawsul (connected). The repeated ones among them, both here and in what preceded, are twelve hadiths, and the rest are unrepeated. Muslim agreed with him in narrating them, except the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf about the killing of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik concerning the slaughtered sheep, the hadith of the delegation of Hawazin from both its routes, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning guarding the zakah of Ramadan, and the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn al-Harith concerning the story of al-Nu'aymān; and in it there are six narrations from the Companions and others. And Allah knows best. End of quote from Fath al-Bari. All these hadiths indicate the permissibility and validity of agency.

As for consensus, the Muslims have agreed on the permissibility and validity of agency in general. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: The Ummah has agreed on the permissibility of agency in general, and because need calls for it, for it is not possible for everyone to do everything they need, so need calls for it. End of quote from him. This is among matters on which there is no dispute.

Branches related to the issue of agency:

The first branch: agency is not permissible except in a matter in which representation is valid. Thus it is not valid in performing a forbidden act, because agency is a form of cooperation, and Allah says: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2].

Nor is it valid in pure acts of worship such as prayer, fasting and the like, because these are required of each person individually, so no one may stand in for another in them, for Allah says: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

As for performing Hajj on behalf of the deceased or the incapacitated, and fasting on behalf of the deceased, other evidences indicate representation in these matters, although many scholars disagreed concerning fasting on behalf of the deceased, because what matters is the sound evidence from revelation and not the opinions of scholars, except where there is no text from revelation.

The second branch: agency is permissible in demanding rights, establishing them and litigating over them, whether the principal is present or absent, healthy or sick. This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and others. Abu Hanifah said: the opponent may refuse to be litigated against through an agent if the principal is present and not excused, because his attendance at the session of judgment and his facing his opponent is a right of his opponent over him, so it is not permissible for him to transfer it to another without the consent of his opponent. We have already mentioned in al-Qurtubi's words that this is also the view of Sahnun from the companions of Malik. The majority argued from the apparent texts, because litigation is a matter in which there is no barrier to delegation.

The author, may Allah forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah knows best, regarding the issue of agency for litigation and adjudication, is that the correct position is a distinction. If the principal is one known for injustice, tyranny and pursuing falsehood, then agency from him is not accepted, based on the apparent saying of Allah: ﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa': 105]. If he is known for other than that, then there is no barrier to appointing an agent for litigation. And Allah knows best.

The third branch: agency is permissible both for a fee and without a fee. The evidence for agency without a fee is that he ﷺ appointed Unays to carry out the prescribed punishment on the woman, and 'Urwah al-Bariqi to buy the sheep without a fee. Many examples of this occur in the hadiths we have mentioned and others.

The evidence for agency with a fee is His saying: ﴿and those who work on it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60], for it is an appointment to collect zakah and distribute it, with a fee from it, as you see.

**The fourth issue:** If the principal dismisses his agent in his absence, and the agent acts after the dismissal but before learning of it, or if the principal dies and the agent acts after his death but before learning of it, is his action valid because of his belief, or is it not valid because of the reality of the matter? On this there is a well-known disagreement among the scholars, which is based on a principle of usul al-fiqh (the foundations of jurisprudence). It is: does a ruling take effect merely by reaching people, even if it has not reached the one who is obligated, or does it take effect only after it reaches the one who is obligated? The disagreement over this principle yields the disagreement over the forty-five prayers that were abrogated from the fifty after they had been prescribed on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey), namely whether that is called abrogation with regard to the Ummah because the ruling reached them, or whether it is not called abrogation with regard to them, because it occurred before the abrogated obligation had reached them. Al-Shanqiti refers to this question in Maraqi al-Su'ud (the poem of Ibn al-Hajib-style principles by al-Sharqawi's tradition) with his verse:

"Does a ruling take effect by its mere arrival,
or only when it reaches what exists?"

"So dismissal by death, or dismissal that occurs,
likewise the judgment of one ignorant of an obligation."

The rules of agency (wakala, the appointment of an agent) are well known and detailed in the books of the furu' (positive rulings) of the four schools. Our aim here is to mention the evidence for its establishment from the Book, the Sunnah and consensus, and to mention examples of its branches as a pointer to others, since it is a major chapter of jurisprudence.

**The second issue:** Some scholars of the Maliki school took from this noble verse the permissibility of partnership (shirka), because they were partners in the silver (al-warq) they sent to buy food with it.

Ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki said: There is no proof in this verse for partnership, since it is possible that each of them sent with him his own share separately, to buy his food separately. What Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned is, as you see, sound. Other evidences have indicated the permissibility of partnership, and we will mention, God willing, on this occasion, the evidences for that, some of its rulings that are needed, and the sayings of the scholars on it.

Know first that partnership is permissible in general by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims.

As for the Book, several verses indicate this in general:

- The saying of God Most High: ﴿But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third﴾ [an-Nisa 4:12].
- The saying of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, many of the partners (al-khulata') oppress one another﴾ [Sad 38:24], according to those who say that al-khulata' means the partners.
- The saying of God Most High: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for God﴾ [al-Anfal 8:41], the verse.

These indicate partnership in two respects.

As for the Sunnah, many hadiths indicate the permissibility of partnership. We will mention here, God willing, a portion of them. Among them is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever frees his share in a slave, and he has wealth that reaches the price of the slave, the slave is valued at a fair price, and he gives his partners their shares; otherwise, what he freed alone is freed." A similar hadith is established in the Sahih from Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ, and in it is an explicit statement from him ﷺ about partnership in slaves. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, in his Sahih, titled the hadiths of Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah mentioned with his saying: "Chapter: Partnership in slaves."

Among them is what Imam Ahmad and al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on them both, narrated: "From Abu al-Minhal, who said: I and a partner of mine bought something, hand to hand and on credit. Then al-Bara' ibn 'Azib came to us and we asked him, and he said: I and my partner Zayd ibn Arqam did the same, and we asked the Prophet ﷺ about that, and he said: 'What was hand to hand, take it; and what was on credit, leave it.'" In it is his ﷺ approval of al-Bara' and Zayd, mentioned, for that partnership. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, titled this hadith in the Book of Partnership with his saying: "Chapter: Partnership in gold and silver, and what involves exchange (al-sarf)."

Among them is his ﷺ giving the land of Khaybar to the Jews to work and cultivate it, on condition that they have half of what comes out of it, which is partnership in the produce that comes from it. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, titled this hadith in the Book of Partnership with his saying: "Chapter: Partnering with the protected people (dhimmis) and polytheists in sharecropping (al-muzara'a)."

Among them is what Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him: "That the Prophet ﷺ decided on pre-emption (al-shufa'a) in everything that has not been divided. When the boundaries are set and the roads are distinguished, there is no pre-emption." Al-Bukhari titled this hadith in the Book of Partnership with his saying: "Chapter: Partnership in lands and other things." Then he narrated the hadith through another chain, and he also titled it with his saying: "Chapter: When partners divide the houses and other things, they have no right of return or pre-emption."

Among them is what Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayrah, raised (marfu'): "God says: 'I am the third of two partners as long as one of them does not betray the other. If one betrays the other, I depart from between them.'" The scholar al-Shawkani, may Allah Most High have mercy on him, said in Nayl al-Awtar regarding this hadith: al-Hakim authenticated it, and Ibn al-Qattan declared it defective (a'allahu) due to ignorance of the state of Sa'id ibn Hayyan. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and Ibn al-Qattan also declared it defective on the basis of irsal (a break in the chain), not mentioning Abu Hurayrah in it, and said that this is the correct version. Only Abu Hammam Muhammad ibn al-Zibriqan narrated it with a chain, and Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi remained silent about this hadith. Abu al-Qasim al-Asbahani narrated something similar in al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib from Hakim ibn Hizam. End of his words.

It is well known about Abu Dawud, may Allah have mercy on him, that he does not remain silent about discussing a hadith unless he believes it is fit to be used as evidence. The chain by which Abu Dawud narrated it apparently shows that it is suitable for use as evidence, for he said: "Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Misisi narrated to us: Muhammad ibn al-Zibriqan narrated to us from Abu Hayyan al-Taymi, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah have mercy on him, raising it, who said: 'God says: "I am the third of two partners."'" until the end of the hadith.

So the first tier of this chain is Muhammad ibn Sulayman, who is Abu Ja'far al-'Allaf al-Kufi, then al-Misisi; his epithet is "Luwayn" (diminutive), and he is trustworthy (thiqa).

The second tier is Muhammad ibn al-Zibriqan, Abu Hammam al-Ahwazi, who is among the narrators of the two Sahihs, and Ibn Hajar said in al-Taqrib: truthful, but he sometimes erred.

The third tier is Abu Hayyan al-Taymi, who is Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn Hayyan al-Kufi, and he is trustworthy.

The fourth tier is his father, Sa'id ibn Hayyan, mentioned above in al-Shawkani's words, that Ibn al-Qattan declared this hadith defective on the basis that he is unknown (majhul). This was answered by the fact that Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and Ibn Hajar said (in al-Taqrib) that al-'Ijli also deemed him trustworthy.

The fifth tier is Abu Hurayrah, who raised it.

This is, as you see, a fit chain. The claim that the hadith is defective because it was narrated as mawquf (stopping at a companion) from another route can be answered: the raising (rafa') is an addition, and the addition of trustworthy narrators is accepted, as established in usul and the sciences of hadith. It is supported by the fact that it came through another route from Hakim ibn Hizam, as we mentioned in al-Shawkani's words above.

Among them is the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Abi al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You were my partner in the Jahiliyyah, and you were the best of partners; you did not deceive me nor dispute with me." Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated it, and its wording is: "You were my partner and the best of partners; you did not deceive nor dispute." Al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim also narrated it and authenticated it. In it is the Prophet's ﷺ affirmation that he was a partner of his. The hadiths indicating partnership are very many.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari at the end of the Book of Partnership, the following text: The Book of Partnership (meaning from Sahih al-Bukhari) includes twenty-seven raised hadiths: one of them is mu'allaq (suspended), and the rest are mawsul (connected). Those repeated in it and in what came before are thirteen hadiths, and the unique ones are fourteen. Muslim agreed with him in narrating them, except the hadith of al-Nu'man: "The likeness of one who stands over the limits of God," and the two hadiths of 'Abd Allah ibn Hisham, and the two hadiths of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr in his story, and the last hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In it there is one athar (report from a companion). And God knows best. End of Ibn Hajar's words. From this you know the abundance of hadiths indicating partnership in general.

As for consensus, all the scholars of the Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of several types of partnerships, and the disagreement among them is only about some of their types.

Know first that partnership is of two kinds: partnership in ownership (shirkat al-amlak), and partnership by contract (shirkat al-'uqud).

Partnership in ownership is that two or more persons own a thing by inheritance, purchase, gift, or the like. It is what is known among the Malikis as the general partnership (al-shirka al-a'ammiyya).

Partnership by contract is divided into: partnership of mufawada (full delegation), partnership of 'inan, partnership of wujuh (partnership based on credit), partnership of abdan (labor partnership), and partnership of mudaraba (profit-sharing). These types may overlap, so some of them combine with others.

As for partnership in ownership, the Noble Qur'an brought it in the saying of God Most High: ﴿But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third﴾ [an-Nisa 4:12], and there is no disagreement about it among the scholars.

As for the types of partnership by contract, we will mention here, God willing, their meanings and the scholars' statements about them, and examples of what is permissible among them as a pointer to others, and the evidences that have come about them.

Know that the partnership of mufawada is derived from tafwid (delegation), because each of the two partners delegates to the other the matter of disposing of the partnership's wealth. From this is the saying of God Most High, about the believer of Pharaoh's family: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir 40:44], the verse.

It was also said: its origin is from equality (musawa), because the two partners are equal in disposal and liability. On this view, it is from fawda (disorder) meaning equality. From it is the saying of al-Afwah al-Awdi:

"People do not prosper in disorder, having no nobles,
nor are they nobles when their ignorant ones rule."

"When the nobles of people take charge of their affair,
the affair of the folk grows and they prosper."

His saying "people do not prosper in disorder" means their affairs do not prosper while they are in a state of disorder, that is, equal, with no nobles who command and forbid them. The first view is correct, and this is its origin in the language.

As for the partnership of 'inan, its linguistic derivation has been disputed. It was said: its origin is from 'anna al-amr ya'inn, with the vowel i or u, 'annan and 'unununan, meaning when a matter presents itself. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"A herd appeared to us, as if its ewes
were virgins wandering in a trailing veil."

Ibn Manzur said in al-Lisan: Shirk al-'inan and shirkat al-'inan: a partnership in a specific thing, to the exclusion of the rest of their property, as if something presented itself to them, so they bought it and partnered in it. He cited for this the saying of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

"So we shared with Quraysh in their piety,
and in their noble lineage, a partnership of 'inan,
with what the women of Bani Hilal bore,
and what the women of Bani Aban bore."

From this you know that the partnership of 'inan is well known in the speech of the Arabs. As for the statement of Ibn al-Qasim, one of the companions of Malik, that he does not know the partnership of 'inan from Malik, and that he did not see anyone of the people of the Hijaz who knew it, and that it is narrated from Malik and al-Shafi'i that they did not apply this name to this partnership, and that they said: it is a word that the people of Kufa adopted so they could distinguish between the general and the specific partnership, without its being used in the speech of the Arabs, all of this is open to scrutiny, since you have learned that it is established from them.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says:

Know that the intent of al-Nabigha in his two verses mentioned is: "with what the women of Bani Hilal bore," the son of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah; among them are Lubaba al-Kubra and Lubaba al-Sughra, who are two sisters, daughters of al-Harith ibn Hazn ibn Bujayr ibn al-Hazm ibn Ruwayba ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Hilal, and they are the sisters of Maymuna bint al-Harith, wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on Surah 18, verse 19 (part 3 of 6):**

As for Lubaba al-Kubra, she was the wife of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him), and the mother of his sons 'Abd Allah, 'Ubayd Allah and al-Fadl, and by him she was known by her kunya (teknonym). About her the reciter (al-rajiz) says:

*"No noble mare has borne from a stallion the like of six from the womb of Umm al-Fadl."*

As for Lubaba al-Sughra, she is the mother of Khalid ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him). Their paternal aunt Safiyya bint Hazn was the mother of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. This is what he means by:

*"With what the women of Banu Hilal bore."*

As for the women of Banu Aban, he means that Abu al-'As, al-'As, Abu al-'Is and al-'Is, the sons of Umayya ibn 'Abd Shams, their mother was Aminah bint Aban ibn Kulayb ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'a. So these mixed kinship ties between the 'Amiriyyin and Quraysh are what al-Nabigha means by their sharing with them in lineage and piety, *shirk al-'inan* (a limited partnership).

It is also said that *shirkat al-'inan* derives from *'inan al-faras* (the bridle of a horse), as will be explained, if Allah wills, and this is the well-known view among the scholars.

It is also said that it derives from *al-mu'anah*, meaning opposition. It is said: *'anantuhu* (I opposed him) when I opposed him with the like of his wealth or his actions. Thus each of the two partners opposes the other with his wealth and his actions.

It is pronounced with a kasra on the 'ayn according to the correct view, contrary to those who claim it is with a fatha. This is reported from 'Iyad and others. The claim that its origin is from *'anan al-sama'* (the clouds of the sky) is very far-fetched, as you can see.

(p-337) As for *shirkat al-wujuh* (partnership of reputation), its origin is from *al-wijaha* (high standing), because the man of standing has his liability pursued for debts, and when he sells something he sells it for more than the obscure man sells it for.

As for *shirkat al-abdan* (partnership of labour), its linguistic origin is clear, because the two share by the work of their bodies. For this reason it is called *shirkat al-'amal* (partnership of work), since the partnership in it is not in wealth but in the labour of the body.

As for *shirkat al-mudaraba*, which is *al-qirad* (profit-sharing), its origin is from *al-darb fi al-ard* (striking in the earth), because the merchant travels in pursuit of profit, and travel is referred to by *al-darb fi al-ard*, as in His saying: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His saying: ﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ [an-Nisa': 101].

Having learned the linguistic meanings of the types of partnership, we will now mention, if Allah the Exalted wills, their meanings as technical terms (*istilah*) as intended by the four Imams and their companions, and their rulings, since they differ regarding what is meant by them as technical terms and regarding some of their rulings.

As for the position of Malik regarding the types of partnership and their rulings, here is its detail:

Know that *shirkat al-mufawada* (full partnership) is permissible according to Malik and his companions. What is meant by *shirkat al-mufawada* according to them is that each of the two gives the other unrestricted authority to dispose of the wealth in which they have partnered, whether in his absence or presence, in sale and purchase, in guaranteeing, in appointing an agent, in surety, and in profit-sharing. Whatever one of them does of that is binding on his companion if it is for the benefit of their partnership.

They are not partners except in what they contract the partnership upon from their wealth, not in what each of them individually owns from his property. It is the same whether they partner in all that they own or in some of their property. The hand of each of them is as the hand of his companion, and his disposal is as his disposal, so long as he does not give away anything that is not in the interest of the partnership.

It is the same whether the full partnership between them covers all types of trade or only one type of it, such as slaves, in which they fully partner for trade only. Each of them may sell on credit and buy on credit, and that binds his companion. This is the correct view, contrary to Khalil in his *Mukhtasar* regarding buying on credit.

Khalil, in his *Mukhtasar*, has indicated the permissibility of the full partnership in the school of Malik, together with its definition and the rulings that its contract entails regarding the two partners, in his saying: *"Then if they both allow unrestricted disposal, even if in one type, it is a full partnership. The independent action of one of them in something does not spoil it. He may give a gift if it wins him goodwill or is light, such as lending a tool or giving a small piece (of food), and he may entrust capital (*yubdi'*), lend it on *qirad* (*yuqarid*), and deposit it (*yuwdi'*) for a valid excuse; otherwise he is liable. He may partner in a specific thing, accept and appoint (an agent), and accept a defective item even if the other refuses, and he may acknowledge a debt to one who is not suspected of it, and he may sell on credit but not buy on credit, such as writing a contract of manumission (*kitaba*) or freeing (a slave) for property, or permitting a slave to trade, and full partnership."* He has already stated that buying on credit is like selling on credit, so one partner may do it without the permission of his partner, according to the correct view of Malik's school, contrary to Khalil. As for *kitaba*, manumission for property, and what is attached to them, none of it is permitted except with the permission of the partner.

Know that this *shirkat al-mufawada* in the school of Malik does not include any of the types of uncertainty (*gharar*) for which the full partnership was prohibited according to the Shafi'is and those who agree with them. This is because what one of the two full partners acquires by another route, such as a gift or inheritance, or by permissible acquisition, such as hunting, gathering wood, and the like, does not belong to his partner in any part. Likewise, what he is liable to pay outside the partnership, such as compensation for a crime, the price of something usurped, and the like, is not a burden on his partner. Rather, all that is between them is limited to what relates to the partnership's wealth. Each of them is an agent for the other and a guarantor for him in everything that relates to the partnership's wealth, and this is what the contract they agreed upon requires. So there is no reason for prohibition and no uncertainty in this partnership according to the Malikis, because they do not make the two full partners partners in everything they both acquire, so that uncertainty would arise from that, nor joint guarantors for everything they both commit, so that uncertainty would arise from that. Rather, it is a contract by which each of them acts on behalf of the other in all dispositions of the partnership's wealth and guarantees everything that relates to the partnership. This is not objectionable, as you see. By this you know that the disagreement of the Malikis and Shafi'is regarding the full partnership is a disagreement about a particular case, not about the reality of the matter.

As for *shirkat al-'inan* (limited partnership), it is permissible according to the four Imams, although they differ in its interpretation. In the school of Malik there are two views about its meaning, and it is permissible according to both views.

The first, which is the well-known one, is that it is the partnership in which each of the two partners stipulates to the other that he will not dispose of the partnership's wealth except in his presence and with his agreement. On this view Khalil proceeded in his *Mukhtasar* with his saying: *"If they stipulate the negation of independent action, it is 'inan."* On this view it is derived from *'inan al-faras*, because the rein of each of the two partners is in the hand of the other, so he cannot act independently of him in any work, like a horse whose rider holds its rein, and it cannot go in any direction without his consent.

The second view among the Malikis is that *shirkat al-'inan* is partnership in a specific thing. This was affirmed by Ibn Rushd, and al-Mawwaq transmitted it in his commentary on Khalil's saying: *"If they stipulate the negation of independent action..."* etc. This latter meaning is closer to what is known in the language, as we have already quoted from Ibn Manzur in *al-Lisan*.

As for *shirkat al-wujuh* (partnership of reputation), it has several meanings among the scholars:

(p-339) The first of them is that two men of standing among the people partner without wealth or craft, but each of them buys on credit in his own name for both of them together. When they sell, the surplus profit over the prices is shared between them.

This type of *shirkat al-wujuh* is known among the Malikis as *shirkat al-dhimam* (partnership of liabilities). It is invalid according to the Malikis and the Shafi'is, contrary to the Hanafis and the Hanbalis. The reason for its invalidity is clear, because it involves uncertainty, since one of them may lose while the other gains, or vice versa. Ibn 'Asim the Maliki alluded to the invalidity of this type of partnership in his *Tuhfa* with his saying:

*"Its annulment if it occurs over liabilities, and dividing the profit is a binding ruling."*

The second meaning of it is that a man of standing sells the property of an obscure man at an increased profit, on condition that he has a share of the profit that was obtained on the sale because of his standing, since the obscure man, had he been the seller himself, would not have obtained that profit. This type too is invalid, because it is a return for standing (*jah*), as stated by more than one of the people of knowledge.

The third meaning is that a man of standing and an obscure man agree that the man of standing buys on credit and the obscure man sells, and the profit is shared between them. This type is also invalid according to the Malikis and the Shafi'is, for the uncertainty we have mentioned previously.

As for *shirkat al-abdan* according to the Malikis, it is permissible under conditions: that the work of the two partners be uniform, such as two tailors, or interlinked, such as one spinning and the other weaving, because weaving necessarily requires spinning; that they be equal in the work in quality, inferiority, slowness and speed, or be close to one another in that; and that cooperation occur between them. Khalil, in his *Mukhtasar*, alluded to the permissibility of this type of partnership with its conditions in his saying:

*"It is permissible in work if it is uniform or interlinked, and they are equal in it, or close to one another and cooperation occurs, even if they are in two places. And regarding the permissibility of each one bringing his own tool and hiring it from the other, or whether ownership or rental is required, there are two interpretations, like two physicians who partner in medicine, and two hunters in hunting with falcons, [and whether if they separate, what they hunt is shared between them, and two diggers for buried treasure (*rikaz*) and a mine, and his heir does not receive the remainder, and the ruler grants it as a fief, and this is restricted to what has not yet appeared, and he is bound by what his partner accepts even if they separate, and illness is disregarded like two days, etc.]."*

By this you know that *shirkat al-abdan* is permissible according to the Malikis in all types of work: crafts of every kind, medicine, and permissible acquisition such as hunting, cutting grass, gathering wood, and other things, under the conditions mentioned. Ibn 'Asim said in his *Tuhfa*:

*"A partnership in wealth, or in work, or in both, is permissible, not for a fixed term."*

(p-340) There remains a type known among the Malikis as one of the types of partnership, which is called in the technical terminology *shirkat al-jabr* (compulsory partnership). Many scholars disagree with them about this type, which is *shirkat al-jabr*.

*Shirkat al-jabr* is this: a person buys a commodity at its customary market, in order to trade in it in the presence of some merchants of that commodity's kind who deal in it, and those merchants present do not speak. If those merchants wish to partner in that commodity with that buyer, they have the right to compel him to do so, and they become his partners in that commodity, whether he likes it or not.

Their partnership with him, compelled upon him, is the *shirkat al-jabr* mentioned. If he bought it to keep for himself and not to trade in, or bought it to travel with to another place, even if to trade there, then they have no right to compel him. Khalil, in his *Mukhtasar*, alluded to *shirkat al-jabr* in his saying: *"He is compelled to it if he buys something at its market, not for keeping or for personal use, while another, a merchant of its kind, is present and did not speak; and whether this applies in the alley but not in his house, there are two views."*

As for *shirkat al-mudaraba*, it is *al-qirad*, which is that one person gives another wealth to trade with, in exchange for a share of its profit that they agree upon. This type is permissible by consensus when it fulfils its conditions, as its evidence will come, if Allah wills.

As for the types of partnership in the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, they are four. Three of them are invalid according to his school, and the fourth is valid.

As for the three invalid ones, the first of them is *shirkat al-abdan*, like the partnership of porters and all craftsmen: tailors, carpenters, brokers, and the like, so that their earnings between them are equal or unequal, whether the craft is the same or different.

The same craft, like two tailors, and different crafts, like a tailor and a carpenter and the like, all of this is invalid according to the school of al-Shafi'i. For him, partnership is not valid except with wealth alone, not with work.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 19 (part 4 of 6):

The reason for the invalidity of the partnership of bodies (shirkat al-abdan) according to the Shafi'is is that it is a partnership in which there is no capital, and that it contains gharar (uncertainty); because each of the two does not know whether his partner will earn anything or not. Also, because each of them is distinct with his own body and his own benefits, so he alone benefits from its returns, just as if the two had partnered in their livestock while it remains distinct, on the condition that the offspring and the milk are shared between them, and (that they partner) in gathering firewood and hunting. This is the Shafi'i reasoning for prohibiting this type of partnership.

You have already learned, in what passed, the conditions for the permissibility of this type according to the Malikis, since with the availability of the mentioned conditions (p-241) the gharar is eliminated.

The second of the invalid types according to the Shafi'is is the comprehensive partnership (shirkat al-mufawada). According to them, it is that the two partner on the basis that all of their earnings, with their wealth and their bodies, will be shared between them, and that all the liabilities that befall each of them, whether from usurpation, destruction, a corrupt sale, or otherwise, will be borne by both of them. There is no doubt that this type includes various kinds of gharar, so its invalidity is clear. It is prohibited according to the Malikis, who do not permit this and do not designate it by the name "shirkat al-mufawada," as we have mentioned.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding this type: "If the comprehensive partnership is not invalid, then I know of no invalid (contract) in this world." He points to the abundance of gharar and uncertainties in it, because it is possible that each of them earns earnings that the other does not, and that each of them incurs liabilities that the other does not. Thus the gharar is very evident in this type.

The third of the invalid types according to the Shafi'is is "shirkat al-wujuh" (partnership of reputation), which according to them is that two men of standing buy on credit, each of them buying on deferred payment in his own name, for both of them together. When they sell, the surplus of the prices is shared between them. This type is known among the Malikis as "shirkat al-dhimam" (partnership of liabilities). Its corruption is clear, because of the gharar in it; since each of them buys in his own name and each gives the other a share of the profit of what he bought in his own name, in exchange for a share of the profit of what the other bought in his own name. Gharar in such a case is very evident. The rest of the kinds of "shirkat al-wujuh" have been mentioned in our discussion of them in the Maliki school, and all of them are prohibited in the Maliki and Shafi'i schools. For this reason we have been content with what we previously mentioned about the rest of their types in the Shafi'i school.

As for the fourth type of partnership, which is valid according to the Shafi'is, it is "shirkat al-inan" (partnership of joint capital), which is: that the two partner in property they own in order to trade with it. According to them, it requires a formula indicating permission to dispose of the partnership's property; so if the two merely use the word "we have partnered," it does not suffice, according to the more correct view among them.

It is required of the two partners that they have the capacity to appoint an agent and to act as an agent, and this condition is agreed upon. According to the Shafi'is, "shirkat al-inan" is valid in fungibles (mithliyyat) absolutely, but not in non-fungible goods (muqawwamat). It has been said that it is restricted to minted currency.

According to them, it is required that the two properties be mixed, such that neither can be distinguished from the other. The device (hilah) according to them for partnership in merchandise (al-'urud) is that each of them sells part of his goods for part of the other's goods (p-241) and authorizes him to dispose of them. According to them, it is not required that the two properties be equal, and the profit and loss are according to the amount of each property, whether they are equal in labor or differ. If they stipulate otherwise, the contract is invalid, and each of them returns to the other for the wage of his work on his property.

The aforementioned partnership contract empowers each of the two to dispose of the partnership's property without harm: so he does not sell on credit, nor at a gross loss, nor entrust it to another without his partner's permission. Each of them may dissolve it whenever he wishes.

As for the detailed classification of partnership types in the school of Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him: partnership is divided into two kinds:
Partnership of ownership (shirkat al-milk) and partnership of contract (shirkat al-'aqd).

Partnership of ownership is clear, such as when two people come to own something by inheritance, gift, or the like, as previously mentioned. Partnership of contract, according to them, is divided into three categories:
Partnership in capital, partnership in labor, and partnership in reputation (wujuh). Each of these three categories, according to them, is divided into two: comprehensive (mufawada) and inan. So the total is six types.

As for the comprehensive partnership according to them, it is permissible if its conditions are met. It is, according to them, the partnership that includes the agency (wakala) of each of the two partners for the other, and the surety (kafala) of each of them for the other. Equality between the two partners in property, religion, and disposal is essential.

By its inclusion of agency, each one's disposal of the other's share is valid.
By its inclusion of surety, each of them may claim from others what is owed to the other.
By the equality of their property, neither may independently take something in which the partnership is valid, to the exclusion of the other. Therefore, if after the contract one of them inherits something in which partnership is valid, such as currency, the comprehensive partnership is annulled and the partnership reverts to an inan partnership.
By its inclusion of equality in religion, it is prohibited between a Muslim and a disbeliever.
By its inclusion of equality in disposal, it is prohibited between an adult and a minor, and between a free person and a slave. Everything that one of the two comprehensive partners buys is shared between them, except the food and clothing of his household. Every debt that befalls one of them through trade, usurpation, or surety falls upon the other.

(p-243) According to them, a comprehensive or inan partnership is not valid except in gold and silver, bullion, and currency in circulation. The device for partnership in merchandise according to them is what we mentioned earlier from the Shafi'is, so they agree on this.

As for inan partnership, it is permissible according to the Hanafis, and we have previously mentioned the consensus on its permissibility under all the meanings intended by the scholars.

Inan partnership according to the Hanafis is the partnership that includes agency alone and does not include surety. It is: that the two partner in a kind of cloth, or food, or in general trade, without mentioning surety.

From this it is known that whatever one of them buys is shared between them, and the liabilities borne by one do not fall upon the other. According to them, the aforementioned inan partnership is valid with equality in property but not in profit, and the reverse is also valid, provided that the greater share of profit goes to the one who does more work; because the increase in profit corresponds to the increase in labor, in agreement with the Hanbalis. According to others, profit must be in proportion to capital. If one of the two partners buys (goods) on credit for the partnership at a price, the seller has no right to demand payment from the other partner, because it does not include surety; rather he demands from the partner who bought from him only. However, the partner returns to his partner for his share. According to them, mixing the two properties is not required in this partnership; so if one of them buys with his own property and the other's property is destroyed, the purchase is shared between them, and he returns to his partner for his share of it.

According to them, this partnership is annulled by the destruction of both properties or of one of them before the purchase. It is corrupted according to them by stipulating a fixed sum of dirhams of the profit for one of them. According to them, each of the two partners in a comprehensive or inan partnership may entrust goods to another for trade (bid'ah), hire, deposit, invest on a profit-sharing basis (mudaraba), and appoint an agent. The hand of each of them over the partnership's property is a hand of trust, like a deposit or a loan (ariya).

As for partnership in labor (shirkat al-a'mal), there is a distinction according to the Hanafis. If the work is among crafts and the like, partnership in labor is permitted according to them, and they do not require that the work be unified or that it be inseparable, in contrast to the Malikis as previously mentioned. Thus it is permitted according to the Hanafis for two tailors, for example, or a tailor and a dyer, to partner on the basis that they undertake jobs and the earnings are shared between them; and every job one of them undertakes binds both of them. If one of them works without the other, then what he earns from his work is shared between them, and the one who did not work is entitled to it only because he guaranteed it by his partner's undertaking it, so he is entitled to his share of it by the guarantee.

This type which the Hanafis permitted is not free of gharar in general when the crafts of the two partners differ, since one of them may earn more than the other. Thus the conditions by which the Malikis permitted "shirkat al-a'mal" are more cautious and further from gharar, as you see.

(p-244) As for work that is of the nature of acquiring permissible resources (mubahat), then partnership in it is not valid according to the Hanafis, such as gathering firewood, cutting grass, hunting, and picking fruit from mountains and deserts, in contrast to the Malikis and the Hanbalis.

The reason for its prohibition according to the Hanafis is that whoever acquires something permissible, such as firewood, grass, or game, comes to own it independently; so there is no basis for part of it belonging to another partner, because agency is not valid in it. Those who permitted it said: each of them gave the other a share of that permissible thing which he acquires in exchange for the share which the other acquires. The Malikis who permit this require that the work be unified or closely similar, so there is no gharar in that and no reason for prohibition. Regarding the requirement of this among the Hanbalis there is a difference of opinion, as will come, Allah willing.

As for "shirkat al-wujuh," which we previously mentioned is known among the Malikis as "shirkat al-dhimam," and whose prohibition among the Malikis and Shafi'is we previously mentioned, it is permitted according to the Hanafis, whether it is comprehensive or inan. You have already learned from what passed that the comprehensive type according to them includes agency and surety, and that inan includes agency only. If the two partners in "shirkat al-wujuh" stipulate that the buyer's profit be split equally or in thirds, then the profit is so divided according to them, and the stipulation of an excess share is void according to them, because profit according to them is only earned by work, like the mudarib, or by capital, like the owner of capital, or by guarantee, like the master craftsman who undertakes work from people and assigns it to an apprentice at less than what he received, so the excess is lawful to him by guarantee. Thus they say, and the gharar in "shirkat al-wujuh" is not hidden.
