*"And a speaker said, 'I have wronged you by striking my waterskin for you,' and does the wrongdoer remain hidden from the one who knows?"*

So his saying "I have wronged you by my waterskin" means: I struck it for you before it churned. From it is also the saying of another about a waterskin of his that he wronged in a similar manner:

*"And a friend of sincerity whose complaint did not trouble me; I wronged him, and in my wronging him I am intentional, a grave error."*

In the riddle of al-Hariri in his Maqamat, about the one who strikes his milk before it churns, he said: "Can a judge be a wrongdoer?" He said: "Yes, if he is learned." From this also is their saying about land that was dug in, when it was not a place for digging previously: "a wronged land" (ardun mazlumah). From it is the saying of Nabighah Dhubyan:

*"Except the pits that I explain with difficulty, and the earthen dam is like a basin, against the land that is wronged and firm."*

What some have claimed, that "the wronged land" in the verse is the one that rain wronged by failing to reach it at its customary time, is not correct. The correct view is what we have mentioned, if Allah, exalted is He, wills. For this reason they call the earth that is brought out of a grave when it is dug zalim, meaning mazlum (wronged), because it has been dug in a place other than the customary place of digging. From it is the saying of the poet describing a man who died and was buried:

*"So he became in the dust after recoil, upon life a ... over which its zalim (wronged earth) is spread."*

His saying: ﴿Surrounded them﴾ means: encircled them from every side. His saying: ﴿its walls [surradiquha]﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. The origin of al-suradiq is the singular of the surradiqat, which are spread above the courtyard of a house. Every tent made of cotton is a surradiq. Al-kursuf is cotton. From it is the saying of Ru'bah or al-Kadhdhab al-Himmazi:

*"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud, the canopy of glory is extended over you."*

A "musardaq" house is one that has been given a surradiq. From it is the saying of Salamah ibn Jandal, mentioning Abarwiz and his killing of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir under the feet of elephants:

*"He is the one who brought al-Nu'man into a house whose roof is the chests of elephants, after a house that was canopied."*

This is the origin of the meaning of surradiq in the language. It is also used in the language for the chamber that is around the tent (fustat).

As for the intended meaning of surradiq in the noble verse, the scholars have several statements, all of which return to one thing: the Fire encircling them from every side. Among the scholars, some say "its surradiq" means its wall; this was said by Ibn al-A'rabi and others. Among them, some say "its surradiq" is a wall of fire, and this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Among them, some say "its surradiq" is a neck that comes out of the Fire and encircles the disbelievers like an enclosure; this was said by al-Kalbi. Among them, some say it is a smoke that surrounds them. This is what is mentioned in Surat al-Mursalat in His saying: ﴿Proceed to a shadow of three branches, neither shading nor averting the blaze﴾ [al-Mursalat: 30–31], and in Surat al-Waqi'ah in His saying: ﴿And a shade of black smoke, neither cool nor pleasant﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43–44].

Among them, some say: it is the sea that encircles the world. Ya'la ibn Umayyah reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The sea is Jahannam," then he recited: ﴿A Fire whose walls will enclose them﴾, then he said, "By Allah, I will never enter it as long as I live, and not a drop of it will touch me." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Mubarak reported from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The surradiq of the Fire has four walls, the thickness of each wall is forty years' journey." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi also narrated it, and said about it: "A hasan sahih gharib hadith." This is the end of what was quoted from al-Qurtubi. This hadith was also narrated by Imam Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim who declared it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya. So said the author of al-Durr al-Manthur, and al-Shawkani followed him. The hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayyah was also narrated by Ibn Jarir in his tafsir. Al-Shawkani said: It was narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih; and the author of al-Durr al-Manthur narrated it from al-Bukhari in his History, and from Ahmad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim who declared it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi. In any case, the meaning of the noble verse is that the Fire encircles them from every side, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them from Jahannam is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41], and He said: ﴿For them from above them are canopies of Fire, and beneath them are canopies﴾ [al-Zumar: 16], and He said: ﴿If only those who disbelieved would know the time when they will not be able to avert the Fire from their faces or from their backs, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Anbiya': 39], and other verses.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And if they call for relief﴾, means: if they seek relief from the distress they are in, they will be relieved; they will be given relief which is water like murky oil. Al-muhl in the language is applied to what has been melted from the substances of the earth, such as molten iron, copper, lead, and the like.

It is also applied to the dregs of oil, which is its sediment. The meaning of al-muhl in the verse is what has been melted from the substances of the earth. It was said: the dregs of oil. It was said: it is a kind of tar. It was said: poison.

If it is said: What relief is there in water like al-muhl, given that it is among the most severe punishments, and how did Allah say: ﴿They will be relieved with water like al-muhl﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]?

The answer is that this is one of the styles of the Arabic language in which the Qur'an was revealed. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

*"Tamim became angry that 'Amir was killed on the day of al-Nisar, so they were pleased with al-Saylam."*

The meaning of his saying "they were pleased with al-Saylam" is: they were satisfied with the sword. That is, there is no satisfaction for them from us except by the sword. And the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*"And cavalry I have advanced against with cavalry, whose greeting between them is a painful blow."*

The meaning is: there is no greeting for them except a painful blow. Since they are relieved only with water like al-muhl, it is known from this that there is no relief for them at all. The ya' in His saying "yastaghithu" (they seek relief) and the alif in His saying "yughathu" (they are relieved) are both substituted from a waw; because the root of al-istighathah is from the hollow verb with a waw middle radical. But the middle radical was altered because of the sound consonant preceding it, according to his statement in the Khulasah:

*"For a sound sakin, move the vowel from the weak letter, the 'ayn of the verb, as in 'abin."*

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿It scalds the faces﴾, meaning: it burns them until the skin of the face falls off. May Allah protect us and the Muslims from it. The Prophet ﷺ, in explaining this noble verse, said: "﴿Like al-muhl, it scalds the faces﴾; it is like the dregs of oil, and when it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off." Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *al-Kafi al-Shafi fi Takhrij Ahadith al-Kashshaf*: al-Tirmidhi narrated it through the chain of Rishdin ibn Sa'd, from 'Amr ibn al-Harith, from Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, and he regarded it as gharib and said: It is not known except from the hadith of Rishdin ibn Sa'd. His statement was criticized: Ahmad and Abu Ya'la narrated it through the route of Ibn Lahi'ah from Darraj, and Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim narrated it through the route of Wahb from 'Amr ibn al-Harith.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Wretched is the drink﴾, the object of the blame in it is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "Wretched is the drink, that water with which they are relieved." The pronoun of the subject in His saying "evil is" (saa'at) refers to the Fire.

Al-murtafaq is the place of reclining (irtifaq). Its origin is that a person reclines, leaning on his elbow. The scholars have several close statements regarding the meaning of al-murtafaq in the verse. It was said: murtafaqan means a dwelling place (manzilan); this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: a resting place (maqarran); this is reported from 'Ata'. It was said: a gathering place (majlisan); this is reported from al-Utbi. Mujahid said: murtafaqan means gathering (mujtama'an). So, according to him, it is the place of irtifaq in the sense of some of them accompanying others in the Fire.

The sum of the meanings of the statements is that the Fire is the wretched place of settlement, and the wretched place of standing. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and standing﴾ [al-Furqan: 66]. That the origin of irtifaq is reclining on the elbow is well known in the speech of the Arabs. From it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*"The one at ease slept, and I spent the night reclining, as if in my eyes is the bitter aloe, slaughtered."*

It is also narrated as "wa bittu al-layla mushtajiran" (and I spent the night in distress), and according to this there is no evidence in the verse. From it is the saying of A'sha Bahilah:

*"I have spent the night reclining, watching the star, bewildered, cautious, though caution would not benefit."*

And the saying of the rajiz (rhymed poet):

*"She said to him, and she reclined, 'Is there not a youth who drives the herd of the wild cows of the forenoon?'"*

This description that Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse, of the qualities of this drink with which the people of the Fire are given to drink, appears in similar form in many other verses, such as His saying: ﴿For them will be a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾ (Al-An'am 6:70); His saying: ﴿and they were given scalding water to drink, which cut up their bowels﴾ (Muhammad 47:15); His saying: ﴿They will be given to drink from a boiling spring﴾ (Al-Ghashiyah 88:5); and His saying: ﴿They will circulate between it and scalding water, intensely hot﴾ (Ar-Rahman 55:44). The *hamim al-ani* (intensely hot scalding water) is water that has reached the utmost degree of heat.

(p-271) And His saying: ﴿And he will be given to drink of purulent water, which he will gulp down but will hardly swallow﴾ (Ibrahim 14:16-17), up to the end of the verse; His saying: ﴿Then indeed for them over it is a mixture of scalding water﴾ (As-Saffat 37:67); and His saying: ﴿Then indeed you will drink upon it of scalding water, drinking like the thirsty camels﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah 56:54-55).

And His saying: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or any drink, except scalding water and *ghassaq* (a dark, intensely cold, or putrid liquid)﴾ (An-Naba' 78:24-25), up to the end of the verse; and His saying: ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and *ghassaq*, and other [punishments] of its kind in pairs﴾ (Sad 38:57-58), and beyond these from the verses. We have already presented several ways of explaining this in Surat "Yunus."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds – indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good in deeds.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that whoever does righteous deeds and does them well, He, majestic and exalted, does not let his reward be lost, i.e., the recompense of his deed. Rather, he is repaid for his good deed with the fullest recompense.

This meaning is explained in very many verses, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I do not let the work of any worker among you be lost, whether male or female"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They rejoice in a favour from Allah and a bounty, and that Allah does not allow the reward of the believers to be lost﴾ [Al 'Imran: 171], and His saying: ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 60]. The verses indicating this meaning are very numerous. Concerning this meaning there are two well-known questions among the scholars:

The first: It may be asked, where is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed) in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30]? If it is said that its predicate is the clause ﴿Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good in deeds﴾ [Al-Kahf: 30], the question is directed at this.

The second: It may be asked, where is the connecting pronoun (rabit) linking the predicative clause to the subject, which is the noun of "inna"?

Know that the predicate of "inna" in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ has been said to be the clause ﴿For them are Gardens of Eden﴾. According to this, His saying ﴿Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good in deeds﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya). On this view, the connecting element exists and there is no difficulty in it. It has also been said that the second "inna" with its noun and predicate, all of it, is the predicate of the first "inna". A parallel in the Qur'an for predicating about "inna" with "inna" and its predicate and noun is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with Allah – indeed, Allah will decide between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ to the end of the verse [Al-Hajj: 17], and the saying of the poet:

Indeed the Caliph, indeed Allah has clothed him with the garment of kingship, by which the final outcomes are hoped for.

This is according to the more apparent of the two views regarding the predicate of the first "inna" in the verse. On this basis, the answer to the second question (p-272) is in two ways:

The first: The connecting pronoun is omitted, its estimated form being: "We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good among them in deeds"; like the saying of the Arabs: "Ghee is two manas for a dirham", meaning: two manas of it for a dirham, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait with themselves [for] four months and ten days﴾ to the end of the verse [Al-Baqarah: 234], meaning: they shall wait after them.

The second way: "one who does good in deeds" refers to those who believe and do righteous deeds. When "those who believe" and "one who does good in deeds" carry one and the same meaning, that takes the place of the connection by pronoun. This is the view of al-Akhfash, and it is the correct one, because the connection is achieved through unity of meaning.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 31:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those—for them are Gardens of Eternity; beneath them rivers flow﴾

up to His saying: ﴿and how good a resting place﴾. In this noble verse, may He be glorified and exalted, He explains the reward of those who do good deeds. He mentions that they will have Gardens of Eternity beneath which rivers flow, and that they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and will wear green garments of fine silk (*sundus*) and brocade (*istabraq*), while reclining therein on couches (*arā'ik*), which are the thrones (*surur*) within the canopied beds (*hijal*). The *hijal* is the plural of *hajlah*, a chamber that is decorated for the bride with every kind of adornment. Then He praised their reward by saying: ﴿How excellent a reward, and how good a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]. What He has explained here regarding the attributes of the recompense of the good-doers, who believed and did righteous deeds, is explained in many other places in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Such as His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat "al-Insan": ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾, up to His saying: ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan: 5–22]. And such as His saying in Surat "al-Waqi'ah": ﴿And the forerunners, the forerunners, those are the ones brought near, in Gardens of Pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–12], up to His saying: ﴿for the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 38]. Similar examples in the Qur'an are numerous.

He has also explained in Surat "as-Sajdah" that what Allah has concealed for them of the comfort of the eyes, no one knows it except Him, may He be exalted. This is in His saying: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], and so on.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Gardens of Eternity﴾ means a settled abode after which there is no departure and no change, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They will not desire to be removed from it﴾ [al-Kahf: 108]. Its root is from *adana bil-makan*, meaning when one settles in a place. The meaning of *sundus* and *istabraq* has already been mentioned in Surat "an-Nahl," which suffices from repeating it here. *Asawir* is the plural of *siwar* (bracelet), and some have said it is the plural of *aswirah*. *Thawab* means recompense in general, according to the verified view (p. 273). From this is the saying of the poet:

*For every brother there is a reward for praise that I have known,*
*but for the praise of al-Bahili there is no reward.*

As for the view of one who says that *thawab* in the language is specific to the recompense of good for good, it is not correct. Rather, *thawab* is also applied to the recompense of evil for evil. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the disbelievers been recompensed for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 36], and His saying: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], up to the end of the verse.

As for His saying: ﴿and how good a resting place﴾, the pronoun in His saying "*hasunat*" (how good it was) refers back to "Gardens of Eternity." As for *murtafaq* (resting place), we have already presented the views of the scholars concerning it. His saying here regarding the Garden, "and how good a resting place," is explained by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for what they patiently endured, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace, abiding therein forever; how good it is as a place of rest and residence﴾ [al-Furqan: 75–76].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I should be returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination.﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and majestic is He, He mentions about this disbelieving man who wronged himself, whom He struck as a parable alongside the believing man in these verses, for the leaders of the disbelievers who boasted of wealth and status over the weak, poor Muslims, as has already been mentioned: that he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said that he did not think his garden would perish or come to an end, because of what he saw of its beauty and freshness. He said that he did not think the Hour would occur, and that if it were supposed that he would be resurrected and returned to his Lord, he would surely find with Him something better than the garden that He had given him in this world.

What this noble verse includes: the ignorance of the disbelievers and their being deceived by the enjoyments of the worldly life, and their thinking that the Hereafter is like this world, in which they will likewise be blessed with wealth and children, just as they were blessed in this world. This is explained in other verses, such as His saying in "Fussilat": ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is for me, and I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I should be returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best.﴾ [Fussilat: 50]; and His saying in "Maryam": ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77]; and His saying in "Saba'": ﴿And they say, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ [Saba': 35]; and His saying in this noble surah: ﴿So he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and stronger in numbers."﴾ [al-Kahf: 34].

Exalted is He has shown their lying and their being deceived in what they claimed: that they would find the blessing of Allah in the Hereafter (p-274) just as He had blessed them with it in this world, in many places, such as His saying: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ ﴿is [because of] Our hastening to them with good? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55-56]; and His saying: ﴿We will gradually lead them [to destruction] from where they do not know.﴾ ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44-45]; and His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is better for themselves. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]; and His saying: ﴿And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in position﴾ — the verse [Saba': 37]; and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned﴾ [al-Masad: 2], in addition to other verses.

His saying "munqalaban" means: a return and a consequence. Its being in the accusative is as a specification (tamyiz). His saying: ﴿I will surely find better than this (minha)﴾ — Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "minhuma" with the dual form of the pronoun, and the rest read "minha" with the singular form of the feminine pronoun. The pronoun, according to the reading of the dual, refers to the two gardens in His saying: ﴿We had made for one of them two gardens﴾ [al-Kahf: 32], and His saying: ﴿Both gardens﴾; and according to the reading of the singular, it refers to the garden in His saying: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾ — the verse [al-Kahf: 35].

If it is said: what is the reason for the singular "garden" when they are two gardens? The answer: he said what Allah mentioned of him when he entered one of them, since it is not possible for him to enter both of them together at one time. What al-Zamakhshari answered regarding this question is clearly untenable, as Abu Hayyan pointed out in al-Bahr.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then proportioned you into a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord.﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and majestic is He, He makes clear that this believing man, who is the parable for the believers upon whom the people of wealth and status among the disbelievers acted arrogantly, said to his other companion, the disbeliever, who is the parable for the people of wealth and status among the disbelievers, rebuking him for his disbelief: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then proportioned you into a man?" Because His creating him from dust, then from a sperm-drop, and then His shaping him into a man, all of this necessitates his belief in his Creator, who brought him from non-existence into existence, made him a complete human being, and makes him regard disbelief in his Creator, who brought him from non-existence into existence, as utterly remote. This meaning made clear here is made clear in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me, and to Him you will be returned?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22], and His saying, exalted is He: (p-275) ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers the former ones? Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds, who created me and it is He who guides me, and who feeds me and gives me drink, and when I am ill it is He who cures me, and who will cause me to die and then bring me to life"...﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 76-79], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who created me, for indeed He will guide me"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 26], and other verses besides these. We have already presented many verses indicating that the criterion for who deserves to be worshipped alone, to the exclusion of others, is that He is the one who creates the created beings and brings them from non-existence into existence, with what suffices without repeating it here.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿from dust﴾ [al-Kahf: 38], the meaning of His creating him from dust is: that is, the creation of Adam, whose origin is dust, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. The verse most similar to the one we are dealing with is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

As for His saying: ﴿then from a sperm-drop﴾, that is: after He created Adam from dust, and created Hawwa' (Eve) from his rib and made her a spouse for him, the way of bringing mankind into existence became through procreation. So after the stage of dust came the stage of the sperm-drop, then the stage of the clinging clot, through to the end of his stages mentioned in His saying: ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾ [Nuh: 14], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses﴾ [az-Zumar: 6]. He has explained this with complete clarity in His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm place. Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-14].

Among what clarifies the creation of man from dust, then from a sperm-drop, is His saying, exalted is He, in "as-Sajdah": ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the Merciful. Who perfected everything He created and began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, despised. Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful﴾ [as-Sajdah: 6-9]. And His saying in this verse: ﴿then proportioned you into a man﴾ [al-Kahf: 38], like His saying: ﴿He created man from a sperm-drop, and at once he is an open adversary﴾ [an-Nahl: 4], and His saying: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a sperm-drop, and at once he is an open adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77]. That is: after he had been a sperm-drop, he became a man, a fierce adversary in the matter of the Oneness of his Lord. (p-276) And His saying: "proportioned you" means: He created you with balanced limbs, of moderate stature and form, sound in your organs, in the most complete form and the best proportion, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [at-Tin: 4], and His saying: ﴿And He shaped you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir: 64], and His saying: ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous? He who created you and proportioned you and balanced you; in whatever form He willed, He assembled you﴾ [al-Infitar: 6-8]. And His saying "a man" means: a male who has reached maturity, the stage of men. The Arabs may sometimes say of a woman "rajulah" (a manly woman), and from it is the saying of the poet:

Every neighbour remained content, except the neighbours of the Banu Jabalah,
They tore the garment of their young woman, and did not observe the sanctity of the man (rajulah).

The accusative of "rajulan" is as a circumstantial state (hal). It has also been said to be a second object of "sawwa" by implicit meaning of "ja'alaka" or "sayyarака" (made you a man). It has also been said to be a specification (tamyiz), but this is not apparent to me. The apparent reading is that the denial indicated by the interrogative particle in His saying: ﴿Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust﴾ [al-Kahf: 37] is implicitly meant as expressing astonishment (istib'ad), because it is greatly unlikely that a creature would disbelieve in his Creator who brought him from non-existence into existence, and it is unlikely that one who knows that Allah created him from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then proportioned him into a man would deny the Resurrection; as in His saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust﴾ ... [al-Hajj: 5]. The verse most similar in indicating astonishment because its cause exists is the poet's saying:

And none removes the calamity except the son of a free woman, who sees the surges of death and then visits them.

Because one who has witnessed the surges of death is considered unlikely to plunge into them.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 38], in it He makes clear that this believing man said to his disbelieving companion: "Are you a disbeliever?! But I am not a disbeliever! Rather, I devote my worship sincerely to my Lord who created me"; that is, because He is the one who deserves from me that I worship Him, because the created being, like me, is in need of a creator who creates him, and worship of his Creator is binding upon him just as it is binding upon me.

The likeness of this believer's statement is what we have already presented about the believing man mentioned in "Ya-Sin," in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22], that is: He who originated me and created me, and to Him you will be returned; and what we have already presented about Abraham in His saying: ﴿Except the Lord of the worlds, who created me and it is He who guides me...﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 77-78], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 26-27].

(p-277) And His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust﴾, after His saying: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever occur﴾, indicates that doubt about the Resurrection is disbelief in Allah, exalted is He. He has explicitly stated this at the beginning of surah "ar-Ra'd" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be [returned] in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord, and those are the ones with shackles around their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 5].

As for His saying in this noble verse: "lakinna" — its origin is "lakin ana" (but I). The hamzah of "ana" was dropped and the nun of "lakin" was assimilated into the nun of "ana" after the hamzah was dropped. Some have said: the vowel of the hamzah was transferred to the nun of "lakin", so the hamzah fell away by transfer of its vowel, and then the nun was assimilated into the nun. A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the poet's saying:

And you strike me with your glance, as if you were the guilty one, and you turn away from me, but I did not turn away from you.

That is: "lakin ana iyyaki lam aqil." Others have said: what was mentioned does not necessarily apply in the verse, since it is possible that the intended form is "lakinni," and the name of "lakinna" was omitted, as in the saying of another poet:

If you were a Dabbi, you would know my kinship, but [you are] a Zanji with large lips.

That is: "lakinnaka" is a Zanji, according to the narration of one who reports "zanjiyyun" with nominative case. Al-Kisa'i recited, as an instance of this omission from "lakinna ana," the saying of another poet:

By God, you are indeed of 'Absiyyah, and beautiful, upon the rumours, whoever speaks them is a liar.

He said: he meant by "lahinnaka" "lillahi innaka," and omitted one of the two lams of "lillah" and omitted the hamzah of "innaka"; this was transmitted by al-Qurtubi from Abu 'Ubayd.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord﴾, the majority of readers recited "lakin" in connection (wasl) without an alif after the doubled nun. Ibn 'Amir, among the seven, recited "lakinna" with the alif in connection, and this is also transmitted from 'Asim; al-Musayyabi transmitted it from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub. All agreed on affirming the alif in pause (waqf). Prolonging the nun of "ana" is the dialect of Tamim when a hamzah follows it. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: affirming the alif of "ana" absolutely in connection is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, while others affirm it only under necessity (poetic license). He said: the reading "lakinna" with the alif in connection came in the dialect of Tamim. Among the evidences of prolonging "ana" before other than a hamzah is the poet's saying:

I am the sword of the tribe, so recognise me, praiseworthy, having raised the chief's shoulder.

And the saying of al-A'sha:

How am I, and the claiming of verses after grey hair has come, is enough shame of that.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿while he was arguing with him﴾, it is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). Al-muhawarah is mutual exchange in speech. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has heard the statement of she who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah; and Allah hears your mutual discourse﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 1], and the saying of 'Antarah in his mu'allaqah:

Had he known what exchange is, he would have complained, and had he known the answer, he would have spoken to me.

As for the statements of the exegetes concerning the two men mentioned here in their story, such as the naming of them and of what people they were, we have set aside discussing that for what we mentioned earlier about its lack of benefit and the absence of a convincing proof for it. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or its water becomes sunk into the earth, and you will not be able to find it.﴾

The meaning of His saying "ghawran" (sunk into the earth) is: ghā'iran (sinking, receding). It is thus among the descriptions by a verbal noun (maṣdar), as he said in al-Khulasah (the summary of Ibn Malik's grammar):

"They often described with a maṣdar, and so they kept it singular and masculine."

Al-ghā'ir is the opposite of al-nābi' (gushing, flowing forth). His saying, ﴿then you will not be able to find it a seeking⁠﴾ [Al-Kahf: 41], is because when Allah causes its water to vanish after it had existed, you will not find anyone other than Him, may He be majestic and exalted, who can bring it to you. He alluded to this same meaning in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunk into the earth, who would bring you flowing water?⁠﴾ [Al-Mulk: 30]. And there is no doubt that the correct answer is: none can bring it to us except Allah alone, as He said here: ﴿then you will not be able to find it a seeking⁠﴾ [Al-Kahf: 41].

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 43:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah, nor could he defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the True. He is best in reward and best in consequence.﴾

Know that this noble verse contains the seven canonical readings (qira'at sab'iyyah) and the opinions of the scholars of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), some of which are supported by other Qur'anic verses. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that a verse may contain several positions of the scholars, each supported by a Qur'anic verse, and we shall mention all of them with their evidence from the Qur'an. Having understood this, know that His words in this verse, ﴿and he had no company (fi'ah)﴾ [al-Kahf: 43], are read by the seven Readers except Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the upper ta' (tā' muthannāh fawqiyyah), while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa lam yakun lahu fi'ah" with the lower ya' (yā' muthannāh taḥtiyyah). As for His words ﴿protection belongs to Allah, the True﴾ [al-Kahf: 44], the seven Readers, except Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, also read "al-walayah" with a fatha on the waw, while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the waw. As for His word "al-Haqq", the seven Readers except Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi'l-khafd) as an attribute (na't) of "lillah" (to Allah), while Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the nominative (bi'l-raf') as an attribute of "al-walayah".

According to the reading of those who read "al-walayah lillah" with a fatha on the waw, its meaning is support and attachment (al-muwalah wa'l-silah). On this reading there are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: the meaning of ﴿there, protection belongs to Allah﴾ is: in that situation and that state, every person's protection belongs to Allah, because the disbeliever, when he sees the punishment, returns to Allah. On this meaning the verse is like His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ [Ghafir: 84], and His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾ ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters."﴾ [Yunus: 90–91], and similar verses.

The second: protection in such a situation and state belongs to Allah alone, so He extends to the believers the protection of mercy (walayat rahmah), as in His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector (wali) of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], and His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11]. He also has over the disbelievers the protection of sovereignty and dominion (walayat al-mulk wa'l-qahr), as in His saying: ﴿And they are returned to Allah, their true Protector (mawlahum al-haqq), and what they used to invent has gone astray from them.﴾ [Yunus: 30].

On the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, "al-wilayah" with a kasra means sovereignty and rule (al-mulk wa'l-sultan), and the verse on this reading is like His saying: ﴿"To whom belongs the dominion today?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾ [Ghafir: 16], His saying: ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26], and His saying: ﴿The dominion that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them﴾ [al-Hajj: 56]. On the reading of "al-Haqq" in the genitive as an attribute of Allah, the verse is like His saying: ﴿And they are returned to Allah, their true Protector﴾ [al-Kahf: 44], and His saying: ﴿So that is Allah, your true Lord﴾ [Yunus: 32], and His saying: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full due, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth.﴾ [al-Nur: 25], and other verses. On the reading of "al-Haqq" in the nominative as an attribute of "al-walayah", taking walayah to mean sovereignty, it is like His saying: ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾.

What He, may He be glorified and exalted, related about this disbeliever, namely that he had no company to help him against Allah, He mentioned something similar about other disbelievers, as in His saying about Qarun: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home, and he had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.﴾ [al-Qasas: 81], and His saying: ﴿Then he has no power nor any helper.﴾ [al-Tariq: 10]. Verses of this kind are very numerous.

As for His word "there" (hunalika), some scholars said it is connected to what follows it, and the pause on "nor could he defend himself" is complete. Others said it is connected to what precedes it. On the first view, the adverbial phrase "there" has as its governing element what follows it, meaning: protection belongs to Allah there. On the second view, the governing element of the adverb is the active participle "defending himself" (muntasiran), meaning: his self-defence did not take place there.

As for His words ﴿He is best in reward﴾, meaning: best in recompense, as previously mentioned. As for His word "consequence" ('uqban), it means outcome and final end. The seven Readers, except 'Asim and Hamzah, read "'uqubun" with two dammas, while the reading of 'Asim and Hamzah, "'uqban" with a damma on the 'ayn and a sukun on the qaf, has the same meaning. Both "thawaban" and "'uqban" are in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) following the comparative form "khayr" (best), as stated in the Khulasah (of Ibn Malik):

"And the agent of meaning, put it in the accusative after a comparative of the form af'al, like 'anta a'la manzilan' (you are higher in rank)."

The word "khayr" and "sharr" both come as comparative forms from which the hamzah has been dropped for lightness, due to frequency of use. Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiyah:

"Usually, khayr and sharr have made them dispensable of saying 'akhar minhu' and 'ashharu'."

* *

Note

His word in this noble verse, "fi'ah", has a letter omitted from it without any disagreement, but the scholars differ about which letter is omitted: is it a ya' or a waw, and is it the 'ayn or the lam? Some said the omitted letter is the 'ayn, and its root is ya'. The root of the word is f-y-', from fa'a yafi'u, meaning to return, because a man's fi'ah is the group to which he returns in his affairs. On this view the ta' is a substitute for the omitted 'ayn, and its morphological pattern (wazn, in sarf) is "fi'lah". Others said the omitted letter is the lam, and its origin is a waw, from fa'attu ra'sahu, meaning I split his head into two halves, and on this view fi'ah means a group of people. On this view its pattern is "fi'ah", and the ta' is a substitute for the lam. Both views were upheld by some scholars, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 46:

Allah's statement, the Exalted: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, and that the enduring good deeds (al-Baqiyat al-Salihat) are better with Allah for reward and better for hope.

The purpose of this noble verse is to alert people to righteous deeds, so that they do not become preoccupied with the adornment of the worldly life, namely wealth and children, to the neglect of the deeds that benefit them in the Hereafter with Allah, the enduring righteous deeds. (p-281) This meaning, which is indicated here, is clarified in other verses, such as His statement: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilth. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but Allah has the excellent return.﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and purified spouses."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14-15]. And His statement: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, those are the losers.﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 9]. And His statement: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15]. And His statement: ﴿And it is not your wealth or your children that will bring you near to Us in position, except for one who believes and does righteousness﴾ [Saba': 37]. And His statement: ﴿The Day when wealth and children will not benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. And other verses indicating that a person should not be preoccupied with the adornment of the worldly life to the neglect of what benefits him in his Hereafter.

The statements of the scholars regarding the enduring righteous deeds all return to one thing, namely the deeds that please Allah. Whether we say they are the five daily prayers, as is related from a group of the early generations (al-Salaf), among them Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Maysara, and 'Amr ibn Shurahbil; or that they are: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is the Greatest, and there is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty." This latter view is held by the majority of scholars (Jumhur al-'Ulama'), and traditions traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) indicate it, narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayra, al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Its annotator, may Allah pardon him, said: The verified position is that "the enduring righteous deeds" is a general term that includes the five prayers, the five words mentioned, and other deeds that please Allah, the Exalted, because they remain for their doer and do not vanish, unlike the adornment of the worldly life, and because they are also suitable to be performed in the manner that pleases Allah, the Exalted. His statement ﴿better for reward﴾ has had its meaning explained previously. His statement ﴿and better for hope﴾ means: what one hopes for from the outcomes of the enduring righteous deeds is better than what the people of this world hope for from the adornment of their worldly life. The root of hope (al-Amal) is a person's longing for the attainment of what he seeks in the future.

A parallel to this noble verse is His statement, the Exalted, in Surah Maryam: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance, and the enduring righteous deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for return.﴾ [Maryam: 76]. Al-Maradd means the return to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. Some scholars said: "maradd" is a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi, a verbal noun formed with the prefix mim), meaning: (p-282) and better for recompense (radd) for the reward upon its doer, so it is not like the deeds of the disbelievers, which return no reward to their doers.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 47:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And (remember) the Day We shall set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We shall gather them together and leave none of them behind﴾.

His statement: "ويَوْمَ" [Al-Kahf: 47] is in the accusative, governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember). Or it is governed by an implied verb of saying before His statement: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [Al-An'am: 94]. That is, "We said to them on the Day We set the mountains in motion: 'You have certainly come to Us alone.'" As for the view of the one who claims that its governing element is "khayr" (better), meaning "and the enduring good deeds are better on the Day We set the mountains in motion," it is very far-fetched, as you can see.

What Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse, that on the Day of Resurrection the order of this worldly existence will be disrupted, so that its mountains are set in motion and its earth remains laid bare, with no stone, no tree, no building, no valley and no landmark in it, He mentions in many other places. He states that on the Day of Resurrection He will lift the earth and the mountains from their places and pound them into one pounding, as in His statement: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown with one blast﴾, ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing blow﴾, ﴿on that Day the Event will occur﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 13-15], to the end of the verse.

What He mentions here about setting the mountains in motion in this noble verse, He also mentions in other places, such as His statement: ﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾, ﴿and the mountains will move, moving away﴾ [At-Tur: 9-10]; His statement: ﴿and the mountains will be set in motion, so they become a mirage﴾ [An-Naba: 20]; His statement: ﴿and when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [At-Takwir: 3]; and His statement: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by like the passing of clouds﴾ to the end of the verse [An-Naml: 88].

Then He mentions in other places that He, exalted is He, will crumble them until their rocky hardness vanishes and they become soft, so that in their lack of hardness and softness they are like carded wool and like scattered sand, as in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass﴾, ﴿and the mountains will be like tufts of wool﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 8-9]; and His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day mankind will be like scattered moths﴾, ﴿and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [Al-Qari'ah: 4-5]. "Al-'ihn" is wool. And His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day the earth and the mountains will quake, and the mountains will become heaps of loose sand﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 14]; and His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized into powder﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 5], meaning they will be crushed until they become like "al-basisah," which is flour kneaded with ghee, according to the most well-known interpretations.

Then He, exalted is He, mentions that He will make them into dust and mirage. He said: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized into powder﴾, ﴿so they become scattered dust﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 5-6], and He said: ﴿and the mountains will be set in motion, so they become a mirage﴾ [An-Naba: 20].

He explains in another place that the mirage is a metaphor for nothing; this is His statement: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾, up to His statement: ﴿he will find it to be nothing﴾ [An-Nur: 39].

As for His statement: ﴿And the Day We shall set the mountains in motion﴾, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited it: "tusayyaru al-jibalu" with a taa' at the beginning and a fatha on the shaddah-ed yaa', from His statement "tusayyaru," in the passive voice, and "al-jibalu" in the nominative as the deputy subject of "tusayyaru," the omitted subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, exalted is He. The rest of the seven readers recited "nusayyiru" with a nun and a kasra on the shaddah-ed yaa', in the active voice, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the direct object. The nun in His statement "nusayyiru" is for magnification.

As for His statement in this noble verse: ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾, "al-buruz" means appearance, that is, you will see the earth visible and uncovered due to the removal of the mountains, the hills, the hillocks, the trees and the buildings that were upon it. This meaning that He mentions here He also explains in other places, such as His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust﴾, ﴿and leave it a level smooth plain, in which you will see no crookedness or elevation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105-106]. The statements of the scholars on the meaning of this come back to one thing, which is that it is a level land with no vegetation, no building, no elevation and no depression. As for the view of one who says that the meaning of ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾ is that what was in its belly of the dead and the treasures comes out, it is very far-fetched, as you can see. The bringing forth of what is in its belly of the dead and the treasures is indicated by other verses, such as His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾, ﴿and casts out what is within it and becomes empty﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq: 3-4]; His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾, ﴿and what is in the breasts is made known﴾ [Al-'Adiyat: 9]; His statement: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [Az-Zalzalah: 2]; and His statement: ﴿and when the graves are overturned﴾ [Al-Infitar: 4].

As for His statement in this noble verse: "wa-hasharnahum," meaning We gathered them for reckoning and recompense. This gathering, expressed here as "hashr," is mentioned in other verses, such as His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed the first and the last﴾, ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known Day﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 49-50]; His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him—will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [An-Nisa: 87]; His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly; that is the Day of mutual loss and gain﴾ [At-Taghabun: 9]; His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud: 103]; and His statement: ﴿And the Day We shall gather them all﴾ to the end of the verse [Al-An'am: 22], among other verses.

He explains in another place that this mentioned hashr includes rational beings and other kinds of creatures, and this is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [Al-An'am: 38].

As for His statement in this noble verse: ﴿and We left none of them behind﴾ [Al-Kahf: 47], meaning We did not leave anyone behind. "Al-mughadarah" means leaving behind, and from it comes "al-ghadr" (betrayal), because it is leaving behind fidelity and trust; and a pool of water is called "ghadir" because the torrent went away and left it behind. From the use of "mughadarah" in the sense of leaving behind is the statement of 'Antarah at the opening of his Mu'allaqah:

"Have the poets left any remains of a dwelling, or do you recognise the abode after its imagining?"

And his statement also:

"I left him rolling in dust, his limbs, while the people were between wounded and felled."

What He mentions in this noble verse, that He gathered them and left none of them behind, is explained in other places, such as His statement: ﴿And the Day We shall gather them all﴾ to the end of the verse [Al-An'am: 22], and similar verses; for gathering them all is the very meaning of not leaving any of them behind.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 48:**

Allah's words: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that all creatures on the Day of Resurrection will be presented before their Lord in rows (ṣaffan), meaning while arranged in ranks. Some scholars said: "in rows after rows." Others said: "in a single row." Some scholars said that "ṣaffan" means "all together," like His words: ﴿Then come forward in rows﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 64], according to the view that this is the meaning there.

Al-Qurṭubī, in his tafsir (exegesis, interpretation) of this noble verse, said: The ḥāfiẓ Abū al-Qāsim ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mandah narrated in the Book of Tawḥīd, from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, will call out on the Day of Resurrection with a loud voice, not a frightening one: 'O My servants, I am Allah. There is no god but Me. I am the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Just of judges, and the Swiftest of reckoners. O My servants, there is no fear upon you today, nor will you grieve. Bring forth your proofs and prepare your answers, for you are to be questioned and held accountable. O My angels, arrange My servants in rows, standing on the tips of their toes, for the reckoning.'" I say: This hadith is an extremely clear explanation of the verse, and many exegetes did not mention it. We wrote it down in our book al-Tadhkirah, and from it we have quoted it. All praise is due to Allah.

End of al-Qurṭubī's words. The hadith mentioned indicates that "ṣaffan" in this verse means "rows" (ṣufūfan), like His words about the angels: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]. A parallel to this verse is His words about the angels: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is right﴾ [al-Naba': 38–39].

Now that you know that Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in this noble verse one of the states of the presentation of creatures before Him on the Day of Resurrection, know that He explained in other places other aspects of their presentation before Him, such as His words: ﴿On that Day you will be presented, and no secret of yours will be hidden﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 18]. He also explained in other places what the disbelievers will encounter and what will be said to them at that presentation before their Lord, such as His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who avert [others] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers"﴾ [Hūd: 18–19].

As for His words in this noble verse, ṣaffan: its origin is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and an indefinite verbal noun may function as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), according to His saying in the Khulāṣah (Ibn Mālik's summary of Arabic grammar):

*"An indefinite verbal noun may come as a ḥāl, frequently, like 'baghtatan' (suddenly) in 'Zayd came suddenly.'"*

His words: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾.

This statement is the object of an omitted verb of saying (maqūl qawl), and omitting the verb of saying is regular in the Arabic language and very common in the Great Qur'an. The meaning is: it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed you have come to Us," that is, "By Allah, you have indeed come to Us just as We created you the first time," meaning barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised (ghurlan), meaning not circumcised. Each one of you is alone, with no wealth with him, no children, no servants, and no attendants.

This meaning has been clarified in other places, such as His words: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners [with Allah] in you. The bond between you has been severed, and what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾ [al-Anʿām: 94]. Also His words: ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them precisely. And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ [Maryam: 94–95]. Also His words: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it. [It is] a promise binding upon Us; indeed, We will do it﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 104], and His words: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 29], which has already passed.

As for His words in this noble verse: ﴿just as We created you﴾, "mā" is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, and the verbal noun formed from it and its clause is an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun, by omitting a modified noun (muḍāf). The clear explanation of this construction is: "You have indeed come to Us just as We created you," meaning a coming like the coming of your creation, that is, barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised, as came in the hadith, and free of wealth and children. This is the parsing required by the statement of Abū Ḥayyān in al-Baḥr (his tafsir). It appears to me that it may also be parsed as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), meaning: "You have come to Us in a state of being like your first state," because comparison is interpreted as a description, as indicated in the Khulāṣah with his words:

*"Stasis occurs in price, and in one who shows interpretation without strain: like 'sell it for a mudd at such-and-such, hand to hand,' and 'Zayd charged as a lion,' meaning like a lion."*

His saying "Zayd charged as a lion, meaning like a lion" is an example of one who shows interpretation: it is interpreted as "charged in a state of being like a lion," as we mentioned. Know that omitting the verb of saying while stating what is said is regular in the Arabic language and common in the Great Qur'an, as we mentioned just now. But the reverse, stating the verb of saying while omitting what is said, is very rare. From it is the words of the poet:

*"We are the ones you said [we would fight]; how then were you filled with terror at the sight of us before you had planned to face us?"*

Because the intended meaning is "We are the ones you said, 'We will fight them,'" so he omitted the clause "we will fight them," which is the content of the saying.

His words: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾ use the past tense while meaning the future, because the certainty of its occurrence makes it as though it has already occurred. Expressing the future with the past tense for the reason we mentioned is very common in the Great Qur'an. From it is His statement here: ﴿and We will gather them﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], and His words: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 48], and His words: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾. From it is His words: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, and His words: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], and His words: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], and His words: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. Similar examples are many in the Qur'an for the reason we mentioned.

\* \*

Allah's words: ﴿Rather, you claimed that We would not appoint for you a promised time﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that the disbelievers claimed that Allah would never appoint for them a promised time (mawʿid). The word mawʿid includes both the time of the promise and its place. The meaning is: they claimed that Allah had not appointed a time or a place for fulfilling what He had promised them through His messengers, of resurrection, recompense, and reckoning. What this noble verse indicates about their denial of resurrection is explained in many verses, such as His words: ﴿The disbelievers claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghābun: 7], and His words about them: ﴿And we are not going to be resurrected﴾ [al-Anʿām: 29], ﴿And we will not be raised again﴾ [al-Dukhān: 35], and similar verses.

Allah has shown their falsehood in denying resurrection in many verses, such as His words in this noble surah: ﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge﴾ [al-Kahf: 58]; and His words: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did"﴾ [al-Taghābun: 7]; and His words: ﴿And they swore by Allah their strongest oaths that Allah will not resurrect those who die. Yes, [He will], as a promise binding upon Him, but most of the people do not know﴾ [al-Naḥl: 38]; and His words: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it, a promise binding upon Us; indeed, We will do it﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 104]. Verses of this kind are very numerous.

We have already presented in (p-287) Surah al-Baqarah and Surah al-Naḥl the proofs that are frequently used in the Great Qur'an to argue for resurrection.

His words in this noble verse: ﴿Rather, you claimed﴾: "bal" here is a transitional (intiqālī) rather than a nullifying (ibṭālī) retraction, moving from one statement to another, as is clear. As for "an" in His words ﴿that We would not appoint﴾, it is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," and the verbal clause following it is its predicate, while its subject is an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), according to His saying in the Khulāṣah:

*"And if you lighten 'anna'..."*, the verse continues.

The verb mentioned is inflected (mutaṣarrif), not a verb of praise or blame (duʿāʾ), so negation was used to separate it from the particle, according to His saying in the Khulāṣah:

*"And if the verb is not one of invocation..."*, the two verses continue.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 18, Verse 49:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Oh woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it!"﴾. In this noble verse, the Majestic and Exalted mentions that the Book will be placed on the Day of Resurrection. What is meant by "the Book" is the genus of books, so it includes all the scrolls in which the deeds of the accountable were recorded in the life of this world. And the criminals are fearful of what is in it, meaning they are afraid of it. They say, ﴿Oh woe to us! What is this Book that leaves [nothing] behind﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], meaning it does not leave, ﴿small or great﴾ of the sins that we committed, ﴿but has enumerated it﴾, meaning it has recorded and encompassed it.

This meaning indicated by this noble verse is clarified in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird [of fate] to his neck, and We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant."﴾ [al-Isra: 13-14]. And He explained that some of them will be given their record in their right hand, some will be given it in their left hand, and some will be given it behind their backs. He said: ﴿But as for one who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record."﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for one who is given his record in his right hand, he will be judged with an easy judgment and will return to his people in joy. But as for one who is given his record behind his back, he will call for destruction and will burn in a Blaze﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 7-12]. We have already mentioned this in Surat "Bani Isra'il". What He mentioned here regarding the placing of the Book, He mentioned in "az-Zumar" in His saying: ﴿And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book will be placed, and the prophets and the martyrs will be brought, and judgment will be made between them in truth﴾ [az-Zumar: 69].

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿you will see the criminals﴾, a similar meaning has preceded in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And you see the sun when it rises﴾ (p-288) [al-Kahf: 17]. "Al-mujrimun" is the plural of "al-mujrim", which is the active participle of "al-ijram". "Al-ijram" is committing a "jarimah", which is a grave sin deserving punishment for its doer. The meaning of their being "fearful of what is in it" is that they are afraid of what is in that Book of the disclosure of their evil deeds, their disgrace before all witnesses, and what follows from that of everlasting punishment. Their saying, "Oh woe to us!" — "al-wailah" is destruction. They called out to their destruction, which they had brought upon themselves specifically from among all destructions, saying: "Oh woe to us!", meaning: "O destruction of ours, be present, for this is the time of your presence!" Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: The one addressed is one who is in their presence; it is as if they said: "O you who are in our presence, look at our destruction." Similarly is what has come of calling to inanimate things, such as His saying: ﴿Oh, my grief over Joseph!﴾ [Yusuf: 84], ﴿Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar: 56], ﴿Oh woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], and His saying: "O wonder at this little she-camel! And O wonder at her heavy load!" It is only intended by it to alert the one who understands through wonder at what has befallen the one called. End of Abu Hayyan's words. The summary of what he mentioned is that the particle of address in "Ya wailatana" is used to address something omitted, and what follows it is the object of an omitted verb, and the estimate, as he mentioned, is: "O you who are in our presence, look at our destruction." It is known that omitting the addressed noun while retaining the particle of address, with the context indicating the omitted addressee, is attested in Arabic speech. From it is the saying of 'Antarah in his mu'allaqah:

"O ewe of the hunted one, for whoever it is lawful to, it is forbidden to me, and I wish it were not forbidden."

meaning: "O people, look at the ewe of the hunt." And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Ah, O (feminine) be safe, O abode of Mayy, in the dew, and may the rain never cease to pour upon your gravel-ground."

meaning: "O you (feminine), be safe."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What is this Book?﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], meaning: what has been established for this Book, ﴿that leaves [nothing]﴾, meaning it does not leave, ﴿small or great﴾, meaning of the sins. As for the statement of whoever says: "The small is the kiss, and the great is fornication," and similar sayings regarding the verse, these are only by way of illustration, not by way of restriction. The scholars have much disagreement regarding the definition of the "great sin," which is well known in the principles of jurisprudence. Allah, the Exalted, has explicitly stated that some prohibited matters are "great sins," and it is understood from this that there are among them "small sins." He also explained that avoiding the great sins causes Allah to expiate the small sins by it. That is in His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [an-Nisa: 31]. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad regarding this verse that he (p-289) said: "They feared the small sins more than the great sins."

The clause "leaves [nothing]" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book."

Remark

From this noble verse it is understood that the disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Shari'ah, because they found in their book of deeds the small sins of their wrongdoing enumerated against them; had they not been addressed by them, they would not have been recorded against them in their book of deeds. And Allah knows best.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾.

In this noble verse the Majestic and Exalted mentions that on the Day of Resurrection they will find their deeds which they did in the world present and enumerated against them. He clarified this also in other places, such as His saying: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a great distance﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 30], His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There every soul will [experience] what it has sent ahead﴾ [Yunus: 30], His saying: ﴿Man will be informed that Day of what he sent ahead and kept back﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13], and His saying: ﴿The Day the secrets will be tested﴾ [at-Tariq: 9], and other verses.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

In this noble verse the Majestic and Exalted mentions that He does not wrong anyone, so He does not diminish the good deeds of the doer of good, nor add to the evil deeds of the evildoer, nor punish for a sin not committed.

He clarified this meaning in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus: 44], His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom. And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [an-Nisa: 40], His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged at all. And if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ [al-Anbiya: 47], His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], His saying: ﴿And Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [an-Nahl: 33], and His saying: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [an-Nahl: 118]. And the verses of similar meaning are numerous.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 50 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾.

We have previously mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:34], may mean that He commanded them to do so before Adam existed, as a command conditional upon his existence; and it may mean that He commanded them to do so immediately after Adam existed. He, majestic and exalted, has also made clear in Surah al-Hijr and Surah Sad that the origin of the command to prostrate preceded the creation of Adam and was conditional upon it. He said in al-Hijr: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "I am going to create a human from clay of altered black mud." So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [al-Hijr 15:28-29]. And He said in Sad: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "I am going to create a human from clay." So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad 38:71-72]. This does not contradict that after Adam existed He renewed the command to them to prostrate to him, immediately.

His saying in this noble verse, "and they prostrated," may mean that they all prostrated or that some of them did; but He made clear in other places that they all prostrated, as in His saying: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely﴾ [al-Hijr 15:30, 38:73], and similar verses.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 18:50], is apparent in that the cause of his defiance of the command of his Lord was that he was of the jinn. It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence, under "the path of the text" and under "the path of allusion and indication," that the fa' (ف) is among the particles indicating causation, as in the saying: "He stole, so his hand was cut off," meaning: because of his theft. And "he forgot, so he performed the prostration of forgetfulness" (sajda al-sahw), meaning: because of his forgetfulness. Of this type is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:38], meaning: because of the cause of their theft. Likewise His saying here, ﴿He was of the jinn, so he defied﴾, meaning: because of the cause of his being of the jinn; for this attribute distinguished him from the angels, since they obeyed the command while he disobeyed. Because of the apparent meaning of this noble verse, a group of scholars held that Iblis was not originally one of the angels but of the jinn, and that he used to worship with them, so the name of the angels was applied to him because he was a follower of theirs, like the ally within a tribe who is called by its name. The disagreement concerning Iblis, whether he was originally an angel whom God transformed into a devil, or whether he was not originally an angel and the word "angels" merely encompassed him because he entered among them and worshipped with them, is well known among the people of knowledge.

The argument of those who said that his origin was not from the angels rests on two matters. The first is the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the angels from committing the disbelief that Iblis committed, as He said of them: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:6], and He said: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:27]. The second is that God explicitly stated in this noble verse that he was of the jinn, and the jinn are other than the angels. They said: "It is a Qur'anic text on the point under dispute."

Those who argued that he was an angel originally cited what recurred in the Qur'anic verses in His saying: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely, except Iblis﴾ [al-Hijr 15:30-31]. They said: his exclusion by the exception from the word "angels" is evidence that he was among them. Some of them said: "Apparent indications, when they multiply, become equivalent to an explicit text." It is known that the basic principle of exception is connection, not disconnection. They said: "There is no proof for those who oppose us in His saying, ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf 18:50], because the jinn are a tribe of the angels, created from among the angels from the fire of the samum wind, as has been related from Ibn 'Abbas; and the Arabs know in their language the application of 'jinn' to the angels." From this is the saying of al-A'sha about Sulayman ibn Dawud:

"And there were subjected to him, of the jinn of the angels, nine, standing before him, working without wage."

They said: From the application of "jinn" to the angels is His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat 37:158], according to those who say that what is meant by it is their saying: "The angels are the daughters of God." Glorified and exalted is He above all that does not befit His perfection and majesty, a great exaltation!

Among those who affirmed decisively that he was not originally one of the angels, on the apparent meaning of this noble verse, were al-Hasan al-Basri; al-Zamakhshari limited himself to this in his tafsir. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of Surah al-Baqarah that his being one of the angels is the view of the majority: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatadah and others. It is the preference of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan, and al-Tabari favoured it, and it is the apparent meaning of His saying "except Iblis." End of quote. What the exegetes report from a group of the early generation, such as Ibn 'Abbas and others, that he was among the nobles of the angels, one of the guardians of Paradise, that he used to manage the affairs of the lowest heaven, and that his name was 'Azazil, is all from the Israelite narrations (isra'iliyyat) on which no reliance may be placed.

The strongest of the arguments on the question is the argument of those who said that he was not an angel, because His saying, ﴿except Iblis, he was of the jinn, so he defied﴾ and the rest of the verse [al-Kahf 18:50], is the clearest thing on the subject among the texts of revelation. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse, ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾, means: he went out of obedience to the command of his Lord. Defiance (fisq) in the language means going out; from this is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:
