Thus his call to them became the cause of the absence of their guidance. This is an error, because this conditional proposition in this noble verse is not a necessary conditional (lazumiyya), such that there is a connection between its condition and its consequent. Rather it is a coincidental conditional (ittifaqiyya), and the coincidental conditional has no connection at all between its two parts, so neither is a cause of the other, nor entails it. This is like if you say: "If man is speaking, then the horse is neighing." There is no link between the two parts, because the consequent in a coincidental conditional has another cause not mentioned, like your saying: "If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." The cause of the absence of disobedience is not the absence of fear, which is the condition, but something else not mentioned, namely the glorification of Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, and His love, which prevents disobedience to Him. Likewise His words here, "fa-lan yahtadu idhan abadan" (then they will never be guided, ever), whose real cause is not mentioned with it. So it is not His words "wa-in tad'uhum" as al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others supposed. Rather its cause is the will of Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, that they not be guided, in accordance with what was previously decreed in His knowledge from eternity.

A parallel to this noble verse in the absence of connection between the two parts of the conditional is His words, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Even if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be killed would have come out to their beds"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], because the cause of their coming out to their beds is something else not mentioned in the verse, namely what has preceded in the knowledge of Allah that their coming out to them is inevitably going to happen. Its cause is not their staying in their houses mentioned in the verse. Likewise His words, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted"﴾ [al-Kahf: 109], and other verses. I have clarified the difference between the necessary conditional and the coincidental conditional in my urjuza (versified poem) on logic and my commentary on it, in my saying:

"The antecedent of the connected conditional, whatever the companionship of that consequent with it,
For a necessitating reason that has required it, like a cause, is the necessary (lazumiyya), then if it goes away.
The necessitating of the association between the two is that; the coincidental (ittifaqiyya) is, according to the scholars."

An example of the necessary connected conditional is your saying: "Whenever the sun is rising, the day exists," because of the evident entailment between the two parts. It suffices for this that there be mere entailment in one direction, not mutual entailment, as in your saying: "Whenever a thing is a human, it is an animal," since its converse is not true.

If you were to say: "Whenever a thing is an animal, it is a human," it would not be true, because the entailment in one of the two parts does not require mutual entailment in both. Mere entailment makes the conditional necessary. But if entailment is entirely absent between its two parts, then it is coincidental, and an example of it is the saying: "If man is speaking, the donkey is braying." Because many grammarians and rhetoricians failed to notice the difference between the necessary conditional and the coincidental conditional, they became confused when discussing the meaning of "law" (if/had), because they wanted to combine in one meaning between your saying "If the sun were rising, the day would exist" and your saying "If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him," although the condition is a cause of the consequent in the first, since it is a necessary conditional, while there is no connection between them in the second, since it is a coincidental conditional. There is no doubt that whoever wants to combine two different things becomes confused. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that He is Forgiving (ghafur), meaning abundant in forgiveness, and that He is the Possessor of mercy, who shows mercy to His believing servants on the Day of Resurrection and shows mercy to creation in this world.

He explains in other places that this forgiveness encompasses all sins by His majestic and exalted will, except shirk, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah - Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 72].

He explains in another place that His mercy is vast, and that He will prescribe it for the righteous, which is His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things, so I will decree it for those who fear Me and give zakah﴾ [Al-A'raf: 156].

He explains in other places the vastness of His forgiveness and mercy, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is of vast forgiveness﴾ [An-Najm: 32], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [Az-Zumar: 53], and what is similar to that of verses.

He explains in other places that, along with the vastness of His mercy and forgiveness, He is severe in punishment, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed, your Lord is severe in penalty﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 6], and His saying: ﴿Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance, Severe in penalty﴾ [Ghafir: 3], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Inform My servants that it is I who am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hijr: 49-50], and other verses besides these.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If Allah were to take them to task for what they earned, He would hasten for them the punishment﴾

In this noble verse He explains that if He were to call the people to account for what they earned of sins, such as disbelief and disobedience, He would hasten the punishment for them because of the enormity of what they commit. But He is Forbearing and does not hasten the punishment; He gives respite and does not neglect.

He clarifies this meaning in other places, as in His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature﴾ [An-Nahl: 61], and His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they earned, He would not leave upon its back a creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. We have already discussed this in Surat an-Nahl in full.

* *

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge other than Him﴾.

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, explains that even though He does not hasten the punishment for them at the present time, He is not unaware of them, nor does He leave their punishment, but rather He, exalted, has set for them an appointed time in which He will punish them; the punishment will neither be delayed from it nor advanced beyond it.

He explains this in other places, as in His saying in An-Nahl: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature, but He delays them until a specified term. And when their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it﴾ [An-Nahl: 61], and His saying at the end of Surat Fatir: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they earned, He would not leave upon its back a creature, but He delays them until a specified term. And when their term comes - indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾ [Fatir: 45], and as in His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], and as in His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 53].

Many verses indicate that Allah does not delay anything from its appointed time, nor does He advance it beyond that, such as His saying: ﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its time has come﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 11], and His saying: ﴿So when their time comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed﴾ [Nuh: 4] and the verse [following it], and His saying: ﴿For every term is a decree﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 38], and His saying: ﴿For every news is a time of fruition﴾ [Al-An'am: 67], and other verses besides these.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿they will find no refuge other than Him﴾ [Al-Kahf: 58], meaning: a place of refuge to which they take shelter and seek protection from that punishment for which the stated appointed time has been set. It is a noun of place, from wa'ala, ya'ilu, wa'lan, wu'ulan, meaning "to seek refuge" (laja'a). It is well known in the science of morphology (sarf) that the verbal noun of mim-form, and the noun of place and time, of a triliteral verb whose first radical is waw, is measured on mafil with a kasra on the 'ayn, as here, provided that its final radical is not weak; if it is weak in the final radical, the measure is with a fatha, as in al-mawla. The Arabs say: "lā wa'alat nafsuhu," meaning: his soul did not find a means of escape by which it could be saved. From this is the saying of the poet:

Lā wa'alat nafsuka khallaytahā lil-'āmiriyyayni wa-lam tukallami
("May your soul find no refuge — you left it to the two 'Amiris, and it was not spoken to.")

And al-A'sha said:

Wa-qad ukhālisu rabba al-bayti ghaflatahu ** wa-qad yuhādhiru minnī thumma mā ya'ilu
("I may steal upon the master of the house while he is unaware, and he may be wary of me, yet he does not escape.")

That is, he does not escape.

The statements of the exegetes regarding "al-mawil" return to what we have mentioned, such as the saying of some: "mawilan, a place of escape," and the saying of some: "a refuge," and the saying of some: "a safeguard," and other sayings; all of them carry the meaning we have mentioned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those cities - We destroyed them when they wronged, and We set for their destruction an appointed time﴾.

In this noble verse He explains that the earlier cities, when they wronged through denying the messengers, persisting in obstinacy and disbelief and disobedience, Allah destroyed them for their sins.

This generality concerning the identification of these cities, the causes of their destruction, and the kinds of destruction that befell them, is detailed in many other verses, as in the Qur'an's account of the people of Nuh, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Shu'ayb, and the people of Musa, some of whose details have already passed. "Al-qura" is the plural of "qaryah" in an irregular pattern; for the broken plural on fu'al, with damma then fatha, is not analogical except in the plural of fu'lah with damma as a noun, such as ghurfah and qirbah, or fu'la when it is the feminine of af'al specifically, such as al-kubra and al-kubar. As indicated for this in al-Khulasah by his saying:

"Fu'al is the plural of fi'lah that is known, and the like of kubrā..." etc. That is: as for other than these, it is a transmitted form that is memorized and not analogized upon. He added in at-Tashil a third type in which fu'al (with damma then fatha) is analogical, namely fu'ulah with two dammas if it is a noun, such as jumu'ah and juma'.

The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿And those cities﴾ [Al-Kahf: 59] is used only for them because they pass by them on their journeys, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not reason?﴾ [As-Saffat: 137-138], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is on a road that remains﴾ [Al-Hijr: 76], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, they are on a clear highway﴾ [Al-Hijr: 79], and similar verses.

His saying "wa-tilka" is a mubtada' (subject), and "al-qura" is its adjective, or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). His saying "ahlaknāhum" is the predicate (khabar). It is permissible for the predicate to be "al-qura," and the clause "ahlaknāhum" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as in His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, ruined because of what they did﴾ [An-Naml: 52]. It is also permissible for His saying "wa-tilka" to be in the accusative position governed by a deleted verb, which is explained by the operative verb occupied with the pronoun, in accordance with the saying in al-Khulasah:

"If the pronoun of a preceding noun is occupied by a verb, [the verb] is governed by its accusative form or its position..."
"So make the preceding noun accusative by a hidden verb, obligatorily, matching what has been made manifest."

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿for their destruction an appointed time﴾ [Al-Kahf: 59]: it was read by most of the Seven except 'Asim, with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, in the form of the passive participle. On this reading it is possible that it is a mim-form verbal noun, meaning: We set for their destruction an appointed time; and that it is a noun of time, meaning (p-319) We set for the time of their destruction an appointed time. It has been established in the science of morphology that every verb whose past tense exceeds three letters, without restriction, has its mim-form verbal noun, noun of place, and noun of time analogically in the passive participle form. The one who destroys with a damma on the mim is the one from whom the quadriliteral "ahlaka" [derived]. Hafs from 'Asim read "li-mahlikihim" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, and Shu'bah from 'Asim read "li-mahlakihim" with a fatha on both the mim and the lam. The apparent reading, on Hafs's recitation, is that it is a noun of time, meaning: We set for the time of their destruction an appointed time; because it comes from halaka, yahlaku with a kasra, and whatever has past form fa'ala with a fatha and present form yaf'ilu with a kasra, like halaka yahlaku, daraba yadribu, and nazala yanzilu, then analogically its noun of place and time is mafil with a kasra, and its mim-form verbal noun is mafal with a fatha. You say: "hadhā manziluhu" with a kasra, meaning the place of his descending or the time of his descending; and "hadhā manzaluhu" with a fatha on the zay, meaning his descent, and so on. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Ina dhakkarat-ka al-dāru manzilahā Jumlun bakayta fa-dam'u al-'aynı munhadirun sajlu"

His saying "manzilahā Jumlun" is with a fatha, meaning: the descent of Jumlun to her. From this you know that on Shu'bah's reading "li-mahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam, it is a mim-form verbal noun, meaning: We set for their destruction an appointed time. The appointed time is the specified time for that event to occur.

Note

The word "lammā" occurs in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech in three types:

The first: lammā negating and jussing the present tense, as in His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 214], and His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove﴾ [Al-Imran: 142]. This is a particle without disagreement, and it is restricted to the present tense. The semantic distinctions between it and the negating lam are mentioned in the science of Arabic grammar, and among those who clarified them is Ibn Hisham and others.

The second: that it is a particle of exception meaning "illa," so it enters upon the nominal clause, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq: 4], in the reading of the one who doubles the mim of "lammā," meaning: no soul except that it has over it a guardian. Of this type is the saying of the Arabs: "Unshiduka Allāh lammā fa'alta," meaning: I ask you only for your doing. And from this is the saying of the rajiz:

"Qālat lahu bi-llāhi yā dhā al-burdayni lammā ghanithta nafasan aw nafasayni"

(p-320) Her saying "ghanithta," with a ghayn, a kasra on the nun, and a thaa, is attached to the second-person pronoun. What is meant by her saying "ghanithta" is that you breathed during drinking, and she used it as a euphemism for intercourse, meaning that he should not continue at that and should breathe in between. This type too is a particle without disagreement, and some people of knowledge say it is the dialect of Hudhayl.

The third type of "lammā" is the type restricted to the past tense, which requires two clauses, the second of which occurs when the first occurs, as in His saying: ﴿When they wronged﴾, meaning: when they wronged, We destroyed them. What precedes it is evidence for the omitted clause. This type is the most common in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. As for this "wa-lammā," which requires the linking of one clause to another, the grammarians differed over whether it is a particle or a noun, and their disagreement is well known. Among those who defended its being a particle is Ibn Kharuf and others; among those who defended its being a noun is Ibn al-Sarraj, al-Farisi, Ibn Jinni, and others. The answer to this "lammā" is always a past verb without disagreement, as in His saying: ﴿So when He delivered you to the land, you turned away﴾ [Al-Isra: 67]; and it may be a nominal clause preceded by the sudden "idhā", as in His saying: ﴿So when He delivered them to the land, immediately they associate others with Him﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 65]; or preceded by fa', as in His saying: ﴿So when He delivered them to the land, some of them are moderate﴾ [Luqman: 32]. Its answer may be a present verb, as Ibn 'Usfur said, as in His saying: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74]. Some of what we have mentioned is not free from discussion among the scholars of Arabic, but it is the apparent view.

These three types are the ones in which "lammā" occurs in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 58 (part 2 of 2):

As for "lammā" (لَمّا) when composed of several words or of two words, it is not the "lammā" that is our subject, because it is other than it. Thus, the one composed of several words is like the view of some exegetes regarding the meaning of God's words, ﴿And surely, to all of them your Lord will pay in full [for their deeds]﴾ [Hud: 111], in the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Hafs from 'Asim, with the nun of "inna" (إنَّ) and the mim of "lammā" (لَمّا) doubled, according to the view of one who claims that the original in this reading is lamman mā, with man (مِن) being the partitive (تبعيضية) and mā having the meaning of man, i.e., "and surely, of the whole of what your Lord will pay them for their deeds." Then the nun of man was changed into a mim and assimilated into mā, and when the mims accumulated, the first was deleted, so it became lammā. According to this view, "lammā" is composed of three words: the first is the particle lām, the second is min, and the third is mā. Although some scholars have held this view, its weakness and remoteness are not hidden, and it is not permissible to interpret the Qur'an by it. Our aim here is merely to give an example of "lammā" composed of several words according to the view of one who said so. As for the one composed of two words, it is like the saying of the poet:

"Lammā ra'aytu Abā Yazīd muqātilan * ad'u al-qitāla wa-ash-hadu al-hayjā'"

("When I saw Abu Yazid fighting, I would abandon fighting and attend the battle.")

Because his saying "lammā" in this verse is composed of "lan" (لَنِ), the negative particle that puts the imperfect verb into the subjunctive, and "mā" (ما), the temporal verbal-masdar particle. That is: "I will never abandon fighting for as long as I see Abu Yazid fighting," i.e., for the duration of my seeing him fighting.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when they reached the junction of the two seas, they forgot their fish﴾.

In this noble verse, the Exalted mentions that Musa and his young companion (fata) forgot their fish when they reached the junction of the two seas. However, He made clear that the forgetting was committed by the companion of Musa, because it was he who had the fish in his care, and it was he who forgot it. The forgetting was attributed to both of them because the use of a plural form while only some of its members are intended (ism al-majmu' muradan ba'duhu) is a common Arabic style, found much in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. We have already explained that among the strongest proofs for this is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i: ﴿And if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], where the killing in both verbs is meant, not the fighting. That is, if some of you are killed, then others of you should kill them. The evidence that the forgetting was done only by the companion of Musa and not by Musa is His saying, concerning the two of them: ﴿Then when they had passed on, he said to his young companion, "Bring us our morning meal; indeed we have suffered fatigue from this journey of ours." He said, "Did you see when we retreated to the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish, and none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it"﴾ [al-Kahf: 62-63]. This is because Musa's saying "Bring us our morning meal" refers to the fish, so he thought that his companion had not forgotten it, as said by more than one scholar. His companion clarified that he had forgotten it by his saying: ﴿Indeed, I forgot the fish, and none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾, and so on.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾ is evidence that forgetting comes from Satan, as other verses indicate, such as His saying: ﴿And if Satan should make you forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-An'am: 68], and His saying: ﴿Satan has overcome them and caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 19].

The companion of Musa is Yusha' ibn Nun. The pronoun in His saying ﴿the junction of the two of them﴾ [al-Kahf: 61] refers to the "two seas" mentioned in His saying: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas﴾ [al-Kahf: 60]. The word majma' (junction) is an ism of place according to the regular pattern (ism makan 'ala al-qiyas), meaning the place where the two of them met.

The scholars differ in identifying the two seas mentioned. Most of them held that they are the Sea of Persia on the eastern side and the Sea of Rome on the western side. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "Majma' al-bahrayn" is near Tangier at the farthest end of the lands of the Maghrib. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through al-Suddi that he said: "They are al-Kar and al-Ra's, where they pour into the sea." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Majma' al-bahrayn is a branch in the land of Persia, on the side of Adharbayjan, which extends from the Surrounding Ocean (al-bahr al-muhit) from its north to its south, and its two ends are on the side of the land of the Levant." It was also said: "They are the Sea of Jordan and the Sea of al-Qulzum." It is narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak that he said: "Some of them said: it is the Sea of Armenia." It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "It is in Ifriqiya," along with other sayings. It is known that identifying the "two seas" belongs to the type we mentioned earlier, for which there is no proof from the Book or the Sunnah, and there is no benefit in knowing it. So searching for it is toil with no profit, and there is no proof requiring that one return to it. Some contemporary heretic disbelievers claimed that Musa did not travel to the junction of two seas, on the pretext that he did not know of that in his history. This claim is utterly false and baseless. Sufficient to decide the matter is that it contradicts His saying: ﴿Then when they reached the junction of the two of them﴾ [al-Kahf: 61], together with the explicit statement that it was a journey involving hardship and fatigue, which can only be the case in a long journey. For this reason the Exalted said concerning Musa: ﴿Indeed, we have suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ [al-Kahf: 62]. It is known that whatever contradicts the Qur'an is false, because the opposite of the truth is false by the consensus of rational people, since it is impossible for two contradictory statements to be both true.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan﴾: all the readers, except Hafs, read anSaniHi (أنْسانِيهِ) with a kasra on the ha' (هاء). Hafs, from 'Asim, read anSaniHu (أنْسانِيهُ) with a damma on the ha'.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 65 (part 1 of 5):

﴿So they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our presence.﴾ This servant mentioned in this noble verse is al-Khidr (peace be upon him), by the consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement) of the scholars, and the indication of the authentic texts for this comes from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for this mercy and this divinely taught knowledge (al-'ilm al-ladunni) by which Allah mentions His favour upon him, the verse does not specify here whether they are the mercy and knowledge of prophethood, or the mercy and knowledge of sainthood (wilaya). The scholars differ regarding al-Khidr: is he a prophet, a messenger, or a saint? As the rajaz poet said:

"The people of intellect have differed concerning Khidr: some said he is a prophet, or a saint, or a messenger."

It was also said that he was an angel. However, it is understood from some verses that the mercy mentioned here is the mercy of prophethood, and that this divinely taught knowledge is the knowledge of revelation (wahy), while knowing that using these as evidence for that has well-known objections among the scholars.

Know first that the word "mercy" is repeatedly used in the Qur'an for prophethood, and likewise the "knowledge from Allah" (al-'ilm al-mu'ta) is repeatedly used in it for the knowledge of revelation. Among the uses of "mercy" for prophethood is His saying, in az-Zukhruf: ﴿And they say, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?" Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [az-Zukhruf 43:31], meaning His prophethood, so that they would dictate the sending down of the Qur'an upon a great man from the two cities. And His saying in surat ad-Dukhan: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct, a command from Us. Indeed, We were sending [messengers], as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [ad-Dukhan 44:4-5], and His saying at the end of al-Qasas: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas 28:86]. Among the uses of "giving knowledge" for prophethood is His saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know. And the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:113], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, he was one of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾ [Yusuf 12:68], along with other verses.

It is well known that mercy and the granting of divine knowledge are more general than whether that is by way of prophethood or otherwise, and using the more general to prove the more specific is flawed, since the existence of the general does not necessitate the existence of the specific, as is known. Among the clearest evidences that the mercy and the divine knowledge by which Allah favoured His servant al-Khidr came by way of prophethood and revelation is His saying about him: ﴿And I did it not of my own accord﴾ [al-Kahf 18:82], meaning: I only did it by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and the command of Allah is only established by way of revelation, since there is no means by which the commands and prohibitions of Allah are known except revelation from Allah, the Exalted. This is especially so regarding the killing of an innocent soul in its apparent form, and the damaging of people's ships by piercing them, because aggression against people's lives and property is not valid except through revelation from Allah, the Most High. Allah, the Most High, has also restricted the means of warning to revelation in His saying: ﴿Say, "I only warn you by revelation"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:45], and "innama" (only) is a construction of restriction.

If it is said: could that be by way of inspiration (ilham)? The answer is that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul) that inspiration from the saints cannot be used as evidence for anything, due to the absence of infallibility ('isma), and the absence of proof that it may be relied upon; rather, there is proof that it is not permissible to rely upon it. As for what some Sufis claim, that acting upon inspiration is permissible for the one inspired and not for others, and what some Jabriyya also claim, that inspiration is a valid proof for the one inspired and for others, treating inspiration as if it were audible revelation, relying on the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So whoever Allah wants to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾ [al-An'am 6:125], and on the report: "Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of Allah" — all of this is false and not to be relied upon, because it is not supported by evidence. A non-infallible person's impulses are not to be trusted, since he is not safe from the subtle deception of Satan. Guidance is guaranteed in following the Sharia, and is not guaranteed in following impulses and inspirations. Inspiration, in technical terms, is the placing of something in the heart which gives the breast peace, without deduction from revelation or consideration of rational proof, which Allah specially grants to whomever He wills among His creation. As for what the prophets are inspired with, which Allah places in their hearts, it is not like the inspiration of others, because they are infallible, unlike others. In Maraqi as-Su'ud, in the book on evidences (al-istidlal), he said:

"Inspiration is to be cast aside in the open, I mean the inspiration of the saints,
and some who claimed Sufism have seen it [as valid],
but the infallibility of the Prophet makes following [him] obligatory."

In sum, one who has familiarity with the knowledge of the religion of Islam will not be unaware that there is no means by which the commands and prohibitions of Allah are known, nor by which one draws near to Him through an action or an abandonment, except by way of revelation. So whoever claims that he is independent in reaching what pleases his Lord, apart from the messengers and what they brought, even in a single matter, then there is no doubt about his heresy (zandaqa). The verses and hadiths indicating this are countless. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15], and He did not say "until We cast inspiration into hearts." And He says: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:165], and He says: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your verses?"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:134], along with other verses and hadiths of this kind, which are very numerous. We have explained a portion of this in surat Bani Isra'il, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15]. And from this you know that what many ignorant people who claim Sufism assert, that they and their shaykhs have a hidden path which agrees with the truth before Allah even if it opposes the apparent Sharia, like the opposition of what al-Khidr did to the apparent knowledge that was with Musa, is heresy (zandaqa), and a means toward complete dissolution from the religion of Islam, under the pretext that truth lies in hidden matters which oppose its apparent form.

Al-Qurtubi (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his tafsir, the text of which is: Our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-'Abbas, said: A group of the heretic Batiniyya (zanadiqa al-Batiniyya) went to a path which does not require these legal rulings. They said: these general legal rulings are applied only to the prophets and the common people. As for the saints and the people of special status, they do not need those texts. Rather, what is required of them is only what falls into their hearts, and they are judged by what prevails over them of their impulses. They said: this is because their hearts are pure from defilements and empty of other things, so the divine knowledge and the lordly truths are made manifest to them, and they come to know the secrets of created things and know the rulings of particulars, and thus they are independent of the universal rulings of the Sharia. Just as happened to al-Khidr: he was independent through what had been manifested to him of knowledge from what Musa had of those understandings. And it has come in what they transmit: "Ask your heart for a fatwa, even if the muftis give you fatwas." Our shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This statement is heresy and disbelief, and its speaker is to be killed without being asked to repent, because it is a denial of what is known from the Sharia. Allah, the Exalted, has established His way and carried out His wisdom that His rulings are known only through His messengers, the emissaries between Him and His creation, who convey from Him His message and His speech, who explain His laws and rulings. He chose them for this and singled them out with what is in that station, as He said: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:75], and He said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 6:124], and He said: ﴿Mankind was one community, so Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213], along with other verses.

In general, there has been established definitive knowledge and necessary certainty, and the consensus of the early and later generations, that there is no path to knowing the rulings of Allah the Exalted, which relate to His command and prohibition, and nothing of them is known except through the messengers. So whoever says that there is another path by which His command and prohibition are known, other than the messengers, such that he becomes independent of the messengers, then he is a disbeliever who is to be killed without being asked to repent, and there is no need with him for question and answer. Moreover, this is a claim of prophets after our Prophet (ﷺ), whom Allah made the seal of His prophets and messengers, so there is no prophet after him and no messenger.

The explanation of this: whoever says, "He takes from his heart, and what falls into it is the ruling of Allah the Exalted, and he acts upon its requirement, and needs no book or Sunna with that," has claimed for himself the special status of prophethood. This is similar to what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Verily the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) breathed into my heart..." [the hadith], ending the quotation from al-Qurtubi's tafsir.

What he mentioned from the words of his shaykh, that the zindiq is not to be asked to repent, is the position of Malik and those who agree with him. We have explained the statements of the scholars on this and their evidences, and what the evidence supports, in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Illusion of Inconsistency from the Verses of the Book), in surat Al 'Imran. As for what some ignorant people who claim Sufism use as evidence, taking inspiration from the apparent meaning of some texts, such as the hadith: "Ask your heart for a fatwa, even if people give you fatwas and they issue fatwas to you," there is absolutely no evidence in it for the validity of inspiration. No one among those whose views are considered has said that the mufti from whom legal rulings are received is the heart. Rather, the hadith is a warning against doubtful matters, since the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that not everyone knows.

So a mufti may give you a ruling of permissibility for something while you know from another source that it may be unlawful, based on the Sharia. The heart of a believer does not find rest in what contains doubt. The hadith, like his saying: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt," and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Righteousness is good character, and sin is that which stirs in your soul and you dislike that people should see it," narrated by Muslim from the hadith of an-Nawwas ibn Sam'an (may Allah be pleased with him), and the hadith of Wabisa ibn Ma'bad (may Allah be pleased with him), mentioned above, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he said: 'Have you come to ask about righteousness?' I said: Yes. He said: 'Ask your heart. Righteousness is that with which the soul is at peace and the heart is at rest, and sin is that which stirs in the soul and wavers in the chest, even if people give you fatwas and they issue fatwas to you.'" An-Nawawi said in *Riyad as-Salihin*: it is a hasan hadith, narrated by Ahmad and ad-Darimi in their Musnads. There is no doubt that the intent of this hadith and the like is to encourage piety (wara') and abandoning doubtful matters. If, for example, a dead animal became mixed with a slaughtered one, or a mahram woman with a non-mahram woman, and some mufti gave you a ruling of permissibility for one of them, on the possibility that the slaughtered one is the first or the non-mahram is the second, then when you ask your heart you will know that it is possible that she is the dead one or the sister. And abandoning the unlawful, and seeking to clear oneself for one's religion and honour, is only achieved by avoiding all of them, because what the abandonment of the unlawful cannot be completed without abandoning is itself obligatory to abandon. So this stirs in the soul and does not bring it peace, because of the possibility of falling into the unlawful in it, as you see. All of this is based on the texts of the Sharia, not on inspiration.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 65 (part 2 of 5):

And among what supports what we have mentioned from the words of the people of Sufism (*al-Sufiyyah*), who are testified to be good in religion and righteousness, is the statement of Shaykh Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Junayd al-Khazzaz al-Qawariri, may Allah have mercy on him: "Our way (*madhhabuna*) is this: it is bound by the Book and the Sunnah." Several of those who wrote his biography transmitted this from him, such as Ibn Kathir, Ibn Khallikan and others, may Allah have mercy on them. There is no doubt that his statement quoted above is the truth, for there is no command or prohibition except through the tongues of the Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace. And from all of this you know that the Khidr's killing of the boy, his damaging of the ship, and his saying ﴿and I did not do it of my own accord﴾ are a clear proof of his prophethood. Al-Fakhr al-Razi, in his *Tafsir*, attributed the view that he was a prophet to the majority. And among what is cited as a supporting indication for the view of his prophethood is Musa's humility toward him, peace be upon him, in his saying: ﴿Musa said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [as] guidance?"﴾ [al-Kahf: 66], and his saying ﴿He said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ [al-Kahf: 69], along with the Khidr's saying to him ﴿And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ [al-Kahf: 68].

* *

**Issue**

Know that the scholars differed about al-Khidr: is he alive until now, or is he not alive, but rather one of those who died in past times? A great number of people of knowledge held that he is alive, and that he drank from a spring called the Spring of Life (*'ayn al-hayah*). Among those who upheld the view of his life are al-Qurtubi in his *Tafsir*, al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim and others, Ibn al-Salah, al-Naqqash and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Al-Naqqash elaborated on this meaning, meaning the life of al-Khidr and his survival until the Day of Resurrection, and he mentioned in his book many things from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and all of them do not stand on a leg," the end, through the transmission of al-Qurtubi in his *Tafsir*.

The accounts of the righteous about al-Khidr are more than can be counted, and their claim that he and Ilyas make the pilgrimage together every year, and that they narrate some supplications from them both, are all well known. But the basis of those who hold this view is very weak, because most of it consists of accounts from some whom they consider to be righteous, dreams, and hadiths traced back to the Prophet (*marfu'*) from Anas and others, and all of them are weak and do not establish a proof.

Among the strongest of what its proponents cite is the report of consolation at the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned in his *Tamhid*, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) died and was covered with a cloth, a caller called out from the side of the house, they heard his voice but did not see his person: 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be upon you, O People of the House. ﴿Every soul will taste death﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185], indeed in Allah is a replacement for every one who perishes, and a compensation for every one who is lost, and a consolation for every calamity. So in Allah place your trust, and to Him turn your hopes, for the one who is afflicted is the one who is deprived of reward.'" They used to think that it was al-Khidr, peace be upon him, meaning the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), the end, through the transmission of al-Qurtubi in his *Tafsir*.

The author of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: Using the report of consolation, such as this report we have just mentioned, as evidence for the life of al-Khidr is rejected on two grounds:

**The first:** This has not been established by a sound chain of transmission. Ibn Kathir said in his *Tafsir*: "Al-Nawawi and others relate two opinions about the survival of al-Khidr until now, and then until the Day of Resurrection. He and Ibn al-Salah inclined to his survival, and they mentioned accounts about him from the early generations (*salaf*) and others, and his mention came in some hadiths, but nothing of that is authentic, and the most famous of them is the hadith of consolation, and its chain is weak." End of quote from him.

**The second:** Even if the hadith of consolation were sound, it does not necessarily follow, rationally, legally or by common understanding, that the one who offered consolation was al-Khidr. Rather, it is possible that he was someone other than al-Khidr from among the believing jinn, because the jinn are those about whom Allah said: ﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you cannot see them﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. The claim that this consoler was al-Khidr is an arbitrary assertion without evidence. And their saying "they used to think that it was al-Khidr" is not a proof to which one must return, because they may have been mistaken in their assumption, and that would not indicate a binding legal consensus (*ijma'*), nor do they have any basis for their claim that it was al-Khidr, as you see.

The author of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to me to be preponderant by evidence in this question is that al-Khidr is not alive, but has died. This is for several proofs:

**The first:** The apparent generality of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, will they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34]. His saying "to any human" (*li-bashar*) is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it encompasses every human. It follows from this that eternity is negated for every human before him, and al-Khidr is a human before him. So if he had drunk from the Spring of Life and become alive and eternal until the Day of Resurrection, then Allah would have granted eternity to that human who is al-Khidr, who came before him.

**The second:** His saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, if You destroy this band of the people of Islam, You will not be worshipped on the earth." Muslim said in his *Sahih*: Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar, Simak al-Hanafi narrated to me, he said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab narrated to me, he said: "When the Day of Badr came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, and his companions, who were three hundred and nineteen men. The Prophet (ﷺ) faced the qiblah, then stretched out his hands and began to call out to his Lord: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if You destroy this band of the people of Islam, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' He continued calling to his Lord, stretching out his hands facing the qiblah, until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr came to him, took his cloak and placed it back on his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, your pleading with your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿When you sought assistance from your Lord, and He responded to you: Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand from the angels, following one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], and Allah reinforced him with the angels." ...the hadith. The point of evidence in it is his saying (ﷺ): "You will not be worshipped on the earth," where the verb in the context of negation means: no worship will occur to You on the earth. This is because the verb, according to the grammarians, resolves into a verbal noun and a time, and according to many rhetoricians into a verbal noun, an attribution and a time. So the verbal noun is latent in its meaning by consensus, and negation applies to it, so it reverts to an indefinite noun in the context of negation, which is among the forms of generality, as was explained earlier in the surah "Bani Isra'il." And the verse of Maraqi al-Su'ud, which points to the fact that the verb in the context of negation and conditionality is among the forms of generality, is in his words, joining it to what implies generality:

*And like "lā shariba" or "in shariba," they agreed that the verbal noun has brought it forth.*

So when you know that the meaning of his saying (ﷺ): "If You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on the earth" is: no worship will occur to You on the earth.

Know that this negation includes, by its generality, the existence of al-Khidr alive on the earth. This is because, on the assumption of his existence alive on the earth, Allah would be worshipped on the earth, even on the assumption that that band of the people of Islam had perished, since al-Khidr, as long as he is alive, worships Allah on the earth. Al-Bukhari said in his *Sahih*: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Hawshab narrated to me, 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, Khalid narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said on the Day of Badr: 'O Allah, I implore You by Your covenant and Your promise. O Allah, if You wish, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' Abu Bakr took his hand and said: 'Enough!' He went out saying: ﴿The multitude will be put to flight and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]." So his saying (ﷺ) in this hadith: "O Allah, if You wish, You will not be worshipped on the earth," means: if You wish the destruction of this group of the people of Islam, You will not be worshipped on the earth. Its meaning therefore returns to the narration we mentioned from Muslim in his *Sahih*, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. We have explained the way of deriving evidence from the hadith concerning the death of al-Khidr.

**The third:** His (ﷺ) report that after a hundred years from the night in which he spoke this hadith, no one who is on the face of the earth that night will remain. So if al-Khidr were alive on the earth, he would not have outlived the mentioned hundred years. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his *Sahih*: Muhammad ibn Rafi' narrated to us, and 'Abd ibn Humayd. Muhammad ibn Rafi' said: "narrated to us," and 'Abd said: "Ibn 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Bakr ibn Sulayman informed me: that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the 'Isha' prayer one night at the end of his life. When he finished the salam, he stood and said: "Do you see this night of yours? Indeed, after a hundred years from it, none of those who are upon its back today will remain." Ibn 'Umar said: "The people made a mistake regarding that statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in what they narrate of these hadiths about a hundred years. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only said: 'None of those who are upon the back of the earth today will remain,' meaning by this that this generation would come to an end."' Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Darimi narrated to me, Abu al-Yaman informed us, Shu'ayb informed us, and al-Layth narrated it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Khalid ibn Musafir, both of them from al-Zuhri with the chain of Ma'mar, like his hadith. Harun ibn 'Abd Allah and Hajjaj ibn al-Sha'ir narrated to me, both saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, he said: Ibn Jurayj said: Abu al-Zubayr informed me that he "heard Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) before his death by a month say: 'You ask me about the Hour, and its knowledge is only with Allah. And Allah has sworn that upon the earth there is no soul created, which will reach a hundred years.'" Muhammad ibn Hatim narrated this to me, Muhammad ibn Bakr narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj informed us with this chain, but he did not mention "a month before his death."

Yahya ibn Habib and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, both from al-Mu'tamir. Ibn Habib said: Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, he said: I heard my father, Abu Nadrah narrated to us: "From Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said that before his death by a month or thereabouts: 'No soul created today will reach a hundred years while it is alive on that day.'" And from 'Abd al-Rahman, companion of the water-supply (*al-siqayah*), from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the like of that. 'Abd al-Rahman explained it: "The decrease of lifespan." Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, Sulayman al-Taymi informed us, with both chains, like it.

Ibn Numayr narrated to us, Abu Khalid narrated to us, from Dawud, and the wording is his. And Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Sulayman ibn Hayyan narrated to us, from Dawud, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk, they asked him about the Hour, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A hundred will not come while upon the earth there is a soul created today.'" Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to me, Abu al-Walid informed us, Abu 'Awanah informed us, from Husayn, from Salim, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'No soul created will reach a hundred years.'" Salim said: "We discussed that in his presence: it is only every created soul on that day." The end, from him, in his own wording.

The hadith reported by Ibn 'Umar, Jabir and Abu Sa'id from the Prophet ﷺ is a clear statement by the Prophet ﷺ that no living soul (nafs mansufah) will remain on the face of the earth after a hundred years. His words "nafs mansufah" and similar expressions in the wordings of the hadith are indefinite nouns (nakirah) in a context of negation (siyaq al-nafy), so they include every created soul on the earth. There is no doubt that this general meaning, by the force of the wording, includes al-Khidr, since he is a living soul upon the earth. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Shu'ayb informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: Salim ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Hathmah narrated to me that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: 'The Prophet ﷺ prayed the 'Isha' prayer at the end of his life. When he finished the salam, the Prophet ﷺ stood up and said: "Do you see this night of yours? At the head of a hundred years, none of those who are upon the back of the earth today will remain.'" The people were confused by the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ statement, and they began to talk about these hadiths concerning a hundred years. The Prophet ﷺ only said: "None of those who are upon the back of the earth today will remain," meaning that it will sweep away that generation." End of quotation in its wording. We have already explained how it indicates the intended meaning.

(p-331) Fourth: If al-Khidr were alive until the time of the Prophet ﷺ, he would have been among his followers, would have supported him and fought alongside him, because he would have been sent to all of the two weighty groups (al-thaqalayn), mankind and the jinn. The verses indicating the universality of his message are very numerous, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 158], and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. What clarifies this is that He, may He be exalted, explained in Surat Al 'Imran that He took from all the prophets a binding covenant that if our Prophet ﷺ came to them confirming what was with them, they would believe in him and support him. This is in His saying: ﴿And [recall] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said, "Have you acknowledged and accepted My commitment on that condition?" They said, "We have acknowledged it." He said, "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿Whoever turns away after that, then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81-82].

This noble verse, according to the view that the "messenger" in it is our Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said, the matter is clear. And according to the view that it is general, he ﷺ enters into its generality in the first place. So if al-Khidr were alive in his time, he would have come to him, supported him and fought under his banner. Among what clarifies that no prophet ever meets another without following him is what Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bazzar related from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him: "'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to the Prophet ﷺ with a book he had obtained from some of the People of the Book, and he read it to him. The Prophet ﷺ became angry and said: 'I have brought you it white and pure. Do not ask them about anything, lest they inform you of the truth and you deny it, or of falsehood and you affirm it. By the One in whose hand is my soul, if Musa were alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me.'" End of quotation. Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: "Its narrators are trustworthy, except that there is weakness in Mujalid." The Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his History, after citing the verse of Al 'Imran mentioned above as evidence that al-Khidr, if he were alive, would have come to the Prophet ﷺ and supported him, the following: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Allah did not send any prophet of ours without taking from him the covenant: 'If Muhammad ﷺ is sent while you are alive, you will surely believe in him and support him.' He commanded him to take the covenant from his own community: 'If Muhammad ﷺ is sent while they are alive, they will surely believe in him and support him.'" Al-Bukhari related it from him.

So al-Khidr, whether he was a prophet or a saint (wali), is included in this covenant. If he were alive in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the best of his conditions would be that he be in his presence, believing in what Allah revealed to him and supporting him against any enemy who might reach him, because if he were a saint, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq is better than him, and if he were a prophet, Musa is better than him.

(p-332) Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad: "Shurayh ibn al-Nu'man narrated to us, Hushaym informed us, Mujalid informed us, from al-Sha'bi, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'By the One in whose hand is my soul, if Musa were alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me.'" This is what is affirmed with certainty and known from the religion as a matter of necessary knowledge (ilm al-darurah).

This noble verse indicates that if all the prophets were supposed to be alive, responsible, in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they would all have been his followers and under his commands, and within the scope of his law. Just as, when they gathered with him during the Night Journey (al-Isra'), he was raised above all of them, and when they descended with him to Bayt al-Maqdis and the prayer time came, Jibril, by the command of Allah, ordered him to lead them, so he led them in prayer in the place of their authority and the abode of their residence. This indicates that he is the greatest Imam and the final, honoured and foremost Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and upon them all.

Once this is known, and it is known to every believer, it follows that if al-Khidr were alive, he would be among the community of Muhammad ﷺ and among those who follow his law, and he could do nothing other than that. Likewise 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, when he descends at the end of time, will judge by this purified law, without departing from it or deviating from it, and he is one of the five Ulu al-'Azm (the messengers of steadfast resolve) and the seal of the prophets of the Children of Israel. And it is known that al-Khidr has not been transmitted by a sound or fair chain that brings the soul to rest, that he met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a single day, or that he witnessed with him any battle at any of the battlefields. Take the day of Badr: the truthful one whose word is believed (al-Sadiq al-Masduq) said, concerning what he called upon his Lord, may He be mighty and majestic, and sought victory and help from Him against those who disbelieved: "O Allah, if You destroy this small band, You will not be worshipped on the earth after it." That band had under it the masters of the Muslims on that day, and the masters of the angels, including Jibril, peace be upon him, as Hassan ibn Thabit said in a poem of his, in a verse said to be the most boastful verse the Arabs ever composed:

"And at the well of Badr, when he turned back their faces, Jibril was beneath our banner, and Muhammad..."

So if al-Khidr were alive, his standing beneath this banner would be the highest of his stations and the greatest of his campaigns. The judge Abu Ya'la Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Farra' al-Hanbali said: One of our companions was asked about al-Khidr: "Has he died?" He said: "Yes." It was also reported to me similarly from Abu Tahir ibn al-'Abbadi, who used to argue that if he were alive he would have come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn al-Jawzi transmitted it in al-'Ujalah. If it is said: Is it said that he was present at all these places but no one saw him?

The answer: The default is the absence of this remote possibility, which would require specifying the general texts merely by suppositions. Then (p-333) what would motivate him to conceal himself in this way? His manifestation would be greater for his reward, higher in his rank, and clearer for his miracle. Moreover, if he had remained after him, his conveying from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the prophetic hadiths and the Qur'anic verses, his rejection of the fabricated hadiths, the distorted narrations and the innovated opinions and partisan desires, his fighting alongside the Muslims in their campaigns, his witnessing their gatherings and congregations, his benefiting them, his averting harm from them from others, his guiding the scholars and rulers, and his establishing of the proofs and rulings would be far better than what is claimed about his being in the cities, traversing the deserts and regions, meeting with servants whose conditions are not known to many of them, and his being like a spokesman who translates on their behalf.

No one who understands this will hesitate about what I have mentioned. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path. End of quotation from al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya of Ibn Kathir, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

Thus it is established that none of the raised (marfu') hadiths indicating that al-Khidr is alive and remaining has been established, and that the evidences mentioned have indicated his death, as we set forth earlier.

Among those who showed the weakness of the hadiths indicating al-Khidr's life and survival were Ibn Kathir in his History and his Tafsir, and Ibn Hajar showed many aspects of their weakness in al-Isabah. Ibn Kathir said in al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, after citing the hadiths and accounts transmitted concerning the life of al-Khidr: "These narrations and accounts are the main reliance of those who have held that he is alive until today, but each of the raised hadiths is very weak and cannot establish a proof in religion. The accounts are mostly not free of weakness in the chain, and at best they are sound up to someone who is not infallible, whether a Companion or other, because error is possible for him (and Allah knows best)." He, may Allah have mercy on him, went on to say: "Shaykh Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi, may Allah have mercy on him, took up in his book 'Ajalat al-Muntazir fi Sharh Halat al-Khidr' the hadiths transmitted on this matter as raised reports, and showed that they are fabricated, and as for the reports from the Companions and the Successors and those after them, he showed the weakness of their chains by clarifying their circumstances and the unknown status of their narrators, and he excelled in this and did an excellent critical examination." End of quotation.

Know that a group of the people of knowledge discussed the evidences we mentioned as indicating his death. They claimed that the general wording of ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34] does not include him, nor does the general wording of the hadith: "Do you see this night of yours? At the head of a hundred years, none of those who are upon the earth today will remain on its back," as mentioned earlier. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him: "There is no proof for those who use the mentioned hadith, meaning the hadith, to invalidate the view of those who say that al-Khidr (p-334) is alive, because the generality of the statement 'there is no living soul' is not a text in that matter. Rather, a general statement, even if its totality is emphasized, is not explicit in it, but is open to specification. Just as it did not include 'Isa, peace be upon him, since he has not died and has not been killed, but is alive by the text and meaning of the Qur'an, and it does not include the Dajjal, although he is alive by the evidence of the hadith of the Jassasah. Likewise it did not include al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and he is not seen by people nor does he mix with them, so that he would come to mind when some of them address others. Such a generality does not include him. It was also said that the People of the Cave are alive and perform Hajj with 'Isa, peace be upon him, as mentioned earlier, and likewise the youth of Musa according to Ibn 'Abbas's statement, as we mentioned." End of quotation.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The words of al-Qurtubi here are manifestly untenable, as will not be hidden from anyone with a grasp of the sciences of the Shari'ah. He acknowledged that the Prophet's ﷺ hadith is general over every living soul with emphasized generality, because the addition of "min" before the indefinite noun in a context of negation makes it an explicit text in generality, not merely an apparent one, as is established in the principles (usul al-fiqh). We have clarified this in Surat al-Ma'idah.

Even if we suppose the correctness of what al-Qurtubi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said, that it is apparent in generality and not explicit, and we affirm that it is open to specification, as is the truth concerning every general text, the scholars are in agreement on the obligation to hold to the generality of a general text until there comes a specifying evidence that is valid for specification both in chain and in text. A bare claim unsupported by evidence from the Book or the Sunnah may not be used to specify any text from the Book or the Sunnah, by consensus.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 65 (part 4 of 5):

As for his saying, "Jesus is not covered by the generality of the hadith" (ʿumūm al-ḥadīth), the reply is that the wording of the hadith from its origin does not cover Jesus, because the Prophet ﷺ said in it: "No one alive upon the earth today from among those who are on it will remain." He restricted that to the surface of the earth, so the wording does not include those in the heavens. Jesus, however, was raised by God from the earth, as He stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Rather, God raised him up to Himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 158]. This is very clear, as you see.

The claim that the Companions of the Cave and the servant of Musa are alive is clearly untenable. Even if we assume they are alive, the hadith indicates their death at the end of the hundred years, as has passed, and nothing has been established that contradicts it.

As for his saying, "Al-Khadir is not visible to people, nor is he among those who mix with them, so that he would come to mind when some of them address others," it may be said that the objection to it comes from two directions:

The first: The claim that al-Khadir is hidden from people's eyes, like the jinn and the angels, is a claim for which there is no evidence, and the default position is contrary to it. The default is that the children of Adam see one another, because they share the same essential attributes and resemble one another.

The second: Even if we assume that the children of Adam do not see him, God, who informed the Prophet of the unseen, namely "the death of every living soul in that hundred years," knows al-Khadir and knows that he is a living soul. Even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that al-Khadir is a rare individual whom the eyes do not see, and that such a one was not intended by the all-inclusive wording of the generality, the more correct of the two opinions among the scholars of usul al-fiqh is that the general (ʿamm) and the unrestricted (muṭlaq) include the rare individual and the individual not intended, contrary to those who claim that the rare individual and the unintended individual are not included in either the general or the unrestricted.

The author of Jam' al-Jawami' (Jam' al-Jawami', a work of usul al-fiqh) said in the section on the general (mabḥath al-ʿamm), in these words: "The correct view is that the rare case and the unintended case are included under it." Here "the rare case and the unintended case" means the rare instance and the unintended instance, and "under it" means under the general. The truth is that the rare instance and the unintended instance are two different instances, and between them there is, on verification, a general and specific relationship from one perspective, because the rare instance may be intended or unintended, and the unintended instance may be rare or not rare. Among the derivative rulings that are built on whether the rare instance is included in the general and the unrestricted or not is the disagreement of the scholars on the permissibility of giving a prize (sabaq, with two fatḥas) in a race involving elephants. The clarification is that a hadith narrated by the compilers of the Sunan and by Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, states that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no prize except in a race involving a camel with a hoof, an arrow-maker's arrow, or a horse." Ibn Majah did not mention "or an arrow-maker's arrow" in it. The elephant has a hoof, and this is a rare instance. So according to the view that the rare instance is included in the general, it is permissible to give a prize (sabaq, with two fatḥas) in a race involving elephants. The prize mentioned is the money set aside for the winner. Some scholars of usul took this hadith as an example of the rare instance being included in the unrestricted but not in the general, saying: "Because his saying 'except in a hoof' is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, since what follows 'except' is affirmed, and an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is unrestricted, not general." Others among the people of usul took it as an example of the rare instance being included in the general.

Shaykh Zakariyya said: "The reason for its generality, despite its being an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, is that it is in the scope of a condition in meaning, since the implied meaning is: 'except if it is with a hoof,' and an indefinite noun in the scope of a condition is general." The criterion of the rare instance according to the people of usul is that this individual does not generally come to the mind of the speaker because its occurrence is rare. Among the examples of disagreement over the rare instance: is it included in the general and the unrestricted or not? There is the disagreement of the scholars on the obligation of ghusl (ritual bath) from the emission of semen that comes out without pleasure, such as one who is stung by a scorpion on his penis so that semen is discharged from it. Likewise, [semen that comes out] with an unusual pleasure, such as one who sinks into hot water or is shaken by an animal so that semen is discharged from him. The discharge of semen without pleasure, or with an unusual pleasure, is a rare instance, and the obligation of ghusl from it follows the disputed question of whether rare instances are included in the general and the unrestricted or not. According to the view that this rare instance is included in the generality of "Water is only from water," ghusl is obligatory; otherwise it is not. Among the examples of this in the unrestricted is the case where a man bequeaths a slave from among his servants, and it is asked whether it is permissible to give a hermaphrodite (khunthā). According to the view that the rare instance is included in the unrestricted, it is permissible to give the hermaphrodite; otherwise it is not. Among the examples of disagreement over whether an unintended instance is included in the unrestricted is the case where a man appoints another as his agent to buy him a slave to serve him, and the agent buys a slave who is freed upon the principal. The principal did not intend the one who would be freed by him; he intended only a servant to serve him. According to the view that the unintended instance is included in the unrestricted, the sale stands and the slave is freed; otherwise it does not. The author of al-Marāqī (Marāqī al-Saʿūd, a work of usul) pointed to these two issues in his verses:

"Is the rare instance included in what is general, or in the unrestricted? There is no reported disagreement [on the matter]."
"So with what is outside of pleasure, and the elephant, and what resembles them, there is disagreement over the saying."
"And what is free of intention is disputed, and it may come with metaphor as an attribute."

Among those who inclined to the view that rare and unintended instances are not included in the general and the unrestricted is Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi, may God have mercy on him.

The one who narrates this (its author), may God pardon him, says: What appears preponderant according to what is established in usul is that the general and the unrestricted include rare instances, because the general is apparent in its generality until a specifying evidence from the Book or the Sunna comes. Once it is established that the general is apparent in its generality and its inclusion of all the individuals, the ruling of the apparent is that one does not turn away from it; rather, acting upon it is obligatory unless there is evidence fit for specification. The Companions, may God be pleased with them, used to act upon the inclusiveness of the general expressions without hesitation in this. By this you know that the inclusion of al-Khadir in the generality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not grant immortality to any human before you﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34], and the generality of the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "Have you considered this night of yours? At the end of a hundred years, not one who is upon the face of the earth today will remain," is the correct view. It is not possible for him to be excluded from those generalities except by a specifier fit for specification.

Among what clarifies this: the hermaphrodite is a very rare case, yet it is included in the generality of the verses of inheritance, retaliation, manumission, and other generalities of the sources of the Shari'a. As for what al-Qurtubi mentioned about the Dajjal being excluded from those generalities by the evidence of the hadith of the Jassasa, there is no proof in it, because the Dajjal was excluded by evidence fit for specification, namely the hadith to which al-Qurtubi pointed. It is a hadith established in the Sahih from the hadith of Fatima bint Qays, may God be pleased with her, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: he told it to her, namely Tamim al-Dari, and that he was impressed by the hadith of Tamim mentioned, because it agreed with what he used to tell his Companions about the news of the Dajjal. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may God have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: "Abd al-Warith ibn Abd al-Samad ibn Abd al-Warith and Hajjaj ibn al-Shair both narrated to us, both from Abd al-Samad, and the wording is that of Abd al-Warith ibn Abd al-Samad; my father narrated to us from my grandfather, from al-Husayn ibn Dhakwan, from Ibn Buraydah, who said: Amir ibn Sharahil al-Sha'bi, of the clan of Hamdan, told me that he asked Fatima bint Qays, who was among the earliest women emigrants, and he said: 'Tell me a hadith you heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ that you do not attribute to anyone else.' She said: 'If you wish, I will certainly do so.' He said to her: 'Yes, tell me.' She said: '...' Then he related the hadith, which is lengthy. The point of evidence in it is the saying of Tamim al-Dari: 'We set off swiftly until we entered the monastery, and there we found the greatest human being we had ever seen in terms of physical form, and the most tightly bound, with his hands gathered to his neck, and iron between his knees and his ankles.' We said: 'Woe to you! What is your state?' ... (the hadith in its entirety) until his saying: 'I am going to inform you about myself: I am al-Masih, and I am about to be given permission to come out, and I will come out and travel through the earth, and I will not leave a town except that I will enter it within forty nights, except Makka and Taba, for they are forbidden to me, both of them.'" (the hadith).

This is a sound and explicit text that the Dajjal is alive and existing on that island in the sea mentioned in the hadith of Tamim al-Dari, and that he remains alive until he emerges at the end of time. This is a text fit for specification, which excludes the Dajjal from the generality of the hadith of the death of every soul within that hundred years. The established principle in usul is that the general must be kept in its generality. What a specifying text excludes is removed from the general, and the general remains a proof for the rest of the individuals for which no evidence of exclusion has come, as we have mentioned repeatedly. This is the truth and the view of the majority. Most of the generalities in the Book and the Sunna are such that some individuals are excluded by a specifying text, while the general remains a proof for what is left. Marāqī al-Suʿūd (a work of usul) pointed to this in its section on specification (takhṣīṣ) with the verse:

"It is a proof for the majority, if a specifier clearly identifies its exception."

By all of this it becomes clear that the texts indicating the death of every person upon the face of the earth within that hundred-year period, and the negation of immortality for every human before him, apparently include al-Khadir, and no text fit for specification has excluded him from them, as you have seen. And God knows best.

Know that the scholars have differed greatly over the lineage of al-Khadir. It has been said that he is the son of Adam by his loins. Ibn Hajar said in al-Isaba: "This is a view narrated by al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad through the route of Rawwad ibn al-Jarrah, from Muqatil ibn Sulayman, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas. Rawwad is weak, Muqatil is abandoned (matrūk), and al-Dahhak did not hear from Ibn Abbas." It has also been said that he is the son of Qabil ibn Adam. Ibn Hajar said: "Abu Hatim al-Sijistani mentioned it in the Book of the Long-Lived (Kitab al-Muʿammarin), then cited its chain and said: it is mursal (broken)." The proponent of this view related that his name is Khadrun, and he is al-Khadir. It has been said that his name is Amir; this was mentioned by Abu al-Khattab ibn Dihya from Ibn Habib al-Baghdadi. It has also been said that his name is Biliyam ibn Malkan ibn Faligh ibn Shalakh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh; Ibn Qutayba mentioned this view in al-Maʿarif from Wahb ibn Munabbih, as stated by Ibn Kathir and others. It has been said that his name is al-Muʿammar ibn Malik ibn Abd Allah ibn Nasr ibn al-Azd; this is the view of Isma'il ibn Abi Uways, which Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from him.

It has been said: Khadrun ibn Amaʾil, from the descendants of Esau (al-ʿIs) son of Isaac son of Abraham the Friend. This view was also related by Ibn Qutayba, and Ibn Hajar cited it from him. It has been said that he is from the lineage of Harun, brother of Musa. This was related from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Hajar also mentioned it and then said: "It is far-fetched." More strange than it is the view of Ibn Ishaq that he is Armiya ibn Halqiya, and Abu Jaʿfar ibn Jarir refuted that. It has been said that he is the son of Pharaoh's daughter, related by Muhammad ibn Ayyub from Ibn Lahi'a.

Some say he was the son of Pharaoh by his own loins, related by al-Naqqash. It is also said that he was al-Yasa', related from Muqatil, but Ibn Hajar said: "It is far-fetched." It is also said that he was of the descendants of Fars.
